fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged only conclusory accusations of racial discrimination without pleading nonconclusory factual matter sufficient to nudge the claim from conceivable to plausible. The complaint failed to allege that plaintiff was a member of a protected class or that similarly situated persons outside the protected class were treated more favorably, falling short of the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act), TILA (Truth in Lending Act), RESPA (Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act), RICO (wire fraud predicate), CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act), 18 U.S.C. § 1010 (false statements to HUD)
fha_claims.reasoning: ECOA claim dismissed for conclusory allegations without factual support. TILA claim dismissed because complaint did not allege failure to provide required disclosures and mere discrepancies between estimates and final disclosure do not suggest TILA violation. RESPA claim dismissed because alleged violation of FHA Handbook 4000.1 is not a RESPA violation and no private cause of action exists for RESPA disclosure violations. RICO claim dismissed for failure to plead pattern of racketeering activity with particularity as required by Rule 9(b). CFAA claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege statutorily recognized harm (damage or loss). § 1010 claim dismissed because the criminal statute provides no private cause of action.

case_name: Brooklynn C. Clark v. GSL Properties, Inc., CBRE GWS Real Estate Services, Inc., One & Three Centerpointe Drive, Monica Ulrig, Anthony Doe, John Doe, Jon/Jane Does 1-20, Bryce Siebenthall, and Kimberly Carpenter

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate rent increases and unequal treatment based on race, gender, and gender-based stereotyping
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged disparate rent increases but failed to allege facts showing the increases were motivated by protected status or that comparators were similarly situated individuals outside her protected class. Conclusory allegations without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facially neutral policies regarding rent increases, law enforcement calls, and security deposit retention
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify any facially neutral practice that adversely or disproportionately impacts persons of a particular type, which is required to state a disparate impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation related to plaintiff's anxiety disability; specific nature of accommodation not detailed in opinion but plaintiff provided doctor's information upon request
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded all four elements of a reasonable accommodation claim: (1) disability (anxiety); (2) defendant's knowledge of disability; (3) necessity of accommodation; and (4) defendant's refusal. Claim survives as to GSL, Siebenthall, Carpenter, and Ulrig but is dismissed as to CBRE, One & Three, Anthony Doe, John Doe, and Jon/Jane Does 1-20 due to lack of personal involvement in the accommodation denial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968; Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII claim dismissed because it does not apply to housing discrimination (applies to employment). ADA claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege that any defendant is a private entity that owns, leases, or operates a place of public accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to add FHA and ADA claims to their amended complaint but did not specify the nature of the accommodation or relief sought.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs failed to allege that purported FHA/ADA violations were motivated by discriminatory purpose. The allegations reflected retaliation for seeking to enforce HOA covenants, not disability-based discrimination, making amendment futile under the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (civil rights) and state law tort claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff Tara Jett's § 1982 and state law tort claims were previously dismissed without prejudice for failure to file an in forma pauperis application. Upon filing a meritorious IFP application, the court reinstated these claims pursuant to Rule 60(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that race was a motivating factor in Defendant's decision to shut down the party and serve an eviction notice. The complaint contains only speculation and conclusory statements that the conduct was race-based, without factual allegations comparing treatment of similarly situated non-African individuals or explaining why guests believed racial prejudice motivated the conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs did not plausibly allege that Defendant interfered with their right to enjoy their apartment free from racial discrimination under § 3617. The allegations do not support the conclusion that Defendant took action against Plaintiffs (serving the eviction notice) because of their race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 (race discrimination in contracts and property rights); NRS 118.120 (Nevada fair housing law); NRS 118A.390 (constructive eviction); breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; unjust enrichment; IIED; NIED
fha_claims.reasoning: Sections 1981 and 1982 claims failed because Plaintiffs did not plausibly allege race was a but-for cause of the injury. Nevada fair housing law claim failed for the same reasons as the FHA claim. Constructive eviction claim failed due to insufficient factual allegations. Breach of implied covenant claim lacked factual specificity. Unjust enrichment claim was barred by the existence of an express written lease. IIED claim failed because the alleged conduct was not extreme and outrageous. NIED claim failed because Plaintiffs did not assert an underlying negligence claim.

case_name: Deborah Morris v. Amtrak, et al.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged various claims including housing-related issues, segregation, transportation, eminent domain, property condemnation, and discrimination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, and the Fair Housing Act, but the complaint was too vague and conclusory to discern specific claims.
fha_claims.disposition: Sua sponte dismissal under Rule 8 and standing doctrine
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to provide fair notice of the claims and grounds for relief under Rule 8(a)(2) and Bell Atlantic v. Twombly. The complaint was too sprawling and conclusory to discern which allegations supported which claims, and plaintiff failed to establish standing by alleging a particularized injury in fact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants failed to provide requested reasonable accommodations related to her disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court ruled on Defendants' affirmative defenses in response to Plaintiff's motion to strike, not on the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself. The claim survives and proceeds to amended answer and further case management.

fha_claims.reasoning: The fourth amended complaint was dismissed as a shotgun pleading under Rule 8 for failing to give defendants adequate notice of claims and grounds, including failure to specify which defendants were responsible for which acts or omissions regarding the dormitory conditions. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The retaliation claim alleging false disciplinary charges and mail withholding after filing the lawsuit was dismissed as part of the shotgun pleading defect; the complaint failed to specify which defendants retaliated against plaintiff and how each defendant participated in the alleged retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional claims under First through Fourteenth Amendments, federal RICO statutes, city and state code enforcement laws, federal statutes concerning hazardous mold/mildew and mismanagement of federal funds
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed as part of the shotgun pleading defect; the complaint cited a bewildering variety of federal and state laws without explaining how factual allegations established violations, making it virtually impossible to know which allegations supported which claims for relief.

case_name: The Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: On appeal from jury verdict, the court held that Ohio House failed to establish facial disparate treatment because the City's zoning regulations facially benefit the disabled by allowing group homes and sober-living homes more favorable treatment than boardinghouses (e.g., ability to operate in R1 zones with permits, whereas boardinghouses are categorically barred). The differential treatment benefits the protected class, defeating the disparate-treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed summary judgment for the City because Ohio House failed to prove the second element of prima facie disparate impact—a significant, adverse, and disproportionate effect on the protected class. Ohio House presented only evidence that group-home applicants were denied permits, not that disabled individuals suffered reduced housing opportunities. Additionally, Ohio House's disparate-impact theory relied on facial discrimination allegations, failing to establish the first element (outwardly neutral policy).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements claim based on facially discriminatory zoning code
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed denial of judgment as a matter of law on the discriminatory-statements claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c). Ohio House's contention that the City violated the FHA by enacting a facially discriminatory zoning code fails because the disparate-treatment claim itself fails. Comments by individual city employees suggesting discriminatory purpose are insufficient standing alone to overturn the jury's verdict that the City did not make unlawful discriminatory statements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with Ohio House's protected activity of providing housing for disabled individuals recovering from addiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed denial of judgment as a matter of law on the § 3617 interference claim. Although Ohio House established protected activity and adverse action, it failed to prove the third element—causation based on discriminatory intent. The City's legitimate, non-discriminatory goals (preserving residential character, addressing traffic/parking/noise concerns, preventing overconcentration) provided sufficient evidence that a reasonable jury could conclude the City's actions were not motivated by discriminatory animus toward the disabled.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver or exception to the 650-foot separation requirement for sober-living homes to allow Ohio House to operate its facility with over six residents per unit in a multi-family residential zone
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed denial of judgment as a matter of law on the reasonable-accommodation claim. Ohio House established elements 1, 2, and 5 (disability, defendant's knowledge, refusal), and element 3 (necessity) was conceded. On element 4 (reasonableness), the jury had an evidentiary basis to find that granting the exception would fundamentally alter the City's zoning scheme because the separation requirement was essential to achieving the City's goals of preventing overconcentration and ensuring disabled persons live in normal residential (not institutional) settings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facial challenge to Costa Mesa Municipal Code § 13-200.62(f)(7), which requires the City to consider whether existing supply of similar facilities is sufficient to provide disabled individuals equal opportunity to live in a residential setting
fha_claims.reasoning: The court rejected Ohio House's facial challenge to subsection 13-200.62(f)(7) because it is not clear that the provision conflicts with the FHA's goal of protecting the right to live in the residence of one's choice. The provision is not facially preempted by the FHA, and even if it were, it would be severable under California law given the ordinance's severability clause and the fact that the remaining seven required findings remain fully functional.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Government Code § 65008 claim for violation of state planning and zoning law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Ohio House's § 65008 claim as time-barred. Although Ohio House characterized its claim as challenging the City's administration of ordinances rather than the ordinances themselves, the claim was effectively a facial challenge to the zoning ordinances' validity. The most recent ordinance (17-06) was adopted May 2, 2017, and Ohio House filed its complaint September 6, 2019, well after the 90-day statute of limitations period under Cal. Govt. Code § 65009(c)(1).

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact remain regarding necessity and reasonableness of the accommodation, and regarding whether defendant failed to engage in the interactive process. Court denied defendant's motion for partial summary judgment on these elements, finding that factual disputes preclude summary judgment and should be resolved by a jury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Damages claim arising from denial of reasonable accommodation for open garage door
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact exist regarding both actual damages (causation between accommodation denial and emotional distress) and punitive damages (whether defendant acted with reckless or callous indifference to plaintiff's federally protected rights). Court held that causation is an intensely factual question best resolved by jury, and that punitive damages remain viable where defendant failed to engage in interactive process.

The court also found the FLSA and § 1983 claims time-barred under applicable statutes of limitations, and other claims either lack a private right of action or do not apply to the facts alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to respond to HUD FHEO investigation in writing or by electronic communication rather than by telephone, citing ADA auxiliary equipment accommodations for her disabilities (memory loss, confusion, brain injuries, anxiety, depression).
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / Lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA provides no express or implied right of action against HUD or its officers for failure to investigate discrimination complaints. The court held that while the FHA authorizes judicial review when HUD charges discriminatory practices, it confers no right of review when HUD fails to issue a charge, and therefore federal courts lack jurisdiction over such claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims for denial of reasonable accommodations during HUD investigation; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 constitutional claims; 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242 criminal civil rights claims; Bivens claims against individual HUD employees; claims based on HUD statutes and regulations (42 U.S.C. § 1437).
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / Lack of subject matter jurisdiction / Sovereign immunity
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II does not apply to the federal government or its agencies; Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act does not waive federal sovereign immunity for monetary damages; § 1983 applies only to state actors, not federal agencies; 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242 are criminal statutes that do not create a private civil cause of action; Bivens claims against individual defendants fail because plaintiff made only conclusory allegations of discriminatory motivation without non-conclusory factual support; HUD statutes and regulations do not confer a private right of action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's complaint alleging that Progress Residential acquired properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods and used race-based statistics to withhold her deposit fails to state a plausible disparate impact claim under the FHA because she provides no details regarding the statistic, how it operates to have discriminatory impact, or how the alleged conduct connects to her claims. The factual allegations are too conclusory and disconnected to survive § 1915(e) frivolity review.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff fails to allege sufficient facts showing intentional racial discrimination by Progress Residential. The complaint lacks details regarding the underlying transaction, how the withholding of deposit or refusal to provide an MLS number constitutes unequal treatment based on race, and how these allegations connect to the claim that Progress Residential targets predominantly Black neighborhoods. The allegations are too vague and conclusory to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state a claim against defendant Tiffany Green because it contains no allegations of any particular action taken by Green. Although Green is named as a defendant and identified as a real estate broker, the complaint does not refer to her again and provides no factual basis for attributing any discriminatory conduct to her individually.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII discrimination claim (race, color, age); Connecticut state law discrimination and retaliation claims under Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 46a-58, 46a-60(b)(1), and 46a-60(b)(4)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII claims against individual defendants dismissed because individuals are not subject to liability under Title VII. Title VII claim against South Oxford dismissed for failure to allege an employer-employee relationship—plaintiffs alleged they were applying for a lease, not that they were hired or received remuneration from defendant. Remaining state law claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction after federal question jurisdiction was eliminated; court declined supplemental jurisdiction. Ms. Williams dismissed for improper service of process under Rule 12(b)(5).

fha_claims.reasoning: Pro se litigant may not bring qui tam action under False Claims Act; complaint not filed in government's name, not under seal, and government not served as required by 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b). Breach of HAP contract claim dismissed for lack of standing because tenant is not a party to or third-party beneficiary of HAP contract between landlord and PHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safe, varied gluten-free dining options and preparation in a certified gluten-free kitchen with adequately trained staff; alternatively, return of entrance fee and payments for services not rendered
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiff's FHA claim accrued in January 2021 when she stopped eating at Broadmead, placing the claim outside the two-year FHA statute of limitations. The court also rejected application of the continuing violation doctrine to failure-to-accommodate claims, finding that discrete incidents of alleged gluten exposure and menu errors do not constitute a systemic practice of recurring unlawful discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA (injunctive relief for discrimination in public accommodation); Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (damages for failure to accommodate disability); breach of contract; negligence; negligent misrepresentation; breach of express warranty; breach of implied warranty of merchantability; breach of implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA claims. For the ADA claim, Plaintiff lacked Article III standing to seek injunctive relief because she failed to demonstrate a concrete and imminent risk of future injury; she had stopped eating at Broadmead and could verify gluten content by inquiry. For breach of contract and negligence claims, Plaintiff failed to produce sufficient evidence that the chicken marsala incident (the only non-time-barred incident) actually contained gluten; her evidence consisted of speculation and inferences rather than probative proof. For negligent misrepresentation, Plaintiff failed to identify timely false statements of present or past fact. For warranty claims, the R&C Agreement is a contract for services (not goods), so UCC warranty provisions do not apply.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants' refusal to rent to housing voucher holders constitutes racial discrimination under the FHA because voucher holders are disproportionately African American and Hispanic (82% of voucher holders are Black or Hispanic). Plaintiff also alleged that defendants published discriminatory advertisements with high income, credit score, and guarantor requirements that disqualify voucher holders.
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA has a two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiff's alleged discriminatory acts (refusals to assist in February and June 2021) occurred outside the limitations period (suit filed August 9, 2023). The discovery rule does not apply because plaintiff knew the critical facts of her injury by June 2021, even if she did not appreciate the legal significance until consulting counsel in September 2021. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because the refusals and advertisements are separate and discrete acts, not a continuous policy. Plaintiff lacks standing to bring a claim based solely on reading discriminatory advertisements without alleging personal injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYSHRL § 296(5)(a) and NYCHRL § 8-107(5)(a) claims for discrimination based on lawful source of income (housing voucher); NYRPL § 441(d) claim for negligent supervision of brokers and salespersons regarding fair housing training.
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing plaintiff's sole federal FHA claim, the district court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims (NYSHRL, NYCHRL, NYRPL) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), as the federal question jurisdiction basis had been eliminated and only state law claims remained.

source_file: 10296755_2024_South Carolina State Conference of NAACP v. South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice_scd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment Due Process violations); Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA); Rehabilitation Act of 1973; and Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Allegations concern unlawful conditions of confinement in juvenile detention facilities, failure to protect children, prolonged solitary confinement, failure to provide rehabilitative services, and substandard conditions.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed organizational standing claims under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to allege that the plaintiff organizations themselves suffered deprivation of constitutional rights; the organizations alleged only that their members' rights were violated and that the organizations suffered resource diversions and mission frustration as a consequence. The court also dismissed associational standing claims as moot because none of the identified constituent juveniles remained in DJJ custody at the time of ruling, and no mootness exception applied.

The court denied the motion to strike and ordered plaintiffs to supplement their expert disclosure with a written report within 30 days. The underlying FHA and other substantive claims have not been adjudicated on the merits and remain pending.

The court assumed plaintiffs did not move for preliminary injunction based on the FHA claim, leaving it unresolved at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and bad faith under Pennsylvania law; Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Act, and Declaratory Judgment Act claims added in amended complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff, not a defendant, attempted removal from state court, which is prohibited by 28 U.S.C. § 1441. Additionally, even if removal were proper, complete diversity did not exist because USAA is a reciprocal interinsurance exchange with members in all fifty states, precluding diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Change of rent due date to align with when plaintiff and her mother received their disability checks; also request to allow payment plans and emergency rental assistance

fha_claims.reasoning: The court found lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint, as properly pleaded, contains no federal question under the well-pleaded complaint rule. Although Defendant asserted FHA violations in the Notice of Removal, the actual complaint is a state landlord-tenant eviction action, and federal defenses or counterclaims cannot create removal jurisdiction. The case was remanded to state court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that GSL not post or stick any information on plaintiff's door; request that GSL not place a trash can in front of the front door entrance because it triggered plaintiff's anxiety
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claims. The court dismissed the amended complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, applying Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards. The court found that Clark failed to allege facts sufficient to support her FHA claims based on race and sex discrimination, and did not separately analyze whether the requested accommodations were reasonable or whether defendants engaged in the interactive process.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate rent increases (30% at each lease renewal compared to neighbors' lower increases) based on race, sex, gender identity, or departure from gender-based norms
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Clark failed to allege that similarly situated individuals outside her protected class were treated more favorably. Although she alleged that neighbors paid less rent, she did not allege the race, sex, or gender identity of those neighbors, and thus failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment based on a protected status under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation through false police reports, attempted assault, false statements to police, trespass order, and eviction notice following Clark's attempts to address disability-related accommodation requests and other grievances
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed Clark's FHA claims (including any retaliation theory under § 3617) for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court found that Clark did not allege facts suggesting that the negative treatment and eviction were because of a protected status, and did not separately analyze the retaliation claim on its merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I (employment discrimination), ADA Title II (public entity services), ADA Title III (public accommodations), and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (employment discrimination)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) and lack of applicability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA claims because Clark did not allege that defendants were a public entity (Title II) or operated a place of public accommodation (Title III), and residential apartment complexes are not covered by the ADA. The court dismissed the Title VII claim because Clark did not allege that any defendants were her employer, that she suffered an adverse employment action, or that defendants treated other employees more favorably.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned handicapped parking space for Angie
fha_claims.reasoning: At Phase One of trial, the Court found that no request for accommodation had been made during the FHA's limitations period, determining that Plaintiff Carlos Cano's testimony regarding when he made the request was not credible based on his embellishment, inconsistent testimony, and conflicting testimony from other credible witnesses.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pedestrian paths suitable for Angie
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that Count Two was not actionable under the FHA and dismissed it with prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification to Angie's bathroom
fha_claims.reasoning: At Phase One of trial, the Court found that no request for accommodation had been made during the limitations period, crediting Defendants' evidence over Plaintiff's testimony that he made a request in 2017, though acknowledging a second request was made in 2018 and granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refinish Angie's bathtub without toxic substances
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court held that the undisputed facts established that Plaintiffs' request to repaint the bathtub in a guest room was not a necessary accommodation under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removing noisy equipment near Plaintiffs' residence
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that there was no evidence that Defendants knew Angie suffered from a disability such that the requested accommodation was necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permit Plaintiffs to keep tape on glass doors and windows
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Six was dismissed with prejudice because it required the Court to speculate about the connection between the accommodation and Angie's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair broken laundry machines
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Seven was dismissed with prejudice as a conclusory assertion that did not explain why Angie's disability required Defendants to fix the laundry facilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for instituting a HUD investigation
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court held that no reasonable jury could find that Plaintiffs had an objectively reasonable and good faith belief that the conduct they protested in Count Nine was unlawful, as Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of retaliation under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing OnCall Parking to harass Plaintiffs
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that there was no evidence that Defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the emails and text messages was pretext for a discriminatory motive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Engaging in intimidation and retaliation by instituting eviction proceedings in retaliation for filing HUD complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court held that the admitted facts and record evidence established that Defendants initiated eviction proceedings before Plaintiffs filed their HUD complaint, and thus the retaliation claim lacked a causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Engaging in intimidation and retaliation by appealing the state court's judgment of retaliatory eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that the premise of Count Twelve was demonstrably false and that Plaintiffs presented no evidence that Defendants appealed the county court judgment to intimidate or retaliate, especially considering that Defendants were successful on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Engaging in intimidation and retaliation by threatening to raise Plaintiffs' rent
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court granted Defendants' Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings on Count 13, determining that the claims and defenses in the prior eviction suit did not allege FHA violations and accordingly could not support the retaliation claim as pled.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Committing familial discrimination by shutting off Plaintiffs' water
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Seventeen was dismissed with prejudice because Plaintiffs failed to allege facts demonstrating a disparate impact to them caused by Defendants' policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failing to maintain the laundry facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Eighteen was dismissed with prejudice as a conclusory assertion that did not explain why Angie's disability required Defendants to maintain the laundry facilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusing to allow Plaintiffs to tape the apartment's glass doors and windows
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Nineteen was dismissed with prejudice for failure to allege facts demonstrating a disparate impact caused by Defendants' policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Statutes Chapter 83 violations (landlord-tenant law); breach of lease covenant of quiet enjoyment; failure to maintain premises; failure to provide notice of entry; failure to repair pedestrian paths; interruption of utilities without notice
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court granted summary judgment on state law claims (Counts 14, 15, and 16) under Florida Statutes Chapter 83, finding insufficient evidence to support Plaintiffs' allegations regarding maintenance obligations, utility interruption, and other landlord-tenant duties.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the original state court petition raised only a forcible detainer action (state law claim), and federal questions cannot be established by counterclaims or defenses. The defendant's FHA and ADA counterclaims do not confer federal question jurisdiction on the district court, and diversity jurisdiction was lacking because both parties were Texas citizens.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible communications in Braille or other accessible format; specific Ring camera model; first-floor apartment unit; mail chute; modified washer/dryer with Braille; Ring Peephole Camera; accessible toilet; light/horn combo in bathroom; sink and tub levers; tub grab bars; accessible range/oven; rocker light switches; wheelchair ramp; orientation and mobility specialist
fha_claims.disposition: 12(c) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation that Ricks failed to allege a plausible FHA claim against OPC because he did not allege that OPC owned, leased, or operated the property; that OPC discriminated against him because of his disability; or that he requested an accommodation from OPC. The court found Ricks' FHA claim failed because he did not allege that he requested an accommodation from OPC, that OPC denied any request, or that OPC had authority to make modifications to his dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA); Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794; Title II of the ADA (auxiliary aids and services in court proceedings)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion because Ricks failed to show a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of his Title III ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims. Ricks did not demonstrate that DMA owns, leases, or operates a place of public accommodation, took adverse action based on disability, or failed to make reasonable modifications. For the Rehabilitation Act claim, Ricks failed to show that DMA received federal financial assistance or that it denied him services because of his disability. The court also found no irreparable injury absent the injunction.

fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint failed to plausibly allege the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHAA: while plaintiff alleged a qualifying disability (asthma) and defendant's knowledge thereof, the complaint did not clearly state what specific accommodation was requested, whether removal of other tenants was reasonable, or what accommodation was actually provided. The court found the allegations too conclusory and lacking sufficient factual detail to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims against Lexington Police Department and officers; ADA Title II claims; state law claims including G.L. 111 § 127 (building code), G.L. 93A (consumer protection), negligence, tortious interference, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and landlord-tenant dispute regarding failure to disclose Lexington Wine & Spirits lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against Lexington Police Department and officers failed to state a plausible § 1983 claim because the complaint did not adequately allege what specific actions the officers took or that such actions violated a clearly established constitutional or statutory right. Claims against landlord defendants regarding failure to disclose the wine store lease failed because plaintiff did not allege that defendants had any duty to make such disclosure or identify the source of any such duty. All claims were dismissed for failure to provide sufficient factual allegations to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA, ECOA, RESPA, FHA, breach of contract, negligence, fraud claims arising from alleged mortgage fraud, faulty construction, and mold exposure causing Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the FHA claim, along with TILA, ECOA, and RESPA claims, consisted of legal conclusions and bald assertions that did not amount to more than labels and formulaic recitations, failing to plausibly allege violations against named defendants. The court could not reasonably infer substantively plausible claims from the facts alleged.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff's FHA claim conclusory and failing to state a claim because the complaint does not clearly identify: (1) plaintiff's specific disability; (2) whether he requested an accommodation; (3) a description of the accommodation requested; or (4) whether defendant failed to provide a reasonable accommodation. Landlord-tenant claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because federal courts do not have federal question jurisdiction over state residential landlord-tenant matters such as rent disputes and repair requests.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that management staff directed personnel not to perform maintenance/repair work on plaintiff's unit based on perceived disability (false perception that plaintiff was a sexual offender and HIV positive).
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual allegations to give rise to an inference of discrimination. The complaint relied on vague, speculative allegations based on information from a confidential source, without explaining why management perceived plaintiff as having a disability or why they interfered with maintenance requests, and without alleging differential treatment of similarly situated individuals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III discrimination claim; NYSHRL discrimination claim; NYCHRL disparate treatment claim; New York Not-for-Profit Corporation Law fiduciary duty claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed because Rochdale is a private housing cooperative, not a place of public accommodation; residential facilities are excluded from Title III coverage. State law claims dismissed by declining supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissal of all federal claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged no facts showing that his disability was at least a motivating factor for the alleged discrimination by Acacia, Basics, Griffiths, Douglas, Crow, Staten, 1212 Grant Realty LLC, and 1412 COL LLC. Allegations were conclusory and lacked factual support under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for bringing previous lawsuit against Acacia and other defendants
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim of retaliation under the FHA. The amended complaint did not cure the deficiencies identified in the prior order.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination claims against Acacia, Basics, NYSOMH, APS (City of New York), 1212 Grant Realty LLC, and 1412 COL LLC; Title II ADA disability discrimination claims against NYSOMH and City of New York; § 1983 claims against NYSOMH, Ben-Atar (official capacity), APS, City of New York, Glenoy (official capacity), Acacia, Basics, Griffiths, Douglas, Crow, Staten, 1212 Grant Realty LLC, and 1412 COL LLC; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Rehabilitation Act and Title II ADA claims dismissed for conclusory allegations lacking factual support regarding denial of services or discrimination based on disability. § 1983 claims against NYSOMH and Ben-Atar (official capacity) dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction due to Eleventh Amendment immunity. § 1983 claims against private defendants dismissed for failure to allege state action. § 1983 claims against City of New York dismissed for failure to allege municipal policy, custom, or practice. § 1983 claims against Ben-Atar and Glenoy (individual capacities) dismissed for failure to allege personal involvement. State law claims declined under supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Title III claims; § 1983 First Amendment retaliation claim; federal health and safety code violations
fha_claims.disposition: Order to Show Cause under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to state viable federal claims: ADA Title II does not apply to private residential housing; Title III does not cover purely residential dwellings; § 1983 First Amendment claim fails because defendants are private actors, not state actors; federal health and safety claims are too vague to constitute a federal claim. Court issued order to show cause rather than outright dismissal to allow pro se plaintiff opportunity to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged unlawful detainer actions and lock-outs but failed to allege she is a member of a protected class under the FHA or that defendants discriminated against her based on protected status. The court found it possible she could state a claim under the FHA but that she had not done so in the amended complaint, and granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourteenth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection claims; Title VII employment discrimination; 18 U.S.C. §§ 242 and 1341 (criminal statutes)

fha_claims.reasoning: Fourteenth Amendment claims against private actors fail because plaintiff did not allege state action; Title VII does not apply because plaintiff did not allege she was employed by defendants; criminal statutes 18 U.S.C. §§ 242 and 1341 provide no private cause of action and no basis for civil liability. No federal question jurisdiction exists over these claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination, ADA Title II disability discrimination, § 1983 federal constitutional violations, state law claims
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and (iii); Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(3)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's Rehabilitation Act claims against Promesa, Basics, NYSOMH, JSAF Management, and 1412 Col LLC fail because he did not allege facts showing denial of services by reason of disability or federal funding (where required). ADA Title II claims against NYSOMH fail for the same reason. § 1983 claims against NYSOMH and Abate in official capacity are barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity (jurisdictional dismissal). § 1983 claims against Abate in individual capacity fail because plaintiff did not allege her direct and personal involvement. § 1983 claims against private defendants (Promesa, Basics, Albors, Douglas, 1412 Col LLC, Crow, Staten, JSAF Management, Safdie) fail because plaintiff did not allege they acted as state actors. fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework for indirect-evidence disparate treatment and found that while a reasonable juror could infer the moratorium was pretextual based on council members' anti-Muslim statements and timing, the evidence at the preliminary injunction stage did not satisfy the heightened Rounds standard for enjoining legislation. The court concluded the success-on-the-merits factor was neutral, and the motion was denied on the basis of failure to demonstrate irreparable harm and the balance of equities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Free Exercise Clause (First Amendment), Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Free Exercise Clause framework from Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye and concluded that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a substantial burden on their ability to practice Islam because the moratorium merely delayed development of a specific property but did not restrict their ability to worship elsewhere or build a mosque elsewhere in the city. The court found the moratorium facially neutral and generally applicable, applying to all development in the covered area regardless of religious affiliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Replacement of non-functioning elevators in the building to provide access to plaintiff's ninth-floor apartment, which plaintiff alleges causes knee pain and exacerbates asthma when forced to use stairs.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that although plaintiff's allegations may state a claim for refusal to make reasonable accommodation, the complaint fails to allege a disability requiring accommodation and fails to identify which specific defendant was responsible for the elevator failure, depriving defendants of fair notice under Rule 8 and Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Provision of used, defective appliances (refrigerator and stove) that infested plaintiff's apartment with roaches, allegedly in violation of Section 8 program requirements.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to connect the appliance allegation to any protected class under the FHA (race, disability, or other enumerated categories), and that source of income/Section 8 status is not a protected class. Complaint also failed to identify which defendant was responsible for the conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination based on disability; also alleged discrimination based on race and income status.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that the ADA does not apply to private landlords and that plaintiff's amended complaint contained no factual allegations indicating any defendant is a public entity or provides public accommodation. Receipt of federal funds (Section 8) does not bring a private landlord within the reach of the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violation of the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a), but the specific accommodation requested is not identifiable from the opinion due to the shotgun pleading defects.
fha_claims.disposition: Struck as shotgun pleading; dismissed with prejudice for failure to comply with court orders and Federal Rules of Civil Procedure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck the second amended complaint as a shotgun pleading that violated the December 5, 2024 Order requiring amendment by December 26, 2024, and dismissed all claims with prejudice under Rule 41(b) for failure to comply with court orders and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure after repeated warnings and a clear record of contumacious conduct.

case_name: Kendrick v. Oakbrook Corporation
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Erickson v. Pardus
Pearle Vision, Inc. v. Romm
Hoskins v. Poelstra

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The plaintiff's FHA claim alleging denial of rental application based on race and criminal conviction occurred on February 4, 2019. The two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) expired on February 4, 2021. The plaintiff did not file a HUD complaint until May 5, 2021, which was outside the one-year period required to initiate an administrative proceeding under 42 U.S.C. § 3610(a)(1)(A)(i), and the complaint filed on July 12, 2021 was time-barred. No basis existed to toll the statute of limitations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing at low-income senior/disabled subsidized housing facility
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff asserted federal-question jurisdiction but the complaint does not allege discrimination under the FHA or any other federal cause of action. Plaintiff merely alleged denial of subsidized housing eligibility without alleging any discriminatory basis, which is insufficient to invoke federal jurisdiction.

case_name: Hartley v. United Student Rentals

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to repair broken front door of rental apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to allege sufficient facts connecting defendants' alleged failure to repair the door to plaintiff's disability or to establish that defendants took any action regarding the door. Plaintiff alleges mental health impairments generally but does not describe how impairments limit major life activities or connect any defendant action to the disability, failing to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First, Sixth, Eighth, Fourteenth Amendment violations); state law breach of warranty of habitability
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims fail because defendants are private parties, not state actors, and complaint alleges no facts supporting any exception (compulsion, joint action, or public function delegation). State law habitability claim dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and § 1332 (no federal question, no diversity, and no supplemental jurisdiction without viable federal claims).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal Tort Claims Act negligence claim against HUD for property conditions (water damage, mold, electrical issues, rodent infestation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies required under 28 U.S.C. § 2675(a) before filing suit against the United States under the FTCA. The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff's communications with HUD did not constitute proper presentment of a tort claim—they did not reference the FTCA, request monetary damages, or state a sum certain for recovery.

case_name: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al.
key_cases_cited: Spieth v. Bucks Cnty. Hous. Auth., 594 F. Supp. 2d 584 (E.D. Pa. 2009)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of mold and repair of water leaks in apartment to accommodate plaintiff Angel Lopez's asthma and severe COPD
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately allege facts supporting a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA. They provided only conclusory allegations that defendants refused to accommodate Lopez's disability without specifying what disability they have, whether defendants knew of it, or how defendants denied specific accommodation requests. The complaint lacks sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on race and national origin in refusing to repair water leaks and remediate mold
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately allege intentional discrimination based on race or national origin under the FHA. They provided only conclusory allegations without specifying how or when discrimination occurred, and a single offensive statement by the landlord about Puerto Ricans does not establish a claim for housing discrimination. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for failure to make reasonable modification; Title II Civil Rights Act claim for discrimination in public accommodation; state law claims for harassment, stalking, invasion of privacy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and public accommodation violations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman, Younger abstention, and Colorado River abstention doctrines because the claims were identical to or inextricably intertwined with pending state court actions. The court also found that Title II claims failed the mandatory notice requirement under 42 U.S.C. § 2000a-3(c), and Title III ADA claims failed to adequately allege disability discrimination in a public accommodation. State law claims against the Broderick Defendants were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits determination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 401 et seq. and 1381 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed the ALJ's determination that plaintiff was not disabled under the Social Security Act's five-step sequential evaluation process. The ALJ's RFC assessment was supported by substantial evidence, and the ALJ properly weighed medical opinions, considered plaintiff's impairments in combination, and provided sufficient narrative explanation for his conclusions.

source_file: 10308231_2025_Washington v. DHS Department of Homeless Services_nysd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide adequate services for person with disability to obtain housing; failure to secure permanent housing in timely manner; inadequate housing voucher funding
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts regarding her disability, what specific services were denied, or whether she alleged intentional discrimination, denial of accommodation, or other theory. Allegations that she did not receive permanent housing within state-law timelines are insufficient to state a claim under ADA Title III or the Rehabilitation Act. Court noted that money damages are unavailable under ADA Title III and that plaintiff failed to allege federal funding for WIN or deliberate indifference required under the Rehabilitation Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional claims for unsanitary shelter conditions, toxic water, physical and mental abuse of residents
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B); lack of state action
fha_claims.reasoning: WIN is a private party and plaintiff made no allegations showing WIN acts as a state actor under § 1983. Provision of homeless services by a private organization, even under contract with the state, does not convert the organization into a state actor. Additionally, plaintiff cannot pursue claims on behalf of other shelter residents as a non-attorney pro se litigant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to secure permanent housing; violation of DHS guidelines; alleged abuse and rights violations of other residents
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissal for lack of capacity to be sued / jurisdictional
fha_claims.reasoning: NYC DHS, as an agency of the City of New York, lacks capacity to be sued in its own name under N.Y. City Charter § 396. All actions must be brought in the name of the City of New York. Court granted leave to amend to name the City as defendant and noted that § 1983 claims against the City require pleading a municipal policy, custom, or practice that caused the constitutional violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act violation alleged in complaint; no specific accommodation identified
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court lacked jurisdiction to reopen the case after remanding it to state court for lack of diversity jurisdiction. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal on jurisdictional grounds without reaching the merits of any FHA or other federal claims alleged in the complaint.

case_name: Gerald Cymbalsky v. 522 Shore Road Owners, Inc.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc.
Logan v. Matveevskii

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability (severe osteoarthritis requiring walker, persistent open leg wound, anxiety disorder, morbid obesity) in connection with co-op's commencement of state court action to access apartment for cleaning.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent or causal nexus to disability. Plaintiff alleged he continues to reside in apartment, was not denied housing opportunity, and did not request any accommodation. Court found no plausible interpretation supporting inference of discriminatory animus—plaintiff alleged co-op sought to profit from his equity, not that disability motivated the action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil RICO (18 U.S.C. § 1961 et seq.), Constitutional rights to privacy/property (§ 1983), Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. § 1692 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: RICO claim failed because plaintiff did not allege two related predicate acts or effect on interstate commerce. Constitutional claims failed because defendants were not state actors. FDCPA claim failed because defendants were not debt collectors—co-op defendants were creditors collecting rent, and Finkelstein defendants were attorneys providing legal services, not regularly collecting debts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO on procedural grounds (failure to show irreparable harm due to delay and failure to comply with Rule 65(b) notice requirements) and on merits (plaintiff failed to allege that eviction resulted from discrimination based on race or other protected class). FHA claim survives the TRO motion but has not been substantively decided on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (Section 8 HAP contract), fraudulent inducement, Title VI Civil Rights Act, Fourteenth Amendment due process and equal protection, Spending Clause violations, intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress, Section 1981 and Section 1982 Civil Rights Act violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO on procedural grounds (delay in seeking relief, failure to comply with Rule 65(b)(1)(B) notice requirements, and failure to clearly show immediate irreparable injury) and on merits (plaintiff failed to plead required elements of fraudulent inducement and failed to establish that DHA was under obligation to pay rent under the lease). Non-FHA claims survive the TRO motion but remain pending.

Fair Housing Center of Metro. Detroit v. Singh Senior Living, LLC, No. 23-3969, 2025 WL 16385 (6th Cir. Jan. 2, 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: The opinion does not specify the particular accommodation(s) at issue; it references only 'allegedly unlawful behavior' by the senior living facility.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court vacated the district court's summary judgment and remanded for reconsideration of standing in light of FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024), which post-dated the district court's November 28, 2023 ruling. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims and expressed no view on the district court's merits ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation moves involving household goods transportation by Reliable and Eco Movers, facilitated by KCHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the § 1983 claim (which incorporated allegations related to the reasonable accommodation moves) as time-barred under Washington's three-year statute of limitations for taking or detaining personal property. The claim accrued no later than March 8, 2021, when plaintiff became aware property was missing, and the suit was filed June 1, 2024—85 days after the March 8, 2024 deadline. The court did not reach the merits of any reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (deprivation of property without due process and unreasonable seizure under Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments); § 1981, § 1982, § 1985; Rehabilitation Act of 1973; Americans With Disabilities Act; Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policies Act of 1970
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claim alleging unlawful deprivation of $177,000 in personal property and documents was time-barred under Washington's three-year statute of limitations. The claim accrued on March 8, 2021, when plaintiff became aware property was missing; the suit was filed June 1, 2024, well after the March 8, 2024 deadline. Amendment would be futile because the underlying chronology cannot be revised.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RCW 48.30A.070 (duty to investigate, enforce, and prosecute violations); RCW 9A.80.010 (official misconduct); RCW 49.60.178 (Washington Law Against Discrimination—unfair practices with respect to insurance transactions during reasonable accommodations move); WAC 284-30-330 (unfair claims settlement practices)
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing the federal § 1983 claim with prejudice, the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims (Second and Third Causes of Action) under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), finding that principles of economy, convenience, fairness, and comity did not favor retention of jurisdiction at this early stage and that state courts were the proper forum for state-law claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA disparate treatment claim based on race discrimination (Puerto Rican identity) survived the prior motion to dismiss and remains pending. The court's July 15, 2024 order granted in part and denied in part the motion to dismiss, allowing the FHA claim to proceed. This opinion addresses only the motion to amend, not the merits of the FHA claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (race-based discrimination), breach of contract, quasi-contract/unjust enrichment/promissory estoppel, third-party beneficiary, UTPCPL
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted leave to amend the breach of contract claim (Count III) and the UTPCPL claim (Count VI), finding them not futile under Rule 15. The court denied leave to amend for the quasi-contract/unjust enrichment/promissory estoppel claim (Count IV) and third-party beneficiary claim (Count V) as futile. The § 1981 claim survived the prior motion to dismiss and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to offer Property for rent to Black and Brown Harlem residents; alleged discrimination by offering Property to migrants instead
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing because they failed to allege an injury in fact. They did not identify any actual or imminent injury to themselves individually, only a generalized grievance about housing availability for the Harlem community generally. The alleged discrimination is hypothetical and conjectural, as there are no current plans to rent the Property to migrants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extra bedroom(s) to provide separate sleeping space for David Samuel (due to ADHD, Autism, PTSD, and Major Depressive Disorder) and minor child AIMS (Autism Spectrum Disorder, non-verbal); later requests for five bedrooms total, housekeeping services, soundproofing, and blackout curtains
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the four-part FHA reasonable accommodation test (disability, defendant's knowledge, necessity, and refusal) but found insufficient evidence for summary judgment because defendants granted the initial three-bedroom accommodation in March 2023, making it unclear whether plaintiffs were denied a benefit, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate entitlement to additional accommodations (five bedrooms, housekeeping) or identify which specific requests remained at issue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA disability discrimination in housing; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act discrimination; Fourteenth Amendment due process violation; accessibility of services claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the prima facie elements for Title II ADA (qualified individual, exclusion/discrimination, by reason of disability) and Section 504 (disability, qualified for benefits, denied solely because of disability, federal funding) but found insufficient evidence for summary judgment on the same grounds as the FHA claim—the March 2023 grant of the three-bedroom accommodation created a genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether plaintiffs were denied benefits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that an adverse employment action was taken because of race or protected status. The complaint alleges all employees, regardless of race, were fired for allegedly stealing packages after video footage verified their participation, establishing no causal nexus between race and the adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts establishing that adverse employment actions (termination) were taken because of race. The complaint alleges all employees were terminated for the same conduct (stealing packages) regardless of race, failing to establish the ultimate element of causation required under Title VII and § 1981.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emergency move/transfer from current apartment due to landlord's failure to follow lease agreements and worsening medical and mental health conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The complaint does not adequately describe the disability, the specific accommodation sought, or the connection between the disability and the requested accommodation, as required by the FHA and the reasonable accommodation form itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim for denial of services in Section 8 housing program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to establish that he is a qualified individual with a disability or that he was denied participation in Section 8 housing. The complaint does not clarify whether the form was rejected for incompleteness or on disability grounds, making it impossible to infer discrimination.

key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a claim under Maryland Fair Housing Act § 20-707 because property tax credits do not constitute a 'source of income' under the statute's plain language. Tax credits reduce the amount owed rather than conferring income or transferring new monies to the plaintiff, and thus fall outside the statutory definition of 'source of income' as 'any lawful source of money paid directly or indirectly to or on behalf of a renter or buyer of housing.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maryland Consumer Debt Collection Act (MCDCA) § 14-202(11) and (8); Maryland Consumer Protection Act (MCPA) §§ 13-301 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege debt collection activity triggering FDCPA/MCDCA protections. The 2022 and 2023 Escrow Statements contained clear disclaimers stating they were 'informational only' and required 'no action,' lacked explicit payment demands, and were not sent for the animating purpose of obtaining payment. Under the commonsense inquiry test, these statements were not attempts to collect a debt. MCPA claims also failed for lack of specificity under Rule 9(b) and failure to allege reasonable reliance on alleged misrepresentations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Credit of $60.00 to cover laundry costs following bed bug incident, framed as accommodation for Fisher's Schizophrenia
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no plausible nexus between Fisher's disability and the requested $60 laundry credit accommodation. The FHA does not require financial accommodations for disabled tenants, and plaintiff failed to allege facts showing the accommodation was necessary to afford Fisher equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged arbitrary enforcement of hotel rules against plaintiffs regarding complementary breakfast and cell phone usage in lobby, allegedly not applied to white guests
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations of race discrimination implausible because complaint provided no explanation of when alleged incidents occurred, no factual basis for inferring discriminatory intent, and only conclusory assertions that rules were applied differently to white people.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for asserting tenancy rights under landlord-tenant law and seeking disability accommodations, including improper charging of credit card and filing of ejectment action
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no plausible causal link between protected activity and alleged retaliation. Facts as pled showed Hilton filed ejectment case once plaintiffs could no longer pay for lodging, not because of any protected activity. Allegations of retaliation were unsupported conclusory assertions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional due process and equal protection claims); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (race discrimination in contract); ADA Title III (public accommodation discrimination); Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (federal financial assistance recipients); Civil Rights Act of 1964 Title II (public accommodation race discrimination); Pennsylvania Constitution and state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims dismissed because private defendants (Hilton, hotel entities, legal counsel, Gasperetti) are not state actors; conclusory allegations of conspiracy and municipal assent insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. ADA Title III and Civil Rights Act Title II claims dismissed as moot because only injunctive relief available and plaintiffs no longer reside at hotel. RA claims dismissed because no allegation defendants receive federal financial assistance. § 1981 claims dismissed for failure to allege facts supporting race discrimination. State law claims dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: General failure to accommodate Fisher's Schizophrenia during hotel stay and ejectment process
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim. Plaintiffs failed to allege specific accommodations requested or necessary to afford Fisher equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Allegations were conclusory and lacked factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under either the McDonnell Douglas framework or direct evidence method, plaintiff plausibly alleged a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on race by showing protected class status, discriminatory conduct (false assault allegations used as pretext), distinct and palpable injury (eviction, reputational and financial harm), and circumstantial evidence of racial animus (timing of allegations after racial incidents, disparate treatment compared to similarly situated non-minority residents).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that defendants' actions created a discriminatory effect upon a protected class or perpetuated housing segregation; allegations were confined to individual harm to plaintiff rather than class-wide impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NRS 118A.390 wrongful eviction, constructive eviction, negligence, defamation
fha_claims.reasoning: Wrongful eviction claim under NRS 118A.390 survives because plaintiff alleged landlord-tenant relationship, unlawful removal, and blocking of entry. Constructive eviction dismissed because plaintiff alleged actual eviction, not conditions rendering premises unfit. Negligence dismissed because allegations describe intentional conduct, not negligence. Defamation dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege unprivileged publication to third parties and did not allege false statements were included in eviction notice or credit reporting.

case_name: Eugene Davis v. Holly Negaard; Holly Negaard as Trustee of the Holly Negaard Revocable Living Trust; Jessica Purdy a/k/a Jessica Shanafelt; and Purdy Investments, LLC d/b/a/ Western Apartments

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Declaratory relief seeking order that eviction judgment was obtained wrongfully through discriminatory actions; request for stipulation and satisfaction of judgment in state court docket
fha_claims.reasoning: Federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to hear claims seeking to declare a state court eviction judgment wrongful or to require filing of stipulations in the state court docket, as such relief would effectively void the state court's decision. The state court properly declined to hear discrimination claims due to lack of subject matter jurisdiction in an eviction proceeding.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Minimum income policy (2015 Policy requiring gross annual income of at least 43 times total monthly rent) that excluded renters receiving rental subsidies
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found the 2015 Policy violated the FHA by disparately impacting renters with disabilities and those receiving rental subsidies. The policy excluded virtually all renters receiving certain rental subsidies, a large percentage of whom have disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Revised minimum income policy (2019 Policy) that maintained 43x income requirement for unsubsidized applicants, eliminated income requirements for fully subsidized applicants, and required 40x income for partially subsidized applicants' share of rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court affirmed district court's finding that the 2019 Policy violated the NYCHRL by continuing to adversely impact applicants with partial subsidies on the basis of source of income. The court rejected defendant's arguments regarding expert methodology and the proper comparison group, finding the district court did not err in comparing partially subsidized to unsubsidized applicants while excluding fully subsidized applicants who were not subject to the challenged income requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York City Human Rights Law (NYCHRL) source of income discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found the 2015 and 2019 Policies violated the NYCHRL's prohibition on housing discrimination based on lawful source of income. Appellate court affirmed, applying NYCHRL's disparate impact framework and rejecting defendant's statistical and legal arguments.

Plaintiff failed to produce sufficient evidence that these reasons were pretextual; his own deposition testimony partially corroborated the complaints, and temporal proximity alone is insufficient to establish pretext without additional evidence.

fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim dismissed because Title III of the ADA does not apply to private residential apartment buildings; plaintiff abandoned the argument that the Monarc was a public accommodation by failing to challenge this ground on appeal. IIED claim dismissed because non-renewal of lease, as a matter of law, constitutes no more than insistence on legal rights in a permissible way and is not conduct 'atrocious and utterly intolerable in a civilized community' under Florida law; allegations about movers' confiscation of belongings were speculative and failed to plausibly connect defendants' conduct to the alleged harm.
