fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged facts plausibly suggesting that race was a but-for cause of the party shutdown and eviction notice by alleging comparator evidence of similarly situated white and other-race tenants who held similar parties without incident and were not evicted. The claim survives the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege what specific policies or procedures regarding the Clubhouse or eviction existed, and in fact cast doubt on whether any such policies existed at all. A disparate impact claim requires identification of a specific policy or practice; allegations of unfair application without identifying the underlying policy are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. Leave to amend is granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on race; party shutdown and eviction notice
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a hostile housing environment claim under § 3604(b) by alleging severe harassment (party shutdown and eviction notice) based on race, with comparator evidence showing white and other-race residents were not similarly treated. The Ninth Circuit recognizes that eviction notices constitute severe harassment sufficient to support a § 3604(b) disparate treatment claim when factually tied to a protected characteristic.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with right to enjoy apartment free from racial discrimination through party shutdown and eviction notice
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a § 3617 violation by alleging that Defendant broke up the party and issued an eviction notice because of Plaintiffs' race, thereby interfering with their right to take and enjoy possession of their home free from racial discrimination. The FAC adds factual allegations supporting this conclusion through comparator evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (equal contracting rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (equal property rights); NRS 118.120 (Nevada fair housing law); NRS 118A.390 (constructive eviction); breach of contract; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; IIED; NIED
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1981 and § 1982 claims survive because Plaintiffs alleged facts plausibly suggesting race was a but-for cause of injury under the Comcast standard. NRS 118.120 survives because it mirrors the FHA and Plaintiffs stated a colorable claim. NRS 118A.390 survives because Plaintiffs alleged an unlawful eviction notice based on illegal discrimination. Breach of contract survives because Plaintiffs alleged the four required elements. Breach of implied covenant survives because Plaintiffs alleged conduct distinct from the breach of contract claim (fabrication of the verbal assault allegation and selective enforcement based on race). IIED is dismissed without leave to amend because Plaintiffs failed to allege facts supporting severe emotional distress beyond conclusory statements, but leave to amend is granted. NIED is dismissed because Plaintiffs failed to allege factual allegations establishing what duty of care was owed or how it was breached, but leave to amend is granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of water heater defect; plaintiff alleges defendants ignored eight written requests to repair and encouraged him to move, constituting retaliation and constructive eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to opine on likelihood of success on merits of FHA claims and denied TRO/PI motion on grounds that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable injury and that requested relief was not narrowly tailored to remedy discrimination under the FHA. Claims survive but injunctive relief denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of water heater defect; plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide reasonable accommodation by ignoring eight written requests to repair a defective water heater
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to opine on likelihood of success on merits and denied TRO/PI motion on grounds that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable injury and that requested relief (halting state court action, preventing dissemination of eviction information, enjoining collection of fees) was not narrowly tailored to remedy the alleged accommodation failure.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II/III claim; § 1983 due process claim; state law claims including breach of contract, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, abuse of process, failure to train, failure to supervise, defamation, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and wrongful eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to opine on likelihood of success on merits of non-FHA claims and denied TRO/PI motion on grounds that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable injury and that requested relief was not narrowly tailored to remedy any alleged violations. Claims survive but injunctive relief denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to install grab bars in shower to accommodate vertigo; defamation claim against Ms. Hall
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA Title III claim as frivolous because private apartment rentals do not fall within the ADA's definition of public accommodations. The defamation claim against Ms. Hall was also dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege the statement was made to a third person, as required under Wisconsin law.

The complaint lacks the factual allegations necessary to state a plausible failure-to-accommodate claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that he informed Defendants of his disabilities or made any specific accommodation request that Defendants could understand. Without notice of the disability and a clear request for accommodation, Defendants cannot be held liable for failure to accommodate under the FHA. The vague allegations regarding requests for 'a quiet, stress-free environment' and 'room modifications' do not plausibly allege that Defendants knew why Plaintiff made these requests or that they refused a known accommodation.

fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed for failure to state a claim (same deficiency as FHA claim—no allegation that Defendants knew of disability) and because Title III defendants cannot be liable for money damages, which is all Plaintiff seeks. State law claims dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims were dismissed and supplemental jurisdiction was declined.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a walker on plaintiff's front patio despite lease provision restricting items on patios; plaintiff sought exception to patio policy due to mobility disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants communicated approval of the accommodation request to plaintiff. Defendants failed to provide documentation of communication, making credibility determination necessary at trial. Viewing evidence in light most favorable to plaintiff, court denied summary judgment on the fifth element of the Dubois test (refusal to accommodate).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim alleges hostile sexual living environment created by co-tenant John McKnight's conduct (sexual assault on July 12, 2021, and subsequent stalking and harassment through August 2021)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied five-part Neudecker test adapted from Eighth Circuit for co-tenant harassment claims. Court found genuine issues of material fact on elements 2 (unwanted harassment), 4 (severity/pervasiveness), and 5 (awareness/failure to remedy). July 12 sexual assault was severe; subsequent daily stalking and threatening gestures created pervasive harassment. Defendants were aware of McKnight's pattern of harassment toward women through AppFolio documentation and direct complaints. Court found conduct resembled or exceeded severity in Ellison v. Brady.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of August 20, 2021 eviction notice (14/30 notice) alleging multiple lease violations including walker on patio, watching McKnight with binoculars, and caretaker's aggressive conduct toward management
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied three-part San Pedro Hotel test for § 3617 retaliation claims. Court found genuine disputes on all three elements: (1) protected activity (reporting McKnight's assault); (2) adverse housing action (eviction notice constitutes coercion/intimidation/threat); (3) causal nexus (timing three months after initial report, disputed factual basis for notice allegations, and walker issue previously unaddressed). Plaintiff's account of events, if believed, would show retaliatory motive. Temporal proximity and circumstantial evidence of retaliatory intent precluded summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of March 2023 eviction notice (14/30 notice) for alleged failure to provide required recertification documents
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on this portion of the retaliation claim because plaintiff offered no evidence linking the March 2023 paperwork miscommunication to her complaints about McKnight from July-August 2021. The temporal gap of one and a half years, combined with no evidence that the new manager (Elrod) was aware of or involved in the McKnight complaints, precluded any reasonable inference of causal nexus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oregon common law negligence claim: (1) negligent violation of duty to recognize obligations under law and refrain from discrimination; (2) negligent violation of duty to provide reasonably safe dwelling. Defendants moved for summary judgment only on the second allegation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Oregon landlord-tenant law foreseeability standard. Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether defendants knew or should have known McKnight posed a danger to plaintiff. Defendants were aware through AppFolio and direct complaints of at least ten allegations against McKnight between September 2018 and March 2021, including stalking, window-staring, threatening comments, gun-display, and at least two explicit sexual misconduct allegations. Common threads between past conduct (stalking, following, threatening, displaying gun) and conduct toward plaintiff (same behaviors plus sexual assault) created foreseeable risk. Court rejected 'mere facilitation' defense and found conduct exceeded what was foreseeable in Miller v. Tabor W. Inv. Co.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie disparate treatment claim under McDonnell Douglas framework. Although plaintiff established membership in protected class (Black), he could not prove he was qualified (credit score 620 vs. 700 requirement), was denied the property (another applicant submitted application first on Dec. 17, two days before plaintiff's Dec. 19 application), or that similarly situated applicant was treated differently (the approved applicant was also Black). Defendants' legitimate nondiscriminatory reason—first-come-first-served policy with earlier qualified applicant—was unrebutted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie disparate impact claim. Although plaintiff presented statistical evidence that Black and Hispanic consumers have lower median credit scores than white consumers, he failed to establish 'robust causality' between defendants' credit score requirement and disparate impact on protected class. Plaintiff provided no evidence regarding how many of defendants' properties require 700+ credit scores, how many Black/Hispanic applicants were denied, or whether defendants' practices disproportionately affected protected classes. The property was ultimately rented to a Black applicant, undermining the disparate impact theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Washington Law Against Discrimination (RCW 49.60.030(1)(c), RCW 49.60.222, RCW 49.60.220); Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress; Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress; Negligent Retention; Negligent Supervision; Breach of Contract; Unfair Business Practices
fha_claims.reasoning: Washington state discrimination claims fail under same McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework as federal FHA claims; plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case. Tort claims for intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress fail because defendants provided unrebutted evidence they did not manipulate rental criteria and plaintiff was not denied based on credit score but rather because another applicant applied first (not outrageous conduct); negligent infliction requires physical manifestation of injury (none alleged); negligent retention and supervision claims fail because no employee acted outside scope of employment. Breach of contract and unfair business practices claims raised for first time in opposition to summary judgment are disregarded.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RESPA claims (failure to respond to qualified written request and notice of error); breach of mortgage agreement; breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing; FCRA violations; ECOA violations; FHA violations for alleged discrimination in compensation offered to similarly situated white borrowers
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to send qualified written request and notice of error to defendants' designated mailing address as required by RESPA and Regulation X; instead, she emailed the correspondence. The Eleventh Circuit in Bivens held that servicers have no duty to respond when correspondence is not sent to the designated address. Additionally, RESPA and Regulation X do not prohibit servicers from committing errors in the first instance or obligate them to respond to CFPB complaints. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

Gov. Code § 845.6), negligent infliction of emotional distress, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Rosado's allegations that he was discriminated against due to his visual impairment were conclusory and speculative, lacking sufficient factual matter to plausibly allege a violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court did not apply any substantive FHA reasonable accommodation standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, § 1983 due process and equal protection claims, First Amendment retaliation, state law tort claims (defamation, property damage, breach of contract)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA federal claims were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim: ADA Title II and Section 504 claims failed because defendants were not public entities or federal funding recipients; § 1983 claims failed because private landlords are not state actors, the police department is not a proper defendant, the magisterial court has Eleventh Amendment immunity, Judge Hipple has judicial immunity, and the First Amendment claim lacked plausible factual support. State law claims were dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 120 percent payment standard exception to allow plaintiff to afford housing units not in high-rises or near busy streets due to epilepsy and transient epileptic amnesia
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff never lost the 120 percent payment standard exception accommodation; it was approved for the Hawai'i Kai unit and continues to apply to her current housing. The rent reasonableness test is not itself a reasonable accommodation but a mechanism to ensure fair market rent. Plaintiff received the accommodation she requested and cannot show defendants denied it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Two-bedroom voucher to accommodate plaintiff's son as a full-time live-in aide to provide 24/7 care for her disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff herself terminated use of the live-in aide accommodation by informing defendants her son was no longer serving in that role. Defendants consistently maintained plaintiff was approved for the accommodation and could identify a replacement aide. Plaintiff's subsequent requests specified overnight care 'when needed' rather than full-time residence, which does not qualify as a live-in aide under HUD regulations requiring the aide to 'reside' with the recipient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to convert two-bedroom Hawai'i Kai unit to one-bedroom by locking or sealing off a bedroom
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that the requested accommodation was reasonable or necessary. She provided no medical evidence or declaration from a doctor showing her disabilities required conversion of the unit. The burden is on plaintiff to show an accommodation 'seems reasonable on its face,' and she did not meet this burden. Defendants' explanation that they must treat units as designated by city tax records is a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Investigation into plaintiff's live-in aide arrangement, questioning about whether her son actually resided with her, and conditioning inspection on answers to questions about the aide's residency status
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff established a prima facie case of retaliation (protected activity of threatening HUD complaint, adverse action of investigation with close temporal proximity of two days), defendants articulated a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason: compliance with HUD regulations requiring live-in aides to actually reside with recipients. Plaintiff failed to prove pretext. The information defendants discovered (son's work email, employment status, plaintiff's statement that son would move in 'as soon as' inspection allowed) reasonably raised compliance concerns under any definition of 'reside.' Temporal proximity alone does not overcome defendants' legitimate reason, especially where the nondiscriminatory reason arose during the same period as the protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged denial of request to convert two-bedroom Hawai'i Kai unit to one-bedroom by locking a door during 2024 move
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of retaliation. Evidence consisted only of unauthenticated emails and letters without sworn declarations. Plaintiff provided no affidavit or deposition testimony and failed to submit required counter-concise statement of facts. Plaintiff did not explain how the denial constituted coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference. Even accepting the conduct occurred, defendants' stated reason (required to treat units as designated by City and County) was not shown to be pretext; plaintiff's only evidence was inadmissible hearsay from an alleged city employee.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed on mootness/standing grounds without reaching the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. El Camino no longer owns the property, rendering declaratory and injunctive relief moot. Compensatory damages claims lack concrete injury in fact: El Camino profited from the sale and operated the property as intended despite never receiving formal authorization. Attorneys' fees cannot independently confer standing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim dismissed on same mootness and standing grounds as FHA claim. Court did not reach merits of either claim, instead finding El Camino lacked Article III standing to pursue any form of relief.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support an inference that defendants discriminated against her on the basis of protected classes (religion and disability). Allegations were conclusory without factual support showing discriminatory intent or animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation under § 3617 for asserting FHA rights, claiming Madden's email and Black's warrantless inspection constituted unlawful retaliation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to specify which FHA rights (§§ 3603-3606) she exercised and failed to allege facts showing defendants acted with discriminatory animus. Conclusory allegations without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim alleging parking closures denied disabled members access; § 1983 claims for First Amendment (Free Exercise and Free Speech), Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment (Takings), and Fourteenth Amendment (Equal Protection and Due Process) violations; § 1985(3) conspiracy; RLUIPA; § 504 Rehabilitation Act; civil RICO; state law claims for defamation, false light, intentional infliction of emotional distress, trespass, conversion, and misappropriation of public funds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to repair defects in newly constructed home (drywall, electrical systems, plumbing, roofing, floor tiles, cabinetry, countertops, trim, framing, insulation) allegedly based on national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim is time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which requires filing within two years of the occurrence or termination of the discriminatory practice. The alleged discrimination terminated on May 5, 2022, when defendants stopped communicating with plaintiffs; the two-year statute of limitations expired on May 5, 2024, but plaintiffs did not file until February 3, 2025. The court rejected arguments for tolling based on subsequent health effects or a state-law prerequisite letter, as these do not constitute continuing discrimination or new occurrences.

The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without the 'who, what, when and where' of what happened, and thus fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for complaining about discriminatory housing practices

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendants knew or reasonably should have known of her disability because she never returned the reasonable accommodation form provided by defendants and never specifically identified her disability to them. Additionally, plaintiff failed to request the accommodation in direct and specific terms as required by law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race, gender, and disability in refusing to fix sewage pipes, raising rent, and declining to renew lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case because she provided no evidence that similarly situated residents outside her protected class were treated more favorably. Even if prima facie case were established, defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their actions (lease violations, failure to enter service requests, unauthorized animals, failure to pay rent), and plaintiff provided only conclusory assertions without evidence that her protected traits were a significant factor in defendants' decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing fair-housing complaint through opening garage remotely, sending unrequested maintenance, and raising rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the third element of retaliation—causal connection between protected activity and adverse action. Even assuming protected activity, defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their actions (holdover rent rate applied when lease expired, not an increase), and plaintiff failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact that defendants' reasons were pretextual.

fha_claims.reasoning: Parties settled claims for $525,000 after thorough settlement conference. fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 conditions of confinement claim; Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment claim regarding constant overhead lighting in prison cell, mold/feces on ceiling, water intrusion from leaky roof, and stale air in cell; Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA) exhaustion requirement
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies as to mold, feces, water intrusion, and stale air claims. As to the exhausted light claim, the court found no Eighth Amendment violation because: (1) the overhead light remaining on for approximately three months does not constitute a deprivation of a basic human need; (2) defendants responded to plaintiff's grievances and worked with maintenance to fix the issue, demonstrating lack of deliberate indifference; (3) plaintiff's medical records indicate his sleep disturbance was caused by mental health issues (nightmares and anxiety) rather than the light; and (4) the PLRA bars recovery for mental or emotional injury without prior showing of physical injury. Defendants also entitled to qualified immunity because no constitutional violation occurred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 12-foot-wide concrete ramp to the lake to provide accessibility for Jennifer Audette, who has multiple sclerosis, to access the lakeshore

The court found that property owners must engage in an interactive dialogue with regulators before undertaking construction, and the failure to do so is fatal to a reasonable accommodation claim under Title II of the ADA.

The Audettes failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact that these reasons were pretextual for disability discrimination, as the Board's comments reflected hostility toward the Audettes' conduct in flouting zoning rules, not toward Jennifer's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim is barred by the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The final alleged discriminatory act occurred on September 10, 2021, when Urimagua-Guraboa killed Arocho. The complaint was not filed until August 23, 2024, nearly a year beyond the September 10, 2023 deadline. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because the plaintiffs failed to allege a series of discriminatory acts emanating from the same discriminatory animus within the limitations period, and the tolling provision does not extend to unrelated administrative proceedings or separate civil actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (Civil Rights Conspiracy)
fha_claims.reasoning: The substantive due process claim fails because the plaintiffs alleged only private violence by a third party (Urimagua-Guraboa), which does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause under DeShaney. The state-created danger exception does not apply because the plaintiffs did not allege an affirmative act by defendants that increased the threat of third-party harm; merely relocating Urimagua-Guraboa next to Laracuente is an allegation of rendering her more vulnerable to risk, not an affirmative act. The equal protection claim fails because the plaintiffs made only conclusory assertions without identifying similarly situated non-Hispanic tenants who received different treatment. The conspiracy claim under § 1985(3) fails because the plaintiffs did not provide minimum factual support for the existence of a conspiracy, did not identify co-conspirators, and did not allege facts showing an agreement to deprive plaintiffs of rights based on race or ethnicity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for disability discrimination; § 1983 Due Process Clause claim; state law tortious interference claim

For the § 1983 due process claim, plaintiff failed to identify what property or liberty interest she was deprived of or what action lacked a hearing or appeal. The complaint alleges claims under § 3604(a) which survive the motion to dismiss because subject matter jurisdiction exists under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and the exemption defense cannot be resolved on the face of the pleadings without factual development.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that § 3604(c) claims for discriminatory statements are not subject to the exemptions in § 3603(b) by their plain language. fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unlawful retaliation for exercise of rights protected under the FHA, specifically the issuance of notice to vacate and initiation of eviction proceedings following plaintiff's termination of sexual relationship with defendant

fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that § 3617 retaliation claims are not subject to the exemptions in § 3603(b) because § 3603(b) explicitly exempts only 'section 3604 of this title' and does not reference § 3617. Accordingly, the court has subject matter jurisdiction over this claim and the motion to dismiss is denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a first-floor apartment unit due to back injury and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her disability (element 2), failed to allege how denial of first-floor unit deprived her of equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3), and failed to allege defendant knew or should have known of her disability. Although plaintiff demonstrated the accommodations were facially reasonable (element 4) and that defendant refused them (element 5), the complaint failed to satisfy all five elements of the reasonable accommodation claim under Dubois.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from use of chemical pesticides in plaintiff's unit due to severe allergies and Stage 3 kidney disease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her allergies and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her disability (element 2), and failed to clearly allege that exemption from pesticides was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3). Although the accommodation appeared facially reasonable and defendant refused it, the complaint did not satisfy all five elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to extend lease, denial of rent payment, and filing of eviction action allegedly in retaliation for requesting accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, plaintiff must allege: (1) protected activity, (2) adverse housing consequence causally linked to that activity, and (3) resulting damage. While plaintiff plausibly alleged protected activity (requesting accommodations) and adverse consequences (lease denial, eviction filing) and damages (emotional/financial harm and risk to Section 8 voucher), she failed to clearly allege the causal nexus between her accommodation requests and the subsequent adverse consequences.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations for first-floor unit and pesticide exemption
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Section 504, plaintiff must show: (1) she is an individual with a disability, (2) she is otherwise qualified to receive the benefit, (3) she was denied benefits solely by reason of disability, and (4) the program receives federal financial assistance. Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to allege the qualifications necessary to live on the first floor and that she meets them (element 2), failed to allege denial was solely based on disability (element 3), and failed to allege sufficient facts that defendant receives federal financial assistance (element 4).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliatory eviction initiated on April 23, 2025, fourteen days after plaintiff's ESA was diagnosed with terminal kidney failure on April 8, 2025.

The court did not reach the substantive merits of the retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil RICO claims alleging pattern of racketeering, housing fraud, wire fraud, obstruction of justice, and fabrication of rental ledgers; California state law retaliatory eviction claim; claim that property was unlawfully rented without Certificate of Occupancy in violation of California Health and Safety Code § 17920.3.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that RICO allegations, while extensive, relied heavily on conclusory assertions of wire fraud and enterprise conduct unsupported by concrete evidence. The court also noted that federal courts lack jurisdiction to review state court eviction proceedings and that Younger abstention applies to this landlord-tenant dispute governed by state law.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly but granted leave to amend, indicating the claims were not frivolous. The opinion does not specify which FHA theory (reasonable accommodation, disparate treatment, etc.) was alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination in making or enforcing contracts); breach of contract; constitutional claims; civil RICO; criminal mail fraud; common law fraud; breach of fiduciary duty
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed non-FHA claims including § 1981, breach of contract, constitutional claims, and others for failure to state a plausible claim. § 1981 claim against certain defendants was weak but not wholly frivolous; plaintiff was granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged disability-based discrimination in housing transaction and failure to accommodate disabled individuals (Mildred and Doris Smith) in connection with property purchase and construction defects causing respiratory issues due to mold
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FHA claim (Count II) as barred by the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a). Discriminatory practice occurred in 2017; plaintiff filed complaint in September 2024. Continuing violations doctrine did not apply because plaintiff alleged only isolated conduct with no facts showing discrimination extending into the limitations period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claims based on disability discrimination in housing transaction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed ADA and Section 504 claims (Count III) as barred by Illinois' two-year statute of limitations for personal injury actions. Discriminatory conduct occurred in 2017; complaint filed September 2024. Continuing violations doctrine did not apply for same reasons as FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged disparate treatment based on immigration status: U.S. citizens were housed in shelters while migrants and asylum seekers were housed in hotels.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court agreed with the magistrate judge that the FHA does not apply to individuals seeking free government shelter, and therefore the FHA disparate treatment claim failed as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; due process claims; claims regarding alleged harms to migrants.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to infer unequal treatment under the Equal Protection Clause; lacked standing to bring claims on behalf of migrants; and failed to allege a deprivation of liberty or property sufficient to support a due process claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA-compliant sidewalk/pathway from plaintiff's patio door across common area to public parking lot, with adequate width (at least 60 inches) to accommodate plaintiff and her seeing-eye dog walking side-by-side, and proper drainage to prevent water runoff into plaintiff's unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff pleaded sufficient factual allegations that the installed walkway was non-ADA compliant (30 inches wide, improper drainage causing mold damage) to survive motion to dismiss. Defendants' attached exhibits did not incontrovertibly contradict plaintiff's allegations because they were not referenced in the complaint and did not confirm actual completion specifications. Whether accommodation is reasonable requires fact-specific balancing inquiry inappropriate for Rule 12(b)(6) stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently alleged all three elements of FHA retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617: (1) protected activity (filing Wisconsin ERD complaint on May 12, 2022); (2) adverse action (delay in providing sidewalk, cancellation of initial approval, non-compliant final product); and (3) causal connection (temporal proximity between complaint and delay, statements from defendants that complex was not built for disabled). Allegations of delay as retaliation and failure to provide compliant accommodation survive at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for discrimination and failure to reasonably accommodate disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff conceded dismissal of ADA Title III claim for lack of available monetary damages. Court granted dismissal without substantive analysis of the claim's merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged Fair Housing Act violations related to alleged religious discrimination in land use decisions, zoning enforcement, and building permit denials. Also alleged violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1982, U.S. Constitution (due process and equal protection), New York State Constitution, New York State Civil Rights Law, and state tort claims (trespass, tortious interference with prospective business advantage).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed plaintiffs' land use claims (including FHA claims) as unripe for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the final decision requirement of Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank. Plaintiffs failed to obtain a final decision by not seeking a variance from the Town Board after their building permit applications were denied, and the futility and discrimination exceptions to the final decision requirement did not apply.

case_name: Cynthia Exline-Johnson v. Rosser Properties, LLC
key_cases_cited: Metropolitan Fair Hous. Council of Oklahoma, Inc. v. Fetock

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statement or advertisement indicating preference, limitation, or discrimination based on religion
fha_claims.reasoning: The statement at issue was not made 'with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling' as required by § 3604(c), and no ordinary listener would interpret Ms. Rosser's skeptical comment about Ms. Johnson's spirituality as expressing a religion-based preference in housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making housing unavailable because of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination under McDonnell Douglas because she presented no evidence that she is handicapped under § 3602(h)(1) or (3). Her testimony of poor sleep without medical evidence, severity, permanence, or long-term impact is insufficient to establish substantial limitation of a major life activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to remain in apartment despite lease non-renewal
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to satisfy the first element of the five-part reasonable accommodation test because she presented no evidence establishing that she is handicapped under the FHA, and no evidence that defendants knew or reasonably should have known of any disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting accommodation and exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present evidence satisfying the third element of the § 3617 retaliation claim—that defendants coerced, threatened, intimidated, or interfered with her on account of her protected activity. Her conclusory allegations of harassment and interference lacked factual support and record citations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oklahoma Discrimination in Housing Act, Oklahoma Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Oklahoma Consumer Protection Act, state-law libel
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all state-law claims without prejudice, finding no compelling reasons to retain supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims that should ordinarily be tried in state court.

fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against New York City Department of Homeless Services dismissed because a municipal agency cannot be sued under New York City Charter § 396; allegations construed as asserted against the City of New York instead. No substantive analysis of any FHA, ADA, or constitutional claims on the merits.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Complaint failed to provide sufficient factual content regarding reasonable accommodation requests and relied instead on conclusory allegations of wrongdoing. No viable cause of action stated under FHA because Plaintiff did not allege facts from which the Court could infer any named Defendant's liability for FHA violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on transgender status and disability in provision of housing accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleged that ECCM and associated landlords discriminated based on transgender status and disability, providing substandard and unsafe housing, but failed to provide sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim. Court could not infer liability from conclusory allegations alone.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate impact based on disability status in housing provision
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleged disparate impact violations but failed to provide factual content sufficient to state a plausible claim. Court found conclusory allegations of wrongdoing insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection, Due Process, First Amendment, Takings Clause); Americans with Disabilities Act Title I and Title II; Rehabilitation Act § 504; state law claims (breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence, unjust enrichment, Pennsylvania Ethics Act)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); Lack of standing / Article III
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims for failure to establish standing (as to taxpayer and citizen claims), failure to identify proper defendants (county departments lack separate legal status), failure to allege color of state law as to private defendants, failure to allege personal involvement, and failure to state plausible constitutional violations. ADA/Rehabilitation Act claims dismissed for failure to allege disability status, employment relationship, or specific adverse actions. State law claims dismissed without prejudice as supplemental jurisdiction declined after dismissal of federal claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination, ADEA age discrimination, Rehabilitation Act interference, Rehabilitation Act and ADEA retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: All five claims brought under the Rehabilitation Act and ADEA, not the FHA. The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework to the disability discrimination and age discrimination claims, and found the BOP articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons (performance issues, concerning conduct, mental health concerns) that were not pretextual. The interference claim failed because denial of leave requests does not constitute unlawful interference under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b), and the retaliation claim failed because plaintiff could not establish causal connection between EEO activity and investigations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Excusal from responding to emergency situations and inmate disturbances; liberal leave and breaks with leave without pay; reassignment to a vacant position at same agency, commuting area, pay grade, and tenure
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the Rehabilitation Act reasonable accommodation framework, plaintiff failed to identify a specific, reasonable accommodation because excusing him from responding to emergencies would strip the correctional counselor role of its essential functions, which the law does not require. Plaintiff's request for reassignment was too amorphous—he never identified a specific vacant position for which he was qualified, failing to meet his burden under Donahue. The court noted that even if the BOP failed to engage in the interactive process, plaintiff's proposed accommodations were facially unreasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from water shutoff for individuals with disabilities, medical conditions, or age-related qualifications; meaningful notice and information regarding exemption procedures and eligibility criteria
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege that they were treated differently as a result of their disabilities or that defendants refused to make a requested accommodation. All plaintiffs received notice of exemptions and ultimately qualified for and received exemptions; no plaintiff alleged water was actually shut off. The complaint does not plausibly allege discrimination or denial of accommodation because of disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims, ADA Title II claims, state and local law claims (CAPA, New York Constitution, New York State Human Rights Law, New York City Human Rights Law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1983 due process claims fail because no plaintiff alleged actual deprivation of water service; mere threats without actual termination do not constitute a deprivation. ADA claims fail because plaintiffs did not allege they were denied benefits or discriminated against because of disability. Injunctive and declaratory relief claims are moot because all plaintiffs received exemptions and no water was shut off. State and local law claims dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicapped accessible parking space, handrails, and ramp access to building entrance (203-building) to accommodate plaintiff's mobility disability (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that a reasonable jury could find the October 12 Letter provided sufficient notice that plaintiff had a disability requiring accommodation, satisfying the second element of the FHA failure-to-accommodate claim. The court distinguished Watters on factual grounds (defendants had no conflicting information about plaintiff's disability, the requested accommodations are not universally desirable, and defendants completely ignored the request rather than engaging in dialogue). Summary judgment denied; case proceeds to trial on whether defendants were aware of plaintiff's disability and whether they failed to reasonably accommodate.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illinois Human Rights Act discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that plaintiff brings state law discrimination claims under the Illinois Human Rights Act, but both parties focused briefing exclusively on the FHA claim. The awareness of disability element is key to all claims, so the denial of summary judgment on the FHA claim implicitly allows the state law claim to proceed as well.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff references Rehabilitation Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and Section 8 in the IFP petition but makes no specific accommodation request in the complaint. The complaint alleges misuse of government funds, tax fraud, racketeering, and racial discrimination but does not allege any failure to provide a reasonable accommodation or any disability-based discrimination.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) and found it fails to state a claim and lacks sufficient factual allegations to establish standing or subject-matter jurisdiction. The complaint is too vague and conclusory to identify who violated plaintiff's rights, what they did, when, or where. Although plaintiff mentions disability-related statutes in the IFP petition, the complaint contains no allegations of disability discrimination or failure to accommodate. The court granted plaintiff leave to amend by August 22, 2025.

fha_claims.reasoning: Second cause of action claims discrimination but fails to articulate whether based on sex or another protected class and lacks factual support. Dismissed as conclusory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in this procedural order

The opinion references that Plaintiff Avila has asserted FHA claims in this and related cases, but no substantive analysis of those claims appears in this order.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA, NYCHRL, NIED

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination, Fair Housing Act violations, unfair business practices, harassment, stalking, and interference by the United States and Irvine Company related to lease termination and housing access; also alleged deprivation of Social Security Disability Benefits.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction under the Tucker Act because plaintiff's claims sounded in tort (harassment, stalking, interference) and fell outside the Tucker Act's scope; claims for social security benefits and criminal actions are also excluded from the Court of Federal Claims's jurisdiction.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting claims under the FHA, ADA, § 1983, HIPAA, Privacy Act, CFAA, or ECPA. The court found that Plaintiff did not allege he is disabled and that a defendant discriminated against him based on disability in a housing matter, nor did he allege any defendant violated his constitutional rights or rights under CFAA/ECPA. HIPAA provides no private right of action, and the Privacy Act applies only to federal agencies.

source_file: 10634417_2025_Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation_ca4

key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from Gibson Island's business-purpose covenant to allow operation of an assisted living group home for elderly people with disabilities on the property
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in analyzing whether removal of the Corporation's four disputed conditions was 'necessary' rather than whether the requested exemption itself was necessary to provide equal housing opportunities. The necessity element is satisfied as a matter of law—without the exemption, disabled elderly persons cannot live on Gibson Island. However, the reasonableness element presents genuine factual disputes regarding whether the Corporation's conditions (septic monitoring, dispute resolution, arbitration escrow, guarantor) are justified or pretextual, requiring jury resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in finding no evidence of adverse action or retaliatory motive. The Corporation's efforts to revoke Lussi's permit, delay the group home opening, and refuse the accommodation request constitute adverse actions. A jury could find these actions were retaliatory for Lussi's years-long advocacy for FHA-protected housing rights, particularly given evidence that the Corporation's stated rationales (litigation risk, administrative burden) may be pretextual and linked to Lussi's protected FHA advocacy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in finding no evidence of discriminatory intent based on disability. Circumstantial evidence supports an inference of discrimination: the Corporation's stated rationales (septic concerns, litigation risk) may be pretextual; community members expressed hostility toward disabled elderly residents; the Corporation President promised to 'defend deeds v FHA' and take a '360 degree' approach to block the project 'even if the group home is by right consistent with FHA'; and the Corporation may have acted in response to community stereotypes about disabled residents. These matters require jury resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maryland fair housing law claims paralleling the FHA reasonable accommodation, retaliation, and discrimination theories
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court's summary judgment on parallel Maryland fair housing law claims is vacated and remanded on the same grounds as the federal FHA claims. Maryland law largely mirrors the FHA, though it shifts the burden of proving reasonableness to the defendant after the plaintiff establishes a prima facie case, a distinction that will apply on remand.

fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot Without Prejudice; Motion to Amend Granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion to amend to add FHA and ECOA claims and denied defendant's motion to dismiss as moot without prejudice, allowing the Second Amended Complaint to proceed as the operative pleading. The court did not reach the merits of any claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory origination of mortgage
fha_claims.reasoning: Against PennyMac: no allegation that PennyMac was involved in origination (occurred 2015, assignment 2019); claim time-barred under applicable statute of limitations. Against Evolve: origination claims time-barred as complained-of conduct occurred more than seven years before filing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of FHA underwriting standards under 24 C.F.R. § 203.500, § 203.606(a), § 203.604 regarding notice of right to face-to-face meeting within 3 pay periods of delinquency
fha_claims.reasoning: Against both defendants: regulations apply only when mortgagee 'commences foreclosure or acquires title.' Plaintiff failed to allege either defendant actually initiated foreclosure proceedings; instead she sold the property voluntarily. Regulations' triggering event did not occur.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA discrimination claim for denying loan modifications and refusing to consider waiting for disability approval; Emotional distress (NIED/IIED); Consumer protection violation (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A § 2); Unjust enrichment; Duress; Unconscionable origination; Mortgage void/never consummated; CARES Act violation; UCC/RESPA violations
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege she is a qualified individual with disability (only alleged 'filed for disability' after 2016 car accident) and failed to show nexus between any discriminatory acts and disability. NIED/IIED: No plausible allegation of negligence or extreme/outrageous conduct; defendants' actions were lawful and typical. Consumer protection: No unfair or deceptive practice alleged; conduct was lawful and typical. Unjust enrichment: Assignment document clearly conveyed interest in mortgage to assignee. CARES Act: No private right of action; complained-of action predated moratorium; no allegation of actual foreclosure initiation.

Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent payment policy requiring disabled residents (those receiving SSDI) to pay rent monthly in full on the first of the month, while non-disabled residents could pay weekly.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found Unity's written rent policy facially discriminatory under the FHAA because it explicitly singled out SSDI recipients for different treatment (monthly vs. weekly payment). Unity's uncorroborated, self-serving testimony about an unwritten policy applying to all fixed-income residents was rejected as contradicted by the record. Unity failed to demonstrate a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason or that no less discriminatory alternatives existed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pennsylvania Landlord Tenant Act wrongful eviction claim; Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (UTPCPL) claims for false representations, failure to return security deposit, and deceptive practices; Pennsylvania intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED) claim; negligence claim against property manager Re/Max.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment to Unity on the IIED claim, finding the conduct did not meet Pennsylvania's extremely high bar for outrageous conduct. However, the court denied summary judgment on all UTPCPL claims (seven separate allegations), finding genuine disputes of material fact on false representations, failure to return security deposit, and deceptive practices. The court also found Unity liable as a matter of law for wrongful eviction under the Landlord Tenant Act (failure to provide 15 days' written notice) and for failure to return the $75 security deposit (awarding $150 in damages). For Re/Max, the court denied summary judgment on negligence and UTPCPL claims, finding Re/Max owed a duty to McCready as property manager with contractual responsibilities for inspection, dispute settlement, tenant screening, and evictions.

source_file: 10636459_2025_Derby v. Pleasant Beach Mobile Home Resort, LLC_mied

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged retaliatory eviction, surveillance, and interruption of therapeutic services in response to protected housing activity and request for accommodation under the ADA
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient factual allegations to state a claim under § 3617. The complaint contained only legal conclusions without facts identifying the protected status, any disability, any specific accommodation requested, or how the Fair Housing Act applied. Plaintiffs did not meet the notice pleading requirements of Rule 8 and Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for accommodation under the ADA (unspecified in the complaint)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to support a reasonable accommodation claim. The complaint vaguely referenced a 'request for accommodation under the ADA' but did not identify any disability, specify what accommodation was requested, or explain how the defendant failed to provide it. The pleading was legally conclusory and failed to meet Rule 8 notice pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim (public accommodation discrimination); § 1982 civil rights claim (racial discrimination in property rights); § 1983 due process claim (constitutional deprivation during eviction); Younger abstention and Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional issues related to state court eviction proceedings
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I (Title II ADA) dismissed because Pleasant Beach and Clarkson are private entities, not public entities subject to Title II. Count III (§ 1982) dismissed because plaintiffs alleged no racial discrimination. Count IV (§ 1983 due process) dismissed because defendants are private actors not subject to § 1983, and because Younger abstention and Rooker-Feldman doctrine bar federal court jurisdiction over ongoing or concluded state court eviction proceedings.

case_name: Connolly v. Lanham
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Alig v. Quicken Loans Inc., 990 F.3d 782 (4th Cir. 2021)
Pinchback v. Armistead Homes Corp., 907 F.2d 1447 (4th Cir. 1990)

Causey v. Ford Motor Credit Co., 162 F.3d 794 (4th Cir. 1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the McDonnell-Douglas burden-shifting framework, plaintiffs established a prima facie case and defendants provided a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason (fair and reasonable appraisal following standard methodology). Plaintiffs failed to create a genuine issue of material fact that the nondiscriminatory reason was pretextual. Expert testimony showed the appraisal was complete, reasonable, and well-explained; plaintiffs' expert lacked appraisal qualifications and could not rebut that the appraisal adhered to professional norms. Isolated discrepancies (neighborhood-level disparities, minor departures from practice, contradictory descriptions of tree buffer) were insufficient to establish pretext for racial discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691(a)(1)), 42 U.S.C. § 1981, 42 U.S.C. § 1982
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (ECOA, § 1981, § 1982) are predicated on the same discriminatory intent standard as the FHA claim. Because plaintiffs failed to establish pretext for racial discrimination under the McDonnell-Douglas framework on the appraisal itself, they likewise failed to establish discriminatory intent under the parallel standards applicable to these statutes. Summary judgment granted on all remaining counts.

key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of multifamily dwelling, including accessible routes to trash dumpsters and public streets, accessible central mailbox, lever-style doorknobs, wheelchair maneuvering space near exterior gates and inside bathrooms, thermostats and light switches at accessible heights, and sufficiently wide doorways for wheelchair passage
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because his complaint failed to allege with sufficient particularity that he personally experienced (rather than merely observed) any accessibility barriers, and he failed to establish a concrete future injury for purposes of seeking equitable relief. The court found the allegations conclusory and devoid of contextual details about when, where, and how plaintiff encountered the barriers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiff's mere invocation of the Fair Housing Act, without establishing federal question jurisdiction or pleading diversity jurisdiction (citizenship and amount in controversy), is insufficient to confer jurisdiction. The complaint was dismissed without issuance and service of process.

case_name: Stephanie Haywood v. Warner Robins Housing Authority, Africa Porter, Reginald Early, Robert Gidney, Andre Washington, Kesha Bray, Betty Ann Faulks, and John Does 1-10

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation, negligence, gross negligence, invasion of privacy, unlawful entry, intentional infliction of emotional distress, Violence Against Women Act violations, Georgia Open Records Act violations, Fourteenth Amendment due process violations, abuse of authority, and unlawful probation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the complaint to be an impermissible shotgun pleading that fails to give defendants adequate notice of claims and grounds, lacks minimum clarity and coherence, and asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which act. The court allowed plaintiff 21 days to file an amended complaint rather than dismissing with prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to meet their burden at step three of the disparate impact framework by failing to propose less discriminatory alternatives that would be equally effective at serving Defendants' legitimate business interests in operating efficiency, cost control, and compliance with HUD and investor guidelines. All seven proposed alternatives either were not true alternatives, were already employed by Defendants, or lacked sufficient specificity and evidentiary support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adduce evidence of discriminatory intent or motive under the McDonnell Douglas framework. Plaintiffs presented no direct evidence of discriminatory motive, no evidence of pretext, and merely questioned the effectiveness of Defendants' cost-saving measures on a property-by-property basis, which is insufficient to rebut Defendants' legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons for their maintenance practices.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Private nuisance claims brought by three Individual Plaintiffs under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court noted that private nuisance claims brought by the three Individual Plaintiffs remain for disposition and have never been addressed on the merits. The court indicated it is inclined to decline supplemental jurisdiction and remand these state law claims to state court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation claim related to false statements regarding rental payments made at a tenant meeting in April 2023; also references misapplication of rental payments, negligent maintenance of tenant ledger, and retaliatory conduct regarding a parking ticket.
fha_claims.reasoning: The defamation claim was filed two years after the allegedly defamatory statements were made in April 2023, exceeding the District of Columbia's one-year statute of limitations under D.C. Code § 12-301(a)(4). Even measuring from the initial complaint filing in May 2024, the claim was thirteen months after the alleged statements, still outside the limitations period.

case_name: Gregory Kelly, et al. v. Max Federal Credit Union, et al.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off., 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Race discrimination in home loan denial; disability discrimination; Fair Housing Act violations; Due Process violations; INA Civil Rights violations; RICO; Internal Revenue Code violations; Fourth Amendment privacy violations; negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint is a frivolous shotgun pleading that fails to provide adequate notice of claims or factual allegations supporting relief. The court found the 72-page complaint contains virtually no meaningful factual allegations, conclusory and vague assertions, and multiple claims against all defendants without specifying individual liability. Amendment is futile given the plaintiff's history of filing similar meritless shotgun pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animal (ESA) accommodation; eviction allegedly retaliatory in response to ESA's terminal illness diagnosis
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO/PI motion on procedural grounds (failure to comply with Rule 65(b) and Local Rule 231 notice requirements) and on merits, finding plaintiffs failed to demonstrate likelihood of success by showing eviction was initiated in response to protected activity or that defendants lacked legitimate, non-retaliatory basis for notice. Claim survives but injunctive relief denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil RICO (wire fraud, obstruction of justice, racketeering); state law retaliatory eviction; California Health and Safety Code § 17920.3 (Certificate of Occupancy violation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO/PI on procedural grounds and on merits, finding RICO allegations rely on conclusory assertions unsupported by concrete evidence, Certificate of Occupancy deficiency does not alone render lease void or entitle immediate injunctive relief, and Younger abstention bars federal intervention in state landlord-tenant dispute. Claims survive but injunctive relief denied.

case_name: Henry Ortiz v. Doug V. Mull, et al.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unit repairs, accommodations, and garage parking access promised by leasing agents but not fulfilled
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's conclusory allegations fail to demonstrate that defendants knew or reasonably should have known of plaintiff's handicap, that plaintiff communicated his disability to defendants, or that defendants refused to make necessary accommodations. The complaint lacks factual specificity required to plead a failure to accommodate claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's conclusory allegations that defendants 'denied housing-related services routinely granted to other tenants without disabilities' and 'selectively enforced policies' lack factual specificity and fail to allege facts demonstrating a similarly situated person treated better or that discriminatory intent motivated defendants' conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of retaliation under the FHA are wholly conclusory and do not adequately identify specific misconduct or allege facts suggesting a causal link between plaintiff's protected acts and defendants' adverse actions, failing to meet the prima facie standard for FHA retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title (unspecified), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process and equal protection, breach of contract, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim fails because defendants are not public entities and apartment residences do not constitute public accommodations; § 1983 claims fail because plaintiff did not adequately allege state action (bare conspiracy allegations are conclusory) and did not adequately allege federal constitutional violations (due process does not require pre-towing hearing; equal protection allegations lack discriminatory intent); state law claims dismissed without prejudice as supplemental jurisdiction declined after dismissal of federal claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claims (5 U.S.C. § 706(1) for unreasonable delay and § 706(2) for arbitrary and capricious action); Appropriations Clause violation; Separation of Powers violation; procedural due process violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found a substantial likelihood of success on the merits on at least two claims: (1) Separation of Powers violation because HUD must follow statutory mandates when appropriated funds are available and no constitutional objection exists, and (2) unreasonable delay under 5 U.S.C. § 706(1) because the TRAC factors weigh in plaintiffs' favor given the congressionally prescribed September 30, 2025 deadline and the concrete harm to fair housing enforcement organizations. The court rejected HUD's threshold arguments regarding Tucker Act jurisdiction, agency discretion under Lincoln v. Vigil, and finality requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Eilleen's race discrimination claim under disparate treatment theory dismissed because Eilleen failed to sign the Second Amended Complaint; pro se litigant Paul cannot represent Eilleen. Claim survives on merits as to Paul, who properly signed and alleged differential treatment (Eilleen subjected to Registration Requirements while other residents were 'grandfathered' in), satisfying the distinct and palpable injury requirement at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Eilleen's disparate impact claim dismissed due to failure to sign the SAC. As to Paul, the court found the Fussells adequately alleged a facially neutral policy (700+ credit score requirement) that disproportionately impacts recent immigrants lacking extensive U.S. credit history, and that facts demonstrate causal connection between the policy and injury; claim survives MTD and may proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim dismissed because the alleged adverse actions (subjecting Eilleen to Registration Requirements and threatening eviction) occurred before the Fussells engaged in protected activity (notifying HUD and requesting resolution). Without temporal proximity, no causal link can be established between protected activity and adverse action. Claim dismissed with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to accommodate Paul's disability by rigidly applying credit score requirements without consideration of his stable federal income (Social Security Disability Insurance)
fha_claims.reasoning: Paul's reasonable accommodation claim dismissed because the SAC fails to allege that Defendants knew or should have known of Paul's disability. The complaint contains only conclusory statements that Paul is disabled and receives SSDI benefits, with no factual allegations demonstrating that the Fussells communicated Paul's disability to Defendants. Claim dismissed with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982 (race discrimination in contracts and property rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional claims under color of state law); First Amendment retaliation; Due Process and Equal Protection claims; 42 U.S.C. § 1985 (conspiracy to deprive civil rights); 8 U.S.C. § 1324b (immigration-related employment discrimination); Arizona Consumer Fraud Act; Americans with Disabilities Act Title III; Equal Access to Justice Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Sections 1981 and 1982 claims dismissed as to both Eilleen and Paul because they are limited to racial discrimination, not national origin discrimination; the SAC alleges only national origin (Filipino) without alleging ancestry or ethnic characteristics. Section 1983 and constitutional claims dismissed because Defendants are private entities and the SAC fails to allege any state actor involvement or color of state law. Section 1985 claims dismissed under all three subsections: (1) no allegation of conspiracy to interfere with federal office; (2) no allegation of obstruction of justice in federal or state courts; (3) no state actor in the alleged conspiracy. Section 1324b dismissed because it applies only to employment discrimination and the SAC alleges a landlord-tenant relationship. ACFA claim dismissed without leave to amend because the SAC does not allege false promise or misrepresentation in connection with sale or advertisement of merchandise. ADA claim dismissed because private mobile home parks are not places of public accommodation, and the SAC does not allege denial of access to the rental office (a common area). EAJA request dismissed because Defendants are not government actors. All claims except Section 1324b and ACFA dismissed with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint alleged Fair Housing Act violations but no substantive details provided in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to respond to defendant's motion for summary judgment despite being given a second chance and a court order to respond. The court dismissed the case with prejudice for failure to prosecute and comply with court orders, not on the merits of the FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Texas Property Code violation, 24 CFR §100.70 HUD regulation violation, breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (Texas Property Code, 24 CFR §100.70, and breach of contract) were dismissed with prejudice for failure to prosecute and comply with court orders, not on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and anxiety; transfer to different shelter; unspecified accommodations related to disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead specific facts describing how he was denied reasonable accommodations, by whom, or how those adverse actions were due to his disability. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations without factual content sufficient to state a plausible claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged he was 'punished due to [his] disability' but failed to plead specific facts describing how he was punished, by whom, or how those adverse actions were due to his disability, failing to meet the two-element test for FHA discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for discrimination in public accommodations (homeless shelter); Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment; 18 U.S.C. § 242 criminal statute claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Eighth Amendment protections apply only to convicted prisoners and plaintiff alleged no conviction; 18 U.S.C. § 242 is a criminal statute that does not confer a private right of action; ADA Title III claim fails for lack of specific factual allegations regarding discrimination and denial of services due to disability, and even if adequately pled, Title III provides only injunctive relief, not the monetary damages sought.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged racial and gender-based housing discrimination in pre-acquisition and post-acquisition conduct. Although plaintiffs established a prima facie case with evidence including discriminatory comments about gender identity and Facebook posts expressing anti-transgender animus, they failed to demonstrate that defendants' proffered non-discriminatory reasons were pretextual. The court granted summary judgment for defendants but found the claim was not frivolous and therefore denied defendants' request for attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(c)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of Florida Condominium Act (§ 718.111(12)(b) and (c), § 718.303, § 718.111); breach of fiduciary duty
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs brought claims under Florida's Condominium Act alleging violations of record inspection requirements, association bylaws, and fiduciary duties. Defendants prevailed on summary judgment. Under § 718.303, the prevailing party is entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees, and the court found defendants were the clear prevailing party on these state law claims.

source_file: 10644815_2025_Derhem v. Bay House Miami Condominium Association_flsd
case_name: Kanayo Derhem et al. v. Bay House Miami Condominium Association et al.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
