fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement — Rental Applications required prospective tenants to submit copies of report cards for persons under age 18
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the Report Card Requirement itself may violate the FHA as discrimination based on familial status, Emanuel and EMS cannot be held liable because Emanuel had no authority to grant or deny rental applications; her role was purely ministerial (checking for required documents and submitting applications to the screening committee). Under Sabal Palm and common law agency principles, an agent cannot be liable for a principal's discriminatory decision when the agent had no authority over that decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proper Attire Rule — Rule requiring all residents to wear proper attire when walking on streets; no shirtless boys; girls must wear cover-up over bathing suit when walking to pool
fha_claims.reasoning: A genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced the Proper Attire Rule against the individual plaintiffs. Emanuel had authority to issue notices of violation and did so on multiple occasions; evidence shows she was present during at least one enforcement action and read rules to a plaintiff. A reasonable jury could conclude Emanuel personally committed or contributed to the FHA violation by enforcing the allegedly discriminatory rule.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loitering Rule — Rule prohibiting loitering (congregating on streets) at any time
fha_claims.reasoning: A genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced the Loitering Rule against the individual plaintiffs. Emanuel had authority to issue notices of violation and did so on multiple occasions; evidence shows she discussed a loitering violation notice with plaintiff Leann Carr regarding her grandson. A reasonable jury could conclude Emanuel personally committed or contributed to the FHA violation by enforcing the allegedly discriminatory rule.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Curfew Rule — Rule requiring persons under age 18 to be in their home or on their patio after sunset
fha_claims.reasoning: A genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced the Curfew Rule against the individual plaintiffs. Emanuel had authority to issue notices of violation and did so on multiple occasions. A reasonable jury could conclude Emanuel personally committed or contributed to the FHA violation by enforcing the allegedly discriminatory rule based on familial status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of equal terms, conditions, and privileges of housing; steering to first-floor unit based on disability; rent increases and eviction based on disability status
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found strong likelihood of success on merits under FHA §§ 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) based on direct evidence of discriminatory intent in defendant's written notes referencing plaintiff's disability, medical problems, and physical condition, combined with pattern of rent increases and eviction notices following plaintiff's refusal to relocate to first-floor unit and complaints to housing authorities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Written statements indicating preference against tenants with disabilities; notes referencing plaintiff's medical problems, medical situation, and physical impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found strong likelihood of success on FHA § 3604(c) claim (unlawful written statements indicating preference based on handicap) because defendant's written notes facially indicate a preference against plaintiff's tenancy based on her perceived physical impairment, and discriminatory intent is not required under this provision; notes clearly show defendant's preference for tenants without disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent increases and eviction notices following plaintiff's complaints to Housing Rights Center and Department of Building and Safety
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that defendant did not present evidence to refute plaintiff's retaliation claim; temporal proximity between plaintiff's complaints to housing authorities and subsequent rent increases and eviction notices supports likelihood of success on retaliation claim under FHA § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), Unruh Civil Rights Act, Disabled Persons Act, negligence, and retaliation claims under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that standards under California FEHA and federal FHA are the same; plaintiff likely to succeed on state law claims under FEHA using same discriminatory conduct analysis as FHA claims; court did not separately analyze negligence or other state tort claims but granted preliminary injunction based on likelihood of success on discrimination and retaliation theories.

key_cases_cited: Alexander v. Choate, 469 U.S. 287 (1985)
Henrietta D. v. Bloomberg, 331 F.3d 261 (2d Cir. 2003)

Taylor ex rel. Wazyluk v. Hous. Auth. of City of New Haven, 645 F.3d 152 (2d Cir. 2011)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of common use portions of dwelling to accommodate Louis's and N.V.S.'s disabilities (mental illness, stroke, seizures, and lung disease requiring monitors and ventilators)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs conflated NYCHA's role as public housing operator with its role administering Section 8 tenant-based program. The Section 8 program provides vouchers and subsidies, not housing or modifications to private dwellings. Plaintiffs' demand for modified housing would substantively alter the benefits provided by the program and does not state a cognizable claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Meaningful assistance in obtaining accessible housing for a family with disabled members participating in Section 8 tenant-based program
fha_claims.reasoning: Although HUD regulations (24 C.F.R. § 8.28(a)) may require PHAs to provide certain assistance in locating accessible housing, plaintiffs failed to allege any factual connection between their inability to find housing and their disabilities. Plaintiffs alleged only that they lacked suitable housing and that NYCHA failed to provide meaningful assistance, without alleging that obstacles to locating housing resulted from disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations under Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act in administration of Section 8 program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs raised Section 504 and Fair Housing Act claims in opposition brief, which the court declined to consider as new claims. Even if considered, they fail for the same reason as Title II claims: plaintiffs did not sufficiently plead that they were denied meaningful access to the Section 8 program because of disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations based on Louis's alleged disability (mental illness, stroke, seizures) under Title II ADA
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead that Louis suffered from a qualifying disability under the ADA. Although the complaint alleged mental illness, stroke, and seizures, it did not allege that these conditions substantially limited any major life activities or major bodily functions during the relevant time period, as required by 42 U.S.C. § 12102.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Executive Law § 296.18(2) disability discrimination; negligence and breach of contract claims related to NYCHA's failure to grant emergency transfer when Louis was sexually harassed by landlord; breach of statutory duties under Housing Act and HUD regulations; breach of 1996 Voluntary Compliance Agreement with HUD; § 1983 procedural due process claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs abandoned non-FHA claims by failing to respond to NYCHA's arguments in opposition brief. Court found no private right of action under Housing Act or HUD regulations; 1996 VCA explicitly disclaims private right of action and applies only to NYCHA-owned housing, not Section 8 administration. Negligence and breach of contract claims were inadequately pleaded and time-barred. § 1983 due process claims lacked factual support and failed to identify protected liberty or property interest. Court declined supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state-law claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege protected activity under § 3617. His complaints about failure to conduct background checks and the presence of sex offenders relate to habitability, not availability of housing, and thus do not constitute a cognizable Fair Housing Act violation under settled Fifth Circuit law. Even under a 'reasonable belief' standard, no reasonable person could believe that such habitability concerns violate the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims for eviction and termination
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only the FHA retaliation claim and grants the motion to dismiss on that claim. State law claims are mentioned but not substantively analyzed or ruled upon in this opinion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff plausibly alleged hostile housing environment sexual harassment under FHA § 3604(b) by alleging unwelcome sexual advances, grabbing of genitals, and pattern of conduct severe and pervasive enough to alter terms and conditions of tenancy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff plausibly alleged quid pro quo sexual harassment under FHA § 3604(b) by alleging that housing benefits (repairs) were implicitly conditioned on sexual favors, with pattern of delayed or failed repairs following plaintiff's rejection of sexual advances.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff plausibly alleged interference and retaliation under FHA § 3617 by alleging that defendant failed to respond to complaints about sexual harassment, continued to direct harasser to contact plaintiff, failed to make repairs after plaintiff complained, and evicted plaintiff in retaliation for withholding rent due to uninhabitable conditions caused by harassment-related repair failures.

Edison v. Douberly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sign language interpreters for Resident Lifestyle Group (RLG) activities and events held at District recreation facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that RLG activities are not services, programs, or activities of the Districts themselves because the Districts do not control the content or presentation of RLG programs, receive no income from them, and the RLGs are operated independently by private residents. The Districts' involvement is limited to facilitating facility use and ensuring compliance with facility guidelines. Therefore, the Districts cannot be held liable under the FHA for the RLGs' alleged failure to provide sign language interpreters, as the RLGs are not instrumentalities of the Districts and participation in them is not a service connected to the dwelling within the meaning of the FHA.

source_file: 7236712_2016_Lowman v. Platinum Property Management Services, Inc._gand

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of rental application based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that his rental application was rejected based on race under the prima facie framework of § 3604(a). The subsequent approval of the application does not negate the prior discriminatory denial, and Plaintiff alleged injury (forced to rent elsewhere at higher rate). Complaint survives motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Imposition of different qualification standards and criteria based on race (differing financial criteria, criminal background investigation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that Defendant imposed different qualification criteria and standards based on race, which constitutes a violation of § 3604(a) as enumerated in 24 C.F.R. § 100.60(b)(4). The regulation provides a list of discriminatory actions that give rise to a § 3604(a) violation. Complaint survives motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (racial discrimination in property rights); Georgia Fair Housing Act, O.C.G.A. § 8-3-200 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims under § 1982 and Georgia FHA are interpreted under the same prima facie standard as the Federal FHA. Because Plaintiff survived dismissal on the Federal FHA claims, the parallel state and federal statutory claims must also survive. Motion to dismiss denied as to all claims.

Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

United States v. JPI Const., L.P., 2011 WL 6963160 (N.D. Tex. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible building entrances on accessible routes; accessible public and common use portions; accessible routes into and through dwellings; reinforcements in bathroom walls for grab bars; usable kitchens and bathrooms for wheelchair users; accessible mailboxes; door widths sufficient for wheelchairs; door thresholds at appropriate heights; adequate clear floor space in kitchens and bathrooms
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether deviations from HUD Guidelines constituted FHA violations. Although defendants' experts testified all properties were accessible, the court determined the question of whether alleged barriers created a pattern or practice of discrimination was ordinarily a question of fact for the jury, precluding summary judgment for either party.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pattern or practice of resistance to full enjoyment of FHA rights; denial to a group of persons of rights granted by the FHA raising an issue of general public importance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the pattern or practice claim because genuine issues of material fact remained regarding whether the alleged accessibility barriers, even if they deviated from HUD Guidelines, constituted unlawful discrimination under the FHA, given that alternative means of achieving compliance existed and defendants presented expert testimony of accessibility.

case_name: Logan v. Matveevskii
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for transfer to a first-floor or lower-level apartment to accommodate plaintiff's heart condition and mobility difficulties (walking up and down three flights of stairs)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege constructive denial of reasonable accommodation. Although plaintiff alleged a 2.5-year delay from August 2008 email to March 2011 offer, courts require more than silence to establish constructive denial; plaintiff offered no factual basis to conclude defendants acted with discriminatory intent or bad faith in the delay, only conclusory allegations that the request was 'ignored.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to establish disparate treatment based on disability. Plaintiff provided only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support that animus against the disabled was a significant factor in defendants' actions. The complaint lacked plausible factual allegations connecting any adverse action to plaintiff's disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged racial discrimination based on defendant Matveevskii's reference to plaintiff having a 'gang' of people coming after her at a tenants meeting
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's racial discrimination claim failed under Iqbal/Twombly. A single reference to 'gang' at a meeting, even if it could have racial connotations, is insufficient to establish discriminatory animus as a significant factor. The word 'gang' has innocuous meanings and plaintiff provided no other factual support for racial animus. Remaining allegations were pure legal conclusions unsupported by facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of Architectural Barriers Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 4151-57), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, ADA Title II, HUD regulations, state law claims (negligence, breach of contract, interference with tenant rights, improper lease termination, improper rent calculations, intentional infliction of emotional distress, violations of Real Property Law and Apartment Law)
fha_claims.reasoning: ABA claim dismissed because plaintiff did not exhaust administrative remedies with the Architectural and Transportation Barriers Compliance Board (ATBCB); the ABA provides no private right of action without first presenting claims to the ATBCB. Rehabilitation Act disparate treatment claim dismissed because it requires showing defendants denied benefits 'solely' because of disability, and plaintiff failed to allege this higher standard. Remaining state law claims dismissed for lack of federal question jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent overcharge claims based on alleged miscalculation of rent, failure to allow medical deductions, and failure to provide rent calculation breakdowns
fha_claims.reasoning: Rent overcharge claims barred by res judicata doctrine. Plaintiff's rent claims arose from the same transaction or series of transactions as a prior New York State Supreme Court judgment (Index No. 50208/2014) that dismissed plaintiff's rent overcharge claim on the merits pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(1). Under New York's transactional approach to res judicata, all claims arising from the same transaction are barred even if based on different theories.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of Planned Development District (PDD) application to establish supportive housing, respite/hospital diversion housing, and mental health services for individuals with mental illness
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found plaintiff established prima facie case of intentional discrimination based on sequence of events, strong community opposition rooted in stereotypes about mental illness, City Council's failure to articulate any non-discriminatory rationale for denial, and departure from normal procedures. City failed to provide legitimate non-discriminatory reason, so discriminatory animus must have been significant factor in denial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of PDD application; plaintiff challenged ARD law as facially neutral but disproportionately impacting mentally ill individuals seeking housing
fha_claims.disposition: Preliminary Injunction Motion - Disparate Impact Claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to establish substantial likelihood of success on disparate impact claim because plaintiff provided no quantitative or qualitative evidence of disproportionate impact on mentally ill persons; plaintiff merely asserted that if it cannot use the Site, there must be disparate impact, which is insufficient at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim for discrimination in municipal zoning decisions
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same McDonnell Douglas disparate treatment framework under ADA § 12132 as applied to FHA claims; plaintiff established substantial likelihood of success on intentional discrimination theory under ADA based on same factual record and reasoning as FHA disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The County adequately alleged a disparate treatment claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3605(a) by identifying the type of discrimination (reverse redlining), the defendants, and the timeframe. The court found the allegations sufficient to state a plausible claim under Twombly/Iqbal and denied the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the FHA under binding Seventh Circuit precedent, and the County adequately alleged specific practices (discretionary pricing, credit approval decisions, appraisal practices) that had disparate impact on minority borrowers. Whether the statistics establish a prima facie case is not decided at the pleading stage.

case_name: Castellano v. Access Premier Realty, Inc.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)

Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
United States v. California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to no-pets policy to allow plaintiff to keep an emotional support cat (Mr. Munchkin) as a reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities including anxiety, depression, panic attacks, psychotic disorder, and PTSD
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element Dubois test and found all elements satisfied: (1) plaintiff has FHA-qualifying handicap (mental and physical impairments substantially limiting major life activities); (2) defendants knew or should have known of disability (multiple letters and rental application disclosed SSI benefits); (3) accommodation was necessary (uncontroverted evidence that emotional support animal alleviated anxiety, depression, and stress, which reduced symptoms of other impairments); (4) accommodation was reasonable (no fundamental alteration or undue burden; defendants had previously granted similar accommodations; cat was well-behaved and plaintiff offered pet deposit); (5) defendants refused accommodation (despite receiving adequate medical documentation, defendants issued cure-or-quit notice and termination notice, and explicitly denied the request). Court applied HUD Notice FHEO-2013-01 with deference and found defendants' concerns about fleas and safety were speculative and not based on individualized assessment of the specific animal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendants interfered with plaintiff's right to request and obtain a reasonable accommodation by issuing cure-or-quit and termination notices in response to accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, defendants violated the FHA by interfering with plaintiff's exercise of her right to obtain a reasonable accommodation. The court found that defendants' issuance of a cure-or-quit notice and termination notice in response to plaintiff's accommodation requests constituted meddling with and hampering her exercise of FHA rights. The approach taken would give a person in plaintiff's position pause in seeking to enforce her right to accommodation. Defendants did not contest these facts, and plaintiff's departure from the apartment due to fear of eviction demonstrated the chilling effect of defendants' conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Vicarious liability of property owner (Defendant Addison) for violations of § 3604(f) and § 3617 committed by her agents (APM, Akulow, Valenzuela)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Meyer v. Holley, property owners may be vicariously liable for FHA violations committed by their agents or property managers. Defendants admitted that APM, Akulow, and Valenzuela acted as agents of Defendant Addison and that Addison directly paid Valenzuela. Defendants presented no evidence suggesting vicarious liability was inappropriate and failed to respond to plaintiff's vicarious liability arguments. Court found Addison vicariously liable for the § 3604(f) and § 3617 violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Right to enjoy dwelling free from interference, coercion, intimidation, and threats based on religion and national origin; alleged pattern of police harassment, selective enforcement, and intimidation designed to force family to abandon property
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants acted with discriminatory intent to interfere with plaintiffs' FHA-protected right to enjoy their dwelling. Evidence of repeated ethnic slurs, selective enforcement, pattern of harassment over 20 years, and explicit statements that police wanted family to leave Bolingbrook supported inference that conduct was frequent and severe enough to constitute interference under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 equal protection claim; 42 U.S.C. § 1982 property rights claim; alleged discriminatory denial of police services, selective enforcement of traffic and municipal regulations, and unlawful stops and seizures based on religion and national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent and effect to survive summary judgment on equal protection and § 1982 claims. Statistical evidence of disparate traffic stops, testimony of ethnic slurs and derogatory language, pattern of selective enforcement, and evidence of pretextual explanations for police conduct supported inference that defendants acted with discriminatory purpose and that selective withdrawal of police protection violated clearly established constitutional rights.

case_name: Handy v. City of New Rochelle
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 57 F. Supp. 3d 234 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie case of discrimination (member of protected class, sought housing, was rejected, housing remained available), but defendants provided legitimate nondiscriminatory reason for termination: plaintiff violated Section 8 regulations by not living in the apartment, as supported by substantial evidence (minimal utility usage, vacant apartment conditions, address discrepancies). Plaintiff failed to demonstrate disability was real reason for termination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to remain in two-bedroom apartment or transfer to one-bedroom apartment to accommodate her mental disability (Major Depressive Disorder, Panic Disorder)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie reasonable accommodation claim because she never requested any accommodation of her disability. Although defendants knew or should have known of her disability, plaintiff did not request a one-bedroom apartment as an accommodation for her mental disability; she merely alleged she needed to move to a one-bedroom apartment after her mother's death. Without a request for accommodation, defendants could not refuse to provide one, and plaintiff incurred no liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourth Amendment unreasonable search and seizure claim; Due Process claim under Fourteenth Amendment (Goldberg v. Kelly procedural safeguards for termination of public benefits)
fha_claims.reasoning: Fourth Amendment: Plaintiff consented to search of apartment; consent was voluntary and extended to closets, drawers, and refrigerator as areas that would contain evidence of residency. Due Process: Hearing officer's determination that plaintiff did not live in apartment was supported by substantial evidence (minimal utility usage, vacant conditions, address discrepancies), and plaintiff was afforded proper Goldberg procedural safeguards including notice, pre-termination hearing, representation by counsel, and impartial decisionmaker.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Sanctions and Preliminary Injunction
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only procedural motions for sanctions and preliminary injunction related to alleged spoliation of Facebook evidence. The underlying FHA claim for disparate treatment based on familial status (refusal to show property due to plaintiff having two minor children) remains pending; the court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission for Ken Bielecki to serve as a live-in aide to assist with activities of daily living due to plaintiff's osteoarthritis and mobility limitations requiring wheelchair use.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found the accommodation reasonable and imposed no undue financial or administrative burdens, but denied summary judgment because genuine dispute exists as to when plaintiff notified VHA of the need for a live-in aide, which affects whether VHA had knowledge of the disability and accommodation need.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of 42 U.S.C. § 1437d(k) and (l) (Housing Act pretermination grievance procedures); Fourteenth Amendment due process; Americans with Disabilities Act Title II; Rehabilitation Act § 504; meaningful access claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on Housing Act § 1437d(k) and (l) claims, finding unequivocal evidence that lease was terminated in violation of statutory requirements: notice was insufficient (less than 30 days required) and no pretermination grievance procedures were afforded. Court denied summary judgment on due process and ADA/Rehabilitation Act failure-to-accommodate claims due to genuine factual disputes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Lease Section 3(A) contains language that singles out tenants with disabilities for eviction threat if they cannot live independently and cannot arrange for someone to aid them, creating discriminatory effect under ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act § 504.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found lease language in Section 3(A) ambiguous and discriminatory under 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(b)(3)(ii), as it has the effect of substantially impairing disabled persons' ability to access and maintain public housing by obfuscating their rights to live-in aides and creating fear of eviction. The ambiguity violated federal law despite no evidence of purposeful intent to mislead.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) violations: failure to provide proper disclosure of debt validation rights and demanding payment before expiration of 30-day validation window
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury resulting from alleged FDCPA violations. The court found bare procedural violations of the FDCPA's disclosure requirements, without more, do not constitute injury in fact under Spokeo v. Robins, and plaintiff never intended to dispute the debt or exercise the rights he claimed were violated.

case_name: Thurmond v. Bowman
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)

McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
United States v. Hylton, 590 Fed.Appx. 13 (2d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent apartment to plaintiff because of her familial status (two minor children)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff presented direct evidence of intentional discrimination: Toombs' admitted statement that he would not rent to her because of her two small children. This statement violated § 3604(a) by refusing to negotiate for rental and making the dwelling unavailable based on familial status. Defendants' proffered safety concerns do not excuse the discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory oral statement indicating preference against renting to families with children
fha_claims.reasoning: Toombs' statement that he would not rent to plaintiff because of her two small children plainly violates § 3604(c), which prohibits discriminatory statements indicating a preference or limitation based on familial status. Under § 3604(c), the speaker's intent is irrelevant; the statement itself, as understood by an ordinary listener, is sufficient to establish liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rezoning of 42-acre parcel from R-1-8 (8,000+ sq ft lots) to R-1-6 (6,000+ sq ft lots) to enable construction of affordable/moderately priced homes ($125,200-$159,800) rather than larger-lot, higher-priced homes ($258,000-$386,000)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs established prima facie disparate impact using HMDA data showing that denial of rezoning disproportionately priced out Hispanic homebuyers (45% Hispanic in proposed price range vs. 30% in larger-lot developments), and that city's stated justifications (neighborhood reliance on preliminary plat and buffer compromise) were not legally sufficient to overcome the disparate impact, creating genuine issues of material fact for jury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rezoning denial based on discriminatory intent evidenced by racially charged code words in neighbor opposition comments and disparate treatment compared to other rezoning approvals
fha_claims.reasoning: Ninth Circuit reversed district court's dismissal of disparate treatment claim, holding that allegations of racially charged code words in public comments, unanimous planning commission approval, and city council's three-year history of approving rezoning requests stated a plausible claim for intentional discrimination under FHA and Equal Protection; case remanded for further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection and substantive due process claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; Arizona constitutional and statutory law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted motion to dismiss all non-FHA claims (§ 1983 equal protection, substantive due process, and state law claims) for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard; Ninth Circuit did not reverse this dismissal.

case_name: Bone v. Village Club, Inc.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1218 (11th Cir. 2016)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support dog (Buttons) in a no-pet section of the mobile home community as a reasonable accommodation for anxiety and mental health disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether defendants constructively denied the accommodation through an overbroad information request, unreasonably short compliance timeline, and accelerated demand for pre-suit mediation rather than engaging in good-faith interactive process. Prior approval by board president and unexplained policy reversal supported inference of bad faith.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intimidation and threats in response to plaintiff's request for reasonable accommodation for emotional support animal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found sufficient evidence of protected activity (requesting accommodation), adverse action (January 6, 2015 letter threatening lawsuit and demanding pre-suit mediation with cost-sharing requirement), and causal nexus. January 6 letter offering choice between paying for mediation or being sued constituted intimidation/threat under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statement by board member Jim Rubert regarding criminal penalties for misrepresenting service dog status, made immediately after board voted to enforce no-pet policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact regarding whether Rubert's statement constituted intimidation under § 3617. Rubert's status as board member with enforcement authority (not mere neighbor) and temporal proximity to board's enforcement vote created arguable nexus to official action. However, ambiguity about whether statement was directed at plaintiff and when she learned of it precluded summary judgment in plaintiff's favor.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Delay or prevention of eviction and destruction of personal property, including motorized wheelchair, during hospitalization due to disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff stated plausible claim regarding preservation of wheelchair and personal property during move-out, applying reasonableness and necessity balancing test. However, court found eviction prevention itself was not a reasonable accommodation because it would prevent bedbug treatment. Claim survives as to property preservation but fails as to eviction prevention.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation under the Americans with Disabilities Act (Title II) for failure to accommodate disability during eviction and property removal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same reasonable accommodation framework as FHAA claim under 42 U.S.C. § 12132, finding plaintiff stated plausible claim under ADA Title II based on identical facts and legal standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation under the Rehabilitation Act for failure to accommodate disability during eviction and property removal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same reasonable accommodation framework as FHAA and ADA claims under 29 U.S.C. § 794(a), finding plaintiff stated plausible claim based on identical facts and legal standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due Process Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), Indiana Due Course of Law (Ind. Const. art. I, § 12), tortious conversion under Indiana law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Equal Protection claim for failure to allege discriminatory intent (required element not plausibly alleged). Court dismissed procedural due process claim because plaintiff received notice of eviction and access to grievance procedures and courts. Court dismissed Indiana Due Course of Law claim as analogous to federal due process. Court denied tortious conversion claim was dismissed in part (claim 7) but allowed in part (claim 5) based on whether anti-discrimination statutes required reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to no-pet policy to allow tenant to keep a service dog (epilepsy alert dog) in the condominium unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element Dubois test and found genuine issues of material fact on all elements: (1) MacArthur's epilepsy qualifies as a disability; (2) defendants knew or should have known of the disability through multiple disclosures and documentation; (3) the service dog was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling; (4) waiving the no-pet policy is a reasonable accommodation absent evidence of direct threat or substantial property damage; and (5) defendants' continued delay in granting approval, imposition of fines, and threats of enforcement constitute an actual or constructive denial. The court found delay as denial doctrine applicable and denied summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the three-element retaliation test under § 3617 and found genuine issues of material fact: (1) plaintiff engaged in protected activity by renting to a person with a disability and requesting accommodation; (2) plaintiff suffered adverse action through imposition of $1,450 in fines, $4,234 in attorney fees, and a $5,684 lien; and (3) causal link exists between protected activity and adverse actions, evidenced by board emails stating counterclaims serve as 'leverage in settlement negotiations' and the board's continued imposition of fines even after allowing the dog to remain. Court denied summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claim for tortious interference with contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Magistrate Judge Wantanabe granted plaintiff's Motion for Leave to Amend Complaint on May 17, 2016, which removed the state law claim from the case. Motion for summary judgment on the tortious interference with contract claim is denied as moot.

case_name: A.S. v. Been
key_cases_cited: Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. Cty. of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of Section 8 voucher transfer and termination of husband's voucher without notice or hearing opportunity; alleged discrimination on the basis of sex under Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff has a protected property interest in her husband's Section 8 voucher under VAWA and that HPD's administration of the Housing Choice Voucher Program falls within the FHA's scope of 'otherwise make unavailable' housing, allowing the disparate treatment claim to survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate impact of HPD's policies regarding Section 8 voucher termination and transfer procedures under Title VIII
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's denial of the motion to dismiss on the disparate treatment claim implicitly allows the disparate impact claim to proceed, as the court found the FHA applies to HPD's administration of the Section 8 program and plaintiff has a protected property interest.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process violation under the Fifth Amendment; disparate treatment and disparate impact under New York City Human Rights Law, N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 8-107(5); arbitrary and capricious action
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff has a sufficient property interest in her husband's Section 8 voucher under VAWA to support a due process claim, and declined to dismiss the state law claims, allowing them to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to HOA restrictive covenant prohibiting parking of large vehicles (Class C RV) in driveway; necessary for disabled resident (Khrizma) to access medical transport vehicle equipped with toilet and shower due to severe incontinence and mobility issues
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the four-part Giebeler test and found: (1) Khrizma has a disability; (2) defendants knew of it; (3) the accommodation was necessary because without the RV parked at home, Khrizma would face injury or pain accessing her medical transport vehicle, and medical evidence established nexus between disability and need for the RV; and (4) defendants refused the accommodation. On reasonableness, plaintiffs met their initial burden by showing the RV fit in the driveway without extending beyond the property line and offering a parabolic mirror to address sight-line concerns. Defendants failed to rebut with objective evidence of direct threat; the single neighbor declaration was insufficient without evidence that the mirror would not mitigate the risk. Plaintiffs entitled to summary judgment on both necessity and reasonableness.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oregon Fair Housing Act claim (Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 659.145(2)(c) & (2)(g)); negligence claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Oregon's fair housing law mirrors federal law and is interpreted identically. The court applied the same Giebeler framework to the state FHA claim and granted summary judgment on liability. The negligence claim was not separately analyzed in the opinion but was part of the overall action; the opinion focuses on the reasonable accommodation claims under federal and state fair housing law.

case_name: Metz v. Herbert
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. and Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Placement of low-income housing (LIHTC-eligible) in plaintiffs' neighborhood; plaintiffs allege disparate impact based on racial composition of neighborhood
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege an FHA disparate impact claim because they did not allege that prospective residents were being excluded from other neighborhoods based on race, nor did they allege facts showing that race was the motivating factor in placement decisions. The complaint contains only vague, conclusory assertions without specific factual allegations about differential treatment of similarly situated neighborhoods or statistical evidence of causal connection required under Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1982 (right to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real property); Section 1981 (right to make and enforce contracts); Title VI (access to federally funded programs); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process and equal protection claims; Tennessee Human Rights Act; Tennessee Constitution due process and equal protection; local zoning ordinances and regulations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim under Section 1982 because they did not allege denial of access to real property but only economic injury to property values from adjacent development. Section 1982 protects access to housing, not economic interests in property value. Procedural due process claim failed because plaintiffs did not allege they were denied notice or opportunity to be heard regarding protected property rights, and they lack a protected property interest in the zoning of adjacent land. Substantive due process claim failed because plaintiffs challenged zoning of adjacent property, not their own property, and cited no authority for such a claim. Equal protection claim failed because plaintiffs did not allege that similarly situated neighborhoods were treated differently. State law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction and for the same reasons federal claims failed.

case_name: Smith v. Avanti
key_cases_cited: Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, 490 U.S. 228 (1989)
Etsitty v. Utah Transit Auth., 502 F.3d 1215 (10th Cir. 2007)
Smith v. City of Salem, 378 F.3d 566 (6th Cir. 2004)
Morgan v. Sec'y of Hous. & Urban Dev., 985 F.2d 1451 (10th Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant refused to rent properties to the Smiths based on sex stereotypes concerning whom a woman should marry, be attracted to, and have children with. Under Price Waterhouse, discrimination based on failure to conform to gender stereotypes constitutes discrimination 'because of sex' under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) and (c). Undisputed material facts establish Defendant's discriminatory intent through her emails referencing the Smiths' 'unique relationship' and 'uniqueness.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant refused to rent to the Smith Family because they had minor children, explicitly stating preference for tenants without children. This violates 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) and (c) prohibitions on discrimination based on familial status. Undisputed facts show Defendant's written refusal was based on the family's status as parents with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act § 24-34-502(1)(a), discrimination based on sex stereotypes is unlawful. Federal FHA case law interpreting sex discrimination is persuasive in interpreting the CADA. Defendant's refusal to rent and her written statements concerning the Smiths' 'uniqueness' constitute unlawful sex discrimination under the CADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act § 24-34-301(7), 'sexual orientation' includes transgender status. Defendant's refusal to rent and written statements referencing the Smiths' 'uniqueness' and her mention of a 'transvestite' friend demonstrate discrimination based on Rachel's transgender status and the Smiths' sexual orientation, violating the CADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act § 24-34-501(1.6), familial status includes minor children domiciled with parents. Defendant refused to rent to the Smith Family because they had minor children, explicitly preferring tenants without children and noise, violating the CADA's familial status protection.

case_name: Lloyd v. Presby's Inspired Life
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condominium Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Castillo v. Condo. Ass'n v. United States HUD, 821 F.3d 92 (1st Cir. 2016)
Taylor v. Harbour Pointe Homeowners Ass'n, 690 F.3d 44 (2d Cir. 2012)
Joint Statement of HUD & Dept. of Justice, Reasonable Accommodations under the Fair Housing Act (May 17, 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from efficiency apartment to one-bedroom, handicapped-accessible apartment to accommodate plaintiff's permanent physical disability affecting mobility (difficulty rising from sitting position, ambulating, unsteady on feet, susceptible to falling)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact regarding whether plaintiff made a proper request for accommodation and whether the accommodation was necessary and reasonable. Defendants failed to establish absence of disputed fact by providing no evidence they requested medical verification from plaintiff or that plaintiff failed to provide it when requested. Court applied three-factor burden-shifting test and found plaintiff's allegations sufficient to survive summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on religion (Jehovah's Witness): (1) prohibition on hosting religious meetings in public spaces while permitting other religious groups to do so; (2) requirement to attend mandatory political meetings contrary to religious beliefs; (3) preferential housing treatment for non-Jehovah's Witnesses; (4) prohibition on leaving religious materials in lobby while allowing other tenants to do so
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on religious discrimination claims based on events prior to March 8, 2011 (statute of limitations bar under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) with tolling). Court denied summary judgment on claims relating to events on or after March 8, 2011, finding defendants failed to meet burden of showing no genuine issue of material fact regarding whether non-Jehovah's Witnesses were permitted to hold religious meetings, received preferential housing treatment, or were exempt from political meeting requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing discrimination complaints with HUD (August 2012, March 2013) and PHRC (August 2012): (1) vandalism and property damage to apartment (breaking water heater and faucet, spreading chemicals, garbage, and feces, contaminating food, attempted poisoning); (2) interception and theft of mail and medication; (3) sabotage of HUD recertification application causing loss of housing subsidy and eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied three-part retaliation test (protected activity, adverse action, causal link). Court granted summary judgment on retaliation claim based on HUD recertification paperwork failure, finding 14-month gap between protected activity (August 2012/March 2013) and alleged adverse action (May 2014) insufficient to create inference of causation without additional evidence, and no other evidence in record created causal link. Court denied summary judgment on vandalism retaliation claim, finding genuine issue of material fact regarding whether alleged vandalism increased in intensity and changed character after protected activity, which could support 'markedly different' treatment inference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No non-FHA claims identified in this opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: No non-FHA claims were raised or addressed in this opinion. All claims were brought under the Fair Housing Act.

source_file: 7243422_2017_de Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. Partnership_vaed
case_name: de Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. Partnership
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Pinchback v. Armistead Homes Corp., 907 F.2d 1447 (4th Cir. 1990)
Miles v. Dell, Inc., 429 F.3d 480 (4th Cir. 2005)
Martin v. Brondum, 535 Fed.Appx. 242 (4th Cir. 2013)
Keller v. City of Fremont, 853 F Supp.2d 959 (D. Neb. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of race or national origin discrimination under the McDonnell Douglas framework. The Policy requiring proof of lawful presence applied uniformly to all residents regardless of race or national origin. The disparate impact on Latino residents was incidental to the Policy's legitimate focus on illegal immigration status, not race or national origin, as established by Espinoza v. Farah Manufacturing Co.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1981 claim alleging discrimination on the basis of alienage and non-citizenship fails because the Policy is facially neutral, applies to all applicants, and permits discrimination based on unlawful immigration status. The burden on female plaintiffs resulted from their illegal presence, not from their non-citizen status as such. § 1981 does not prohibit discrimination based on unlawful presence in the United States.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Virginia Fair Housing Law (VFHL), Va. Code § 36-96.3 et seq.; Virginia Manufactured Home Lot Rental Act, Va. Code § 55-248.41 et seq.; breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Genuine disputes of material fact preclude summary judgment on the Virginia Rental Act and breach of contract claims. Factual disputes exist regarding whether defendants were entitled to terminate leases immediately without 60 days' notice under Va. Code § 55-248.31 (threat to health or safety), whether defendants waived their right to terminate by accepting rent with knowledge of non-compliance, and whether plaintiffs committed fraud. These claims proceed to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) claims for false, deceptive, or misleading representations in debt collection letters (15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e(2)(A), 1692e(5), 1692e(10), and 1692f)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied Midland's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Article III standing (12(b)(1)) and motion for judgment on the pleadings (12(c)). The court held that Haddad alleged a concrete injury sufficient for standing by alleging receipt of misleading debt collection letters in violation of the FDCPA's prohibition on false, deceptive, or misleading representations. The court found that Haddad stated plausible claims under § 1692e(2)(A) (false representation of debt character/amount), § 1692e(5) (threat of action not intended to be taken), and § 1692e(10) (false representation to collect debt), and that Midland Funding could be held vicariously liable for MCM's conduct as its agent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on disability-based harassment and abuse by staff at residential facility
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to dismiss FHA claim for hostile housing environment under § 3604(f)(2), finding that the statute reaches post-acquisition discrimination in the provision of services and that plaintiffs adequately alleged sufficiently pervasive and severe harassment based on disability. Court applied Title VII hostile environment standard adapted to housing context.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 (Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment excessive force, deliberate indifference, abuse and neglect); § 504 Rehabilitation Act; Title II ADA; New York State Human Rights Law; New York City Human Rights Law; state tort claims (assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motions to dismiss on § 1983 excessive force claims (Staff Defendants adequately alleged unprovoked violence against persons with disabilities; Supervisor Defendants and higher-level officials adequately alleged deliberate indifference through failure to respond to reports of abuse), state tort claims (assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence), and federal disability statutes (§ 504 and Title II ADA for injunctive relief; § 504 for damages against White and Minter-Brooks in official capacity). fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep Kyla, an emotional support animal/service dog, in the condominium unit to assist Bruno Jr. with PTSD-related panic attacks
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged undue delay in the Board's response to the accommodation request (October 2015 through January 2016 with no response, followed by demands for documentation with impossibly short deadlines), satisfying the prima facie elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The Board's failure to engage in the interactive process and its evasion of requests for dialogue constitute plausible allegations of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for exercising FHA rights by requesting reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court did not separately analyze the § 3617 interference/retaliation claim but noted in footnote 10 that defendants failed to separately address its elements. The claim survives the motion to dismiss as part of Count II, though the court's analysis focused primarily on the reasonable accommodation theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Massachusetts Chapter 151B state law discrimination claim; claims against Attorney Gaines and Law Firm under various theories including conspiracy
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against Attorney Gaines and the Law Firm were dismissed under the Massachusetts litigation privilege because the attorney's communications were made in his capacity as counsel for the Board in connection with potential litigation. The privilege applies absolutely to statements made by attorneys in their professional function, even if made maliciously or in bad faith. Chapter 151B claims against the Board survive but exhaustion of administrative remedies is an affirmative defense not appropriate for motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the Life Safety Code's limitation on the maximum number of unrelated persons who can reside together as a family; interpretation of 'family' to include Oxford House residents and treatment of the property as a single-family dwelling rather than a lodging or rooming house
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-element reasonable accommodation test and found that: (1) residents are disabled (substance use disorder substantially limiting major life activities); (2) accommodation was requested and refused; (3) accommodation is reasonable because it does not undermine the basic purpose of the Life Safety Code—residents exhibit hierarchical social structures and familial bonds comparable to traditional families, creating equivalent fire safety; and (4) accommodation is necessary because at least six unrelated individuals must reside together for the Oxford House model to achieve its empirically proven ameliorative effects, and without the accommodation residents would be forced to vacate due to prohibitive costs of fire safety upgrades.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Rehabilitation Act (RA) reasonable accommodation claims; analysis treated identically to FHA claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that reasonable accommodation claims under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act are analyzed identically to FHA claims. The court rejected defendant's arguments that: (1) the sole-causation standard of the Rehabilitation Act applies to reasonable accommodation claims (it does not—causation is irrelevant to RA accommodation claims); and (2) the federal funding must be connected to the specific program at issue (the Civil Rights Restoration Act overturned this requirement, making the entire agency subject to RA obligations when any part receives federal funding). Plaintiffs prevailed on the same four-element test applied to the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence of intentional racial discrimination through statements by property manager Brittany Allen and affidavit testimony from employee Khelsi Harvest showing discriminatory motive. Genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether defendants' stated non-discriminatory reasons for the rules were pretext for racial discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found all five disputed rules (Adult Supervision, Curfew, Playground, Pool, and Gym rules) are facially discriminatory on the basis of familial status. Genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether defendants justified the disparate treatment by showing the restrictions benefit the protected class or respond to legitimate safety concerns rather than stereotypes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination claim under § 3604(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment because plaintiffs failed to cite any evidence that defendants discriminated against them because of a disability and did not address their disability-based claims in briefing. Plaintiffs did not direct the court to evidence satisfying the elements of a disability discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact on African-American residents based on enforcement of five rules
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient statistical evidence demonstrating proportional disparate effect on African-Americans as a group. General comparisons and anecdotal evidence without proportional numbers or statistics do not meet the Eleventh Circuit standard for disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact on disabled persons based on enforcement of five rules
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment because plaintiffs did not address this argument in briefing and did not direct the court to any evidence of disparate impact on disabled persons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact on families with children based on enforcement of five rules
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs failed to demonstrate proportional disparate effect on tenants with children compared to tenants without children. Evidence showed only that a few tenants with families were adversely affected, which is insufficient to establish disparate impact under Eleventh Circuit precedent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation through threats, harassment, and fines for complaining about rules and attempting to enjoy complex facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs presented sufficient evidence to establish prima facie case of retaliation under § 3617. Affidavit testimony regarding threats and harassment, combined with evidence of racially discriminatory motive, allows reasonable fact-finder to conclude defendants promulgated and enforced rules in response to plaintiffs' enjoyment of facilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Steering of African-American residents to back of complex while steering white residents to front
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on steering claim because plaintiffs did not direct the court to any evidence of steering practices and did not address this issue in briefing. Court declined to search the record and make plaintiffs' arguments for them.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alabama Fair Housing Law (ALFHL) claims for racial discrimination, familial status discrimination, disparate impact on race/disability/familial status, and retaliation; Alabama common law claims for negligent hiring/supervision/training, breach of contract, breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment, and negligence per se
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same legal analysis to ALFHL claims as FHA claims. Court granted summary judgment on ALFHL disability discrimination and disparate impact claims (race, disability, familial status) for same reasons as FHA claims. Court denied summary judgment on ALFHL racial discrimination, familial status discrimination, and retaliation claims. Court granted summary judgment on negligent hiring/supervision/training because plaintiffs failed to direct court to evidence of defendants' knowledge of employee incompetency. Court denied summary judgment on breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment, finding genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants' actions materially interfered with plaintiffs' use and enjoyment of premises. Court denied summary judgment on compensatory and punitive damages claims.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Mr. Andrews's conduct was sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter terms and conditions of tenancy, and whether DJ Mortgage is vicariously liable. Sexual assault combined with repeated sexual advances, requests for nude photos, and contemporaneous repair requests created triable issues for jury on hostile environment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Quid pro quo sexual harassment claim based on conditioning repairs and housing benefits on sexual favors
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence that Mr. Andrews explicitly requested nude photos in exchange for repairs and delayed or refused repairs after plaintiff rebuffed sexual advances. Temporal proximity between sexual advances and repair requests, combined with pattern of delayed/denied repairs, created triable question whether repairs were conditioned on sexual favors.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unlawful interference with FHA rights by failing to make repairs and evicting plaintiff in retaliation for filing sexual harassment complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent and interference for period October 21–December 2013 (close timing of Notice to Pay or Quit after complaint, contradictory December 11 agreement followed by December 19 notice), creating triable issue. However, court found insufficient evidence of discrimination for April 2014 eviction based on multiple months of unpaid rent, as plaintiff had alternative remedies under Georgia law and passage of time attenuated inference of retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Georgia negligence doctrine claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court did not reach merits of state negligence claim, instead ordering mediation and administratively closing case pending resolution of FHA claims. Court indicated it would decline supplemental jurisdiction over negligence claim if FHA claims were dismissed, but did not dismiss the claim at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that Habitat consider his food stamps and monthly familial support (from his father) as income to meet Habitat's minimum gross annual income requirement of $10,170. Plaintiff also requested that Habitat accept a notarized letter from his father as proof of familial support, rather than requiring a trust or annuity.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Eleventh Circuit's framework requiring that accommodations address needs created by the disability itself, not financial conditions unrelated to disability. The court held that Schaw's requested accommodations addressed his financial condition, not his quadriplegia, and would have given him a better (not equal) opportunity than non-disabled applicants. Alternatively, the court found Habitat provided a reasonable accommodation by offering to accept an annuity as proof of familial support, and was not required to provide Schaw's preferred alternative of accepting only a notarized letter.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Habitat's minimum gross annual income requirement of $10,170 for a family of one, applied equally to all applicants regardless of disability status.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Schaw failed to present sufficient comparative evidence of disparate impact on SSDI recipients. Schaw provided only bare statistics about average SSDI amounts in Florida without showing how Habitat's policy affected SSDI recipients differently than non-disabled applicants. Habitat presented evidence that at least eight SSDI recipients had been approved for housing since 2013, and Schaw conceded that some disabled SSDI recipients do qualify, undermining any inference of causation.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that the complaint states a plausible claim for failure to accommodate under the FHA. Court also rejected the direct threat defense as premature at the pleading stage, finding allegations of post-conviction treatment and stabilization sufficient to survive dismissal.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Iqbal/Twombly standard to non-FHA claims. Plaintiff was offered two reasonable options and chose to wait for the three-bedroom unit. No reasonable juror could find Plaintiff was denied a reasonable accommodation in the form of a transfer.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of wheelchair ramp, grab bars in bathroom, and tub transfer bench at Plaintiff's current residence
fha_claims.reasoning: Under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(A), a tenant must personally fund reasonable modifications. Plaintiff never offered to pay for the modifications and was not capable of paying. However, under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Defendant may have been obligated to fund modifications. Defendant immediately responded to Plaintiff's January 25, 2016 request, obtained three contractor quotes, secured HUD funding approval, and within six weeks offered Plaintiff two viable options: structural modification of her current unit or transfer to an accessible three-bedroom unit. Plaintiff elected to wait for the three-bedroom unit. No reasonable juror could conclude Plaintiff was denied a reasonable modification.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constructive denial of reasonable accommodation/modification through unreasonable delay
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff argued she was constructively denied accommodation through unreasonable delay. The Fourth Circuit recognizes constructive denial when a defendant delays responding to an accommodation request. Here, Defendant immediately began investigation on January 25, 2016, stayed in contact with Plaintiff weekly and almost daily, obtained three contractor quotes, consulted with HUD and Virginia Fair Housing Office, and by March 7, 2016 (within six weeks) had finalized two reasonable options. The delay was not indeterminate; it was driven by legitimate need to investigate Plaintiff's medical condition, obtain funding approvals, and secure contractor estimates. No reasonable juror could find constructive denial based on the temporal analysis and absence of evidence of discriminatory animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to provide reasonable modifications/accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff also brought a claim under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which applies to programs receiving federal funding. The Rehabilitation Act has a stricter causation standard, requiring plaintiff to demonstrate that exclusion from benefits resulted solely by reason of disability. Defendant acknowledged potential obligation under Section 504 to fund structural modifications. However, applying the same factual analysis as the FHA claim, Defendant did not deny Plaintiff a reasonable modification; rather, Defendant offered two reasonable options within six weeks, and Plaintiff chose the option with the longer timeline. Summary judgment is warranted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act (FCA), New Mexico Medicaid False Claims Act (MFCA), New Mexico Fraud Against Taxpayers Act (FATA), ADA Title I, Title VII, NMHRA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on FCA, MFCA, and FATA claims against Family Smiles, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Dr. Shafer knowingly submitted false claims and whether Family Smiles is vicariously liable. Court also denied summary judgment on reverse false claims, finding questions of fact regarding whether Family Smiles received overpayments and failed to exercise reasonable diligence in identifying and reporting them.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to bring Boscoe, a service dog in training, to the dental clinic to assist with his Generalized Anxiety Disorder and PTSD. The dog was trained to detect panic attacks and provide cues to alert Plaintiff. Plaintiff proposed housing the dog in an office where he could see it; Defendants proposed a cage in a back office.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Boscoe was a service animal (despite being in training, evidence showed he was trained to perform tasks for Plaintiff's disability), whether the accommodation was reasonable, whether it imposed undue hardship, and whether Defendants engaged in the interactive process in good faith. Court found that Khurram Hussain refused to consider documentation and closed off discussion of accommodations, suggesting bad faith.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination based on disability (Generalized Anxiety Disorder and PTSD)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that timing of termination very shortly after disclosure of disability, combined with evidence of pretext (Defendants' stated reasons contradicted by company policy and evidence), created genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Plaintiff was fired because of his disability under the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation for disability under ADA, Title VII, and NMHRA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiff engaged in protected opposition to discrimination by requesting accommodation for his disability and complaining about sexual harassment. Temporal proximity between protected activity and termination (within days) created inference of causation. Genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether termination was in retaliation for protected conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination based on sexual orientation (sex discrimination under Title VII and NMHRA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiff established prima facie case of sex discrimination based on sexual orientation. Defendants' stated reasons (refusal to stop bringing dog, unprofessional behavior) were pretextual: Family Smiles had a policy permitting service dogs, Defendants acted contrary to that policy, and evidence of patient/staff complaints was created after termination. Temporal proximity to disclosure of sexual orientation supported inference of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for reporting fraudulent billing practices (FCA, MFCA, FATA whistleblower protection)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiff took action in furtherance of FCA enforcement by reporting fraudulent billing practices to managers, using words 'fraud' and 'illegal,' and requesting audit. Temporal proximity between protected activity (reports made within days of termination) and adverse action created inference of causation. Genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Khurram Hussain knew of protected activity and whether it motivated the termination.

case_name: Tejada v. Littlecity Realty LLC
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly, finding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional discrimination based on race, color, and national origin through a pattern of discriminatory practices including requiring only Latino tenants to disclose immigration status, filing frivolous evictions against them, and engaging in harassment to displace them.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York City Human Rights Law § 8-107(5) (discrimination based on perceived national origin, alienage, citizenship status); New York City Housing Maintenance Code § 27-2004(a)(48) (harassment); New York Rent Stabilization Law § 26-516(a)(2) (overcharges in rent-stabilized apartments)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to dismiss state and local law claims, finding supplemental jurisdiction appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 because the federal and state claims derive from a common nucleus of operative fact (the alleged discriminatory scheme to displace Latino tenants and deregulate apartments). Court also found continuing violations doctrine applicable to extend statute of limitations for all claims through 2017, and found fraud adequately pled for rent stabilization overcharge claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exclusion of dementia care homes from permitted-as-of-right residential zoning; requirement that such facilities undergo local municipal land use review rather than being automatically permitted in residential districts
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff stated a plausible claim of facial discrimination under the FHA by alleging that the 2015 Act applies different rules to persons with dementia (requiring local zoning approval) than to other persons with head injuries (permitted as of right). The court applied the burden-shifting framework for disparate treatment and found the complaint adequately alleged discriminatory effect, denying the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim alleging discrimination in housing based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that ADA and FHA claims overlapped and applied FHA analysis, finding the standards similar. The ADA claim survives the motion to dismiss on the same factual basis as the FHA claim.

case_name: Sanders v. SWS Hilltop, LLC
key_cases_cited: Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

McGinest v. GTE Service Corp., 360 F.3d 1103 (9th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found direct evidence of discriminatory intent: defendants explicitly stated they would impose conditions (inflated deposit, refusal to replace carpet) because Jo Sanders owned a service animal. Defendants' conduct of imposing more burdensome application procedures and delaying tactics violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1). Even viewing evidence in light most favorable to defendants, no rational trier of fact could find defendants' actions were motivated by anything other than discriminatory intent based on disability.

key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
