fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unit mix composition (number of one-, two-, three-, four-, and six-bedroom units) in replacement public housing units
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1) on ripeness grounds. The alleged discriminatory unit mix was not final—it was merely a 'possible' mix in a July 2014 letter that was not incorporated into the Zoning Commission's Order. The unit mix will be determined in future second-stage PUD applications subject to Zoning Commission approval, making the claim premature and unfit for judicial review.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unit mix composition (number of one-, two-, three-, four-, and six-bedroom units) in replacement public housing units under D.C. Human Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Same ripeness analysis as Count I. The court lacked supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claim after dismissing the federal FHA claim, and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) based on judicial economy and comity considerations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constructive demolition claim under United States Housing Act (USHA), 42 U.S.C. § 1437p and 24 C.F.R. § 970.25; also alleged under D.C. Human Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 1437p(a)(1)(A) and (a)(3) do not confer a federal right enforceable through Section 1983 under the Blessing/Gonzaga framework. The relevant subsections lack 'right-creating language' focused on the benefitted class, are directed at the HUD Secretary rather than public housing residents, and Congress removed the post-Edwards clarifying language in the 1998 amendments without including alternative rights-creating language.

key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged that PEC employee stated PEC 'does not care to have folks of Islamic religion' in their programs and that Plaintiff was denied lease signing on ribbon-cutting day while other tenants were permitted to sign. The alleged discriminatory statement is 'so revealing of discriminatory animus' as to survive the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, Plaintiff alleged harassment through continual lease infractions and denial of community room use based on discriminatory animus. Liberally construing pro se allegations and accepting them as true, Plaintiff alleged harassment 'sufficiently severe or pervasive as to create a hostile environment,' satisfying the four-element test for interference claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 3631 (criminal statute prohibiting use of force or threat of force); 18 U.S.C. § 112 (criminal statute protecting internationally protected persons); 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq. (ADA Title II and Title III)
fha_claims.reasoning: 42 U.S.C. § 3631 does not create a private right of action; 18 U.S.C. § 112 does not provide a private right of action and Plaintiff alleged no facts showing he is an 'internationally protected person'; ADA Title II and Title III do not apply because Plaintiff did not allege Defendants are a public entity or place of public accommodation (apartments and condominiums are not public accommodations under Title III).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Wells Fargo's Product Validation Process and practice of allowing lender credits on FHA loans caused disparate impact on minority borrowers by steering them into higher-cost loans.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of disparate impact because: (1) only two loans alleged to be higher-cost, insufficient to show statistically-imbalanced lending patterns; (2) no evidence of robust causality linking neutral policies to statistical disparity; (3) struck plaintiff's key expert declaration as unreliable; (4) plaintiff failed to identify facially-neutral policy causing the disparity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Wells Fargo issued loans to minority borrowers at higher rates than similarly-situated non-minority borrowers (two matched pairs: HC6 vs. NHW8, and HC2 vs. NHW8).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case because the loan comparators were not 'nearly identical' as required by Boykin: minority borrowers received substantially different lender credits ($1,878 and $8,000) compared to non-minority borrower ($479), originated at different times, and received different promotional discounts. Even if prima facie case could be made, defendant established legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons (lender credits, promotional pricing, origination timing) and plaintiff presented no evidence that these reasons were pretextual for discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act challenge to HUD's withdrawal of the LG2017 Assessment Tool and reversion to the Analysis of Impediments process; claims that withdrawal violated notice-and-comment requirements and was arbitrary and capricious
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked Article III organizational standing because they failed to establish a cognizable injury in fact. Although HUD's withdrawal of the LG2017 Tool suspended certain AFH procedures, key portions of the AFFH Rule remained active (definitions, community participation requirements, recordkeeping, certification), and plaintiffs' mission-driven activities were not perceptibly impaired. Plaintiffs also failed to show they diverted resources beyond normal operational costs, and any redressability was too speculative because it depended on third-party (local government) conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide adequate repairs and maintenance services (heating, water, plumbing, doors, fixtures) in violation of FHA § 3604(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs established prima facie case of race-based discrimination in provision of repairs and maintenance services. Material issues of fact remain regarding defendants' intent and whether alleged disparate treatment was motivated by race. Summary judgment denied; case proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to lease vacant apartments to plaintiffs based on race (FHA § 3604(d) and 42 U.S.C. § 1982)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie case under McDonnell Douglas framework. Plaintiffs never sought to rent vacant apartments and were denied; Oyola's 2011-2012 inquiry was outside statute of limitations. Futile gesture doctrine does not apply because plaintiffs lacked direct contact with defendants regarding leasing policies and were not reliably informed of discriminatory rental practices.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYHRL § 296(5) and NYCHRL § 8-107(5)(a) claims for race-based discrimination in repairs and maintenance; 42 U.S.C. § 1982 claim for race-based discrimination in leasing
fha_claims.reasoning: NYHRL and NYCHRL repair claims analyzed under same standard as FHA § 3604(b) and survive summary judgment on same basis. § 1982 leasing claim dismissed on same grounds as FHA § 3604(d) claim—failure to establish prima facie case.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Thelma Martinez, Blanca's sister and primary caretaker, to live in Blanca's Section 8 apartment to provide full-time care and assistance with activities of daily living (cooking, eating, using restroom, dressing). Blanca is intellectually and developmentally disabled with Cerebral Palsy and cannot live alone.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element reasonable accommodation test and found no genuine dispute of material fact: (1) Blanca is disabled within the FHA definition; (2) defendants knew of her disability; (3) the accommodation is necessary because Blanca cannot live alone and has no other willing/able caretakers; (4) the accommodation is reasonable because the cost to defendants is modest (same Section 8 rent regardless of occupancy), Thelma has demonstrated ability to pay rent, and the burden on defendants does not outweigh Blanca's critical need for full-time care; and (5) defendants refused the accommodation. The court rejected defendants' reliance on neutral screening policies (credit/rental history), holding that FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B) expressly requires deviations from neutral rules when necessary and reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act § 504 (29 U.S.C. § 794), New York State Human Rights Law (N.Y. Exec. Law. § 296 et seq.), New York City Human Rights Law (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 8-107(5))
fha_claims.reasoning: Court analyzed Rehabilitation Act and state/local human rights law claims under the same reasonable accommodation framework as the FHA, finding that the standards are nearly identical. The court noted that NYCHRL claims must be analyzed separately and independently but that defendants' conduct violates all applicable statutes. The court applied the same balancing analysis and reached the same conclusion: defendants must permit Thelma to live in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claim for damages under New York Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law (RPAPL) § 1951(2) for monetary value of restrictive covenant deemed unenforceable due to FHA violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The Sisters' counterclaim under RPAPL § 1951(2) is preempted by the FHA because allowing state law compensation to an FHA violator would undermine Congress's regulatory and deterrent purposes. The FHA's broad, results-oriented language and legislative focus on housing availability preclude state law claims that would compensate violators or make housing less available to protected persons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that Emigrant intentionally discriminated by offering STAR NINA loans that were grossly unfavorable and intentionally targeted certain communities based in part on race, color, or national origin. The court upheld the jury's verdict against Emigrant's post-trial motion for judgment as a matter of law, finding sufficient evidence of targeting through advertising, broker recruitment, and loan product design.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that Emigrant's practice of making STAR NINA loans had a discriminatory effect on African-American and Hispanic borrowers. The court rejected Emigrant's argument that the instruction relieved plaintiffs of their burden to show causality, finding that the instruction properly required plaintiffs to establish that the STAR NINA loan product itself (not mere economic disparities) caused the adverse impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691 et seq.), New York City Human Rights Law, Truth in Lending Act (15 U.S.C. § 1601 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found violations of ECOA and NYCHRL on the same intentional discrimination and disparate impact theories as the FHA claims. The TILA claim (Edith Saint-Jean only) survived motion to dismiss and was strengthened by trial evidence showing the 18% default interest rate was not unanticipated. Court granted new trial on damages for all claims due to inability to determine how jury calculated awards across different types of losses (equity loss, home ownership loss, emotional distress).

case_name: Heine v. Comm'r of the Dep't of Cmty. Affairs of State

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that the DCA's regulation of the Property as a rooming house and enforcement of fire safety and health code violations discriminated against occupants based on familial status (unrelated individuals and non-traditional family configurations).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of FHA discrimination. The regulations at issue were facially neutral health and safety requirements (fire codes, smoke detectors, egress requirements) that did not target families with children and applied equally to all occupants regardless of family status. The court found no evidence that the enforcement disproportionately impacted families with children, the only protected class under FHA's familial status provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims for constitutional violations (due process, property rights, equal protection) related to the closure of the Property and enforcement of rooming house regulations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish personal involvement of the Commissioner in the alleged constitutional violations. The Property was closed by the City of Garfield based on imminent fire and safety hazards, not by the DCA. The court found no evidence that the DCA or Commissioner, through policy or direct action, caused the closure or eviction. Additionally, the § 1983 claims were vague, failed to specify which constitutional provisions were violated, and were not tied to any occupant's family status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that Villa de Paz's published notices requiring supervision of minor children at all times constitute facial discrimination under FHA § 3604(c) as a matter of law, following precedent in Iniestra, Pack, and related cases. Plaintiffs need not show injury to establish the violation; the discriminatory nature of the policy itself is sufficient.

case_name: Phyllis Davis v. Echo Valley Condominium Association
key_cases_cited: Matarese v. Archstone Pentagon City, 808 F.3d 961 (4th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Smoking ban throughout the entire Echo Valley condominium complex, including private residential units, to prevent secondhand smoke infiltration into plaintiff's unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-part reasonable accommodation test (equal opportunity, necessity, reasonableness) and found that plaintiff failed to establish the accommodation was necessary because she offered only conclusory medical opinion without expert testimony showing the smoking ban would ameliorate her disability specifically (not just general burden shared by all exposed to smoke). More critically, the court found the accommodation unreasonable as a matter of law because it would require the HOA to impose a use restriction on co-owners' lawful activity in their own homes without the two-thirds consent required by Michigan law, which the co-owners had already rejected in a vote. The court balanced the burden on defendants (violation of state law and co-owner rights) against the benefit to plaintiff and found the accommodation imposed a fundamental alteration and undue burden.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Michigan Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (PWDCRA) claim; private nuisance claim under Michigan common law; breach of contract claim under condominium bylaws
fha_claims.reasoning: The PWDCRA claim was analyzed under the same reasonable accommodation framework as the FHAA and failed for identical reasons. The private nuisance claim failed because the remaining defendants (HOA and property manager) lacked control over the smoking conduct; under Michigan law, a landlord cannot be held liable for a nuisance created by a tenant, and a condominium association cannot be liable for lawful conduct by co-owners within their own units absent a bylaw violation. The breach of contract claim failed because plaintiff offered no evidence that smoking increases insurance rates, that units were not maintained in safe/clean/sanitary condition, or that smoking constitutes an 'annoyance or nuisance' under the bylaws absent a controlling rule or statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) challenge to asylum eligibility rule; no FHA claim present. Plaintiffs challenge the validity of a Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security interim final rule that categorically bars asylum eligibility for aliens who enter the United States outside designated ports of entry in violation of a presidential proclamation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the Immigration Organizations likely to succeed on the merits of their APA claim that the Rule violates 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1) by creating a categorical bar to asylum eligibility based on manner of entry, which Congress explicitly stated should not disqualify an alien from applying for asylum. The court also found serious questions going to the merits regarding the Rule's compliance with APA notice-and-comment requirements and granted a temporary restraining order pending preliminary injunction hearing.

source_file: 7251500_2019_Walsh v. Friendship Vill. of S. Cnty._moed
case_name: Walsh v. Friendship Village of S. Cnty.

Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, 490 U.S. 228 (1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs' claim of sex discrimination based on the 'but-for' sex argument (that if Ms. Walsh had been a man married to Ms. Nance, they would not have been denied housing) fails because the claim is fundamentally based on sexual orientation, which is not a protected class under the FHA under Eighth Circuit precedent. The court found the allegations boil down to discrimination based on sexual orientation rather than sex alone.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected plaintiffs' associational discrimination theory (that they were treated less favorably because of association with a same-sex spouse) because sexual orientation is an unprotected class under the FHA, and plaintiffs presented no evidence that associational discrimination claims are actionable with respect to unprotected classes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs' sex-stereotyping claim fails because the alleged gender non-conforming behavior is based solely on sexual orientation. The court found that sexual orientation alone cannot be the basis for an actionable sex-stereotyping claim under the FHA, as this would impermissibly bootstrap protection for sexual orientation into the statute contrary to binding Eighth Circuit precedent.

source_file: 7252515_2019_Greater New Orleans Fair Hous. Action Ctr. v. Kelly_laed
case_name: Greater New Orleans Fair Housing Action Center v. Kelly
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Quigley v. Winter
OCA-Greater Houston v. Texas

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent and making housing unavailable based on sex; differential treatment of male and female testers regarding availability of rental units
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a disparate treatment claim under § 3604(a) by alleging a pattern of treating male and female testers differently with respect to unit availability, responsiveness to inquiries, and appointment confirmations. The pattern of differential treatment moves allegations from speculative to plausible under Iqbal/Twombly, particularly when viewed alongside other allegations of Kelly's preference for renting to women.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, and privileges of rental; different application requirements (credit check waived for female tester but required for male tester)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a § 3604(b) claim by alleging Kelly placed different conditions on application materials for male and female testers seeking the same rental unit. The allegation that Kelly told female tester #4 he would forego her credit check because she was a 'grown woman' isolates sex as a factor in his decision, satisfying the plausibility standard when viewed in context of other allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual harassment creating hostile housing environment; unwanted touching, sexually suggestive comments, and repeated unauthorized entry into tenant's apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a hostile housing environment claim under § 3604(b) by alleging Kelly's harassment of tenant B.C. was sufficiently severe and pervasive to alter conditions of her housing arrangement. Allegations of unwanted touching, sexually suggestive comments, and repeated unauthorized apartment entry—viewed in context of similar harassment of other female tenants—satisfy the plausibility standard for hostile environment discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oral statements indicating preference for renting to women; statements made during lease signing and apartment tours indicating sex-based rental preferences
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a § 3604(c) claim by alleging Kelly made statements indicating sex-based rental preferences 'with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling.' Kelly's statement to B.C. that he returned her call because she sounded attractive, and his statements to female tester #4 about her appearance and credit check waiver, were made during rental transactions and would suggest to an ordinary listener a preference for renting to women.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act claims under La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(1), (A)(2), and (A)(3), which contain language nearly identical to FHA §§ 3604(a), (b), and (c)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the same analysis to state law claims as to federal FHA claims, finding that because the language in the relevant sections of the Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act is nearly identical to the FHA, plaintiff's allegations sufficiently state claims under state law as well.

case_name: Sanzaro v. Ardiente Homeowners Ass'n, LLC
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Fair Housing Council of San Diego v. Penasquitos Casablanca Owners' Ass'n, 381 Fed. Appx. 674 (9th Cir. 2010)
Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Mrs. Sanzaro to bring her service dog (Angel, a Chihuahua) into the Ardiente HOA clubhouse. Angel was trained to assist Mrs. Sanzaro with her mobility disability by retrieving her walker and helping her manage acute pain attacks.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the five-element FHA reasonable accommodation test and found: (1) Mrs. Sanzaro is handicapped; (2) defendants knew or should have known of her handicap; (3) accommodation was necessary for equal enjoyment of the dwelling; (4) allowing Angel in the clubhouse was reasonable because the dog was not disruptive, posed no risk, and defendants provided no legitimate reason why the accommodation would be unreasonable; and (5) defendants refused the accommodation on three separate occasions despite receiving sufficient documentation of Angel's assistance tasks.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of access to the Ardiente clubhouse based on disability (refusal to allow Mrs. Sanzaro to enter with her service animal while similarly situated non-disabled persons were permitted to use the clubhouse).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's analysis of the reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) necessarily established disparate treatment: Mrs. Sanzaro was denied access to a common facility available to other homeowners solely because of her disability and her use of a service animal, despite providing documentation of the disability and the animal's assistance function.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III public accommodation claim; NRS § 651.075 Nevada state law claim for denial of service to person with disability accompanied by service animal.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the Ardiente clubhouse does not qualify as a place of public accommodation under the ADA or Nevada law because the community and clubhouse were private establishments with restricted access. Although members of the public could participate in 'Stay and Play' and 'Taste of the Good Life' marketing programs, access was conditioned on explicit written indication of interest in purchasing a home and was not advertised or available to the general public as a hotel or lodging facility would be. Therefore, neither the ADA nor NRS § 651.075 applied.

source_file: 7252923_2019_Conn. Fair Hous. Ctr. v. Corelogic Rental Prop. Solutions, LLC_ctd
case_name: Connecticut Fair Housing Center v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Aff. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Automatic criminal record screening without individualized assessment or disclosure of underlying records; disparate impact on racial minorities (African Americans and Latinos)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a facially neutral policy (automated CrimSAFE screening without individualized assessment) with disproportionate impact on minorities, supported by allegations that minorities are more likely to be arrested and charged. Court found allegations satisfy prima facie burden at motion to dismiss stage under Inclusive Communities Project framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination based on race through use of automated criminal record screening without individualized assessment
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Swierkiewicz, plaintiffs need not allege prima facie case under McDonnell Douglas at pleading stage. Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged membership in protected class (race), adverse treatment (disqualification without individualized assessment), and minimal facts suggesting inference of discriminatory intent (defendant's knowledge of racial disparities in criminal justice system and HUD guidance, yet continued offering automated product).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policies requiring power of attorney from conserved individuals and refusing to accept conservatorship documentation; disparate impact on disabled individuals more likely to be conserved and unable to execute power of attorney
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged two facially neutral policies with disproportionate impact on disabled individuals. Court rejected defendant's argument that statistical evidence was required at pleading stage, finding allegations sufficient to satisfy prima facie burden under Inclusive Communities Project framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for disclosure of underlying tenant screening report to conservator (Ms. Arroyo) in lieu of power of attorney requirement; necessary to allow conservator to challenge disqualification and request individualized assessment from housing provider
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged all five elements of failure to accommodate: (1) Mikhail Arroyo had significant disabilities; (2) defendant knew of disabilities; (3) accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwelling; (4) accommodation was reasonable because conservatorship gave Ms. Arroyo more power than power of attorney; (5) defendant refused. Defendant's argument that no different treatment of non-disabled individuals was alleged lacks support at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA) claim based on unfair and deceptive practices: failure to make individualized assessment of criminal records, failure to disclose underlying records, marketing CrimSAFE as improving fair housing compliance while knowing of discriminatory effect, requiring power of attorney instead of accepting conservatorship, and discrimination based on race and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged unfair or deceptive practices under CUTPA's cigarette rule by showing practices offend public policy (FHA, FCRA, conservatorship statute), are unethical and unscrupulous, and cause substantial injury. Plaintiffs alleged ascertainable loss (housing denial, deprivation of FCRA rights) proximately caused by defendant's conduct. File disclosure practices sufficiently related to defendant's commercial relationship with WinnResidential to constitute trade or commerce.

source_file: 7253536_2019_Nat'l Ass'n of the Deaf v. Harvard Univ._dcd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Captioning and audio description for online video content; auxiliary aids and services to provide meaningful access to deaf and hard of hearing individuals to online educational content, lectures, videos, and other audiovisual materials
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) - Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied Harvard's motion for judgment on the pleadings on Title III ADA and Section 504 claims. Court held that plaintiffs adequately pleaded a nexus between online content and physical locations at Harvard, and that auxiliary aids/services obligations apply to online content. CDA immunity applies only to embedded third-party content not created or developed by Harvard; claims as to Harvard-created content and third-party content hosted on Harvard platforms survive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a distinct and palpable injury under ADA § 12203(b). The defendant's statement that the State Bar would be interested in plaintiff's conduct was not conditioned on plaintiff forgoing ADA rights, and plaintiff did not allege he was forced to abandon any ADA claims or suffered injury from the alleged threat.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III public accommodations access claim; Hawaii state law accessibility claims; unfair and deceptive practices; nondisclosure; negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff and defendant KLC filed a stipulation to dismiss with prejudice all claims against KLC on April 26, 2019, resolving the non-FHA claims by agreement.

source_file: 7253788_2019_Poursaied v. Reserve at Research Park LLC_alnd
case_name: Shahnaz Poursaied v. Reserve at Research Park LLC
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condominium Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendant's apartment personnel promised a quiet, sound-proof apartment and failed to accommodate her for a disability related to noise sensitivity. Plaintiff requested either a move-out option or transfer to another unit.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to allege any facts establishing she was disabled within the meaning of the FHA or that she had a disability involving noise sensitivity. The court also found plaintiff failed to allege facts showing defendant refused to accommodate her within the 19-day window between lease signing and filing suit, noting defendant offered her options (move out in 30 days or wait 6 months for another unit). Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the four elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alabama Uniform Residential Landlord Tenant Act (AURLTA) claim for failure to maintain apartments in good repair to prevent noise penetration; invasion of privacy claim based on alleged criminal noise torture from neighbors and traffic.
fha_claims.reasoning: Under AURLTA, plaintiff failed to allege defendant violated any applicable building or housing codes; no codes require sound-proof apartments and the lease contained no warranties regarding sound. Under invasion of privacy, plaintiff failed to allege defendant caused the intrusion or failed to remedy it; defendant is not liable for unforeseeable criminal actions of third parties (neighbors and traffic). Court could not draw reasonable inference of liability from facts pleaded.

case_name: Noah v. Assor
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lawrence v. Courtyards at Deerwood Ass'n, Inc., 318 F. Supp. 2d 1133 (S.D. Fla. 2004)
West v. DJ Mortg., LLC, 164 F. Supp. 3d 1393 (N.D. Ga. 2016)
Quigley v. Winter, 598 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment under § 3617 interference theory, applying HUD regulations and totality of circumstances test. Defendant's motion to dismiss this claim was denied; claim survives and proceeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege she is disabled, which is required to state a claim under § 3604(f)(1)-(2). Court granted motion to dismiss but allowed plaintiff leave to amend to correct inadvertent pleading error by citing §§ 3604(b)-(c) instead.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II under Fla. Stat. § 760.37 (state counterpart to § 3617) survives motion to dismiss on identical reasoning as federal § 3617 claim. Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged interference through quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(3) survives motion to dismiss. Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendant made oral and written statements indicating sex-based preference/limitation with respect to rental (lease renewal), satisfying all three elements of the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IV under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(2) dismissed for failure to plead the 'ready, willing, and able' element. Plaintiff alleged only that she was current on rent but did not allege intent or willingness to renew. Dismissal without prejudice; plaintiff granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Common law intentional infliction of emotional distress (Florida state tort law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Count V dismissed because plaintiff's allegations of sexual harassment, without physical contact or threats of physical harm, do not meet Florida's extremely high standard for outrageous conduct required for intentional infliction of emotional distress. Dismissal with prejudice.

case_name: Rayantha Favourite v. 55 Halley Street, Inc.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett
Cain v. Rambert
United States v. Weisz

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on race under § 3604(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory animus as an essential element of a hostile housing environment claim. The court found that the defendants' legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for the noise complaints and lease termination notices was supported by extensive documentation of noise violations and other residents' complaints, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate this was pretextual discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation under § 3617 for opposing discriminatory conduct
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendants acted with retaliatory motive. The court found no evidence that plaintiff engaged in protected activity by opposing FHA-prohibited conduct prior to filing suit, and the adverse actions (notices to cure and terminate) were based on documented noise violations and lease breaches, not retaliation for protected activity.

Plaintiff's §§ 1981 and 1982 claims failed for the same reasons as the FHA claims—lack of evidence of racial animus. Section 1983 claims failed because defendants were private entities and no state action was shown. Section 1985 conspiracy claim failed because plaintiff did not establish that racial animus motivated the alleged conspiracy. New York state discrimination claims failed under the McDonnell Douglas framework for lack of discriminatory animus.

source_file: 7253955_2019_Diamond House of SE Idaho, LLC v. City of Ammon_idd
case_name: Diamond House of SE Idaho, LLC v. City of Ammon
key_cases_cited: Children's Alliance v. City of Bellevue, 950 F. Supp. 1491 (W.D. Wash. 1997)
Cmty. House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2006)
Gladstone, Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Trafficante v. Metro. Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ordinance 598 restricts group foster homes to R2-A zone while allowing unlimited unrelated adults and day care facilities in R-1 zone
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Ordinance 598 is facially discriminatory under § 3604(a) and (c) because it expressly treats households with minors (protected familial status) differently than similarly situated households without children, and the City provided no justification for the restriction. Plaintiffs demonstrated likelihood of success on merits, irreparable harm, balance of equities in their favor, and public interest in FHA enforcement.

source_file: 7254034_2019_Morris v. W. Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc._idd
case_name: Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc.
key_cases_cited: Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Prods., Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 917 F.3d 109 (2d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-element test for § 3604(b) disparate treatment and found that plaintiffs failed to prove intentional discrimination based on religion. The January 2015 Letter, the strongest evidence, did not support a finding of discriminatory intent; the Board's edits to remove inflammatory language and the rushed context of the letter's drafting demonstrated lack of intent to discriminate. The court granted judgment as a matter of law because no reasonable jury could find intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), plaintiffs were required to show that an ordinary reader would interpret the January 2015 Letter as expressing a preference that a non-religious individual purchase their home. The court found the letter's clearest statement was 'It is not the intention of the Board to discourage you from becoming part of our great neighborhood,' which an ordinary reader would not interpret as expressing a preference for non-religious purchasers. Judgment as a matter of law was appropriate.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3617, plaintiffs were required to prove the Homeowners Association threatened, intimidated, or interfered with their exercise of protected rights based on religion. The court found that because plaintiffs failed to prove the underlying § 3604(b) violation, they could not establish § 3617 liability. Additionally, plaintiffs purchased the home and hosted the Christmas program in both 2015 and 2016 despite the Board's objections, demonstrating no meaningful interference with their rights.

case_name: Wilson v. Guardian Management, LLC
key_cases_cited: Bouley v. Young-Sabourin, 394 F. Supp. 2d 675 (D. Vt. 2005)
Dickinson v. Zanesville Metro. Hous. Auth., 975 F. Supp. 2d 863 (S.D. Ohio 2013)
Creason v. Singh, 2013 WL 6185596 (N.D. Cal. 2013)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Tex. Dep't of Cmty. Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248 (1981)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of sex/gender discrimination under the FHA based on her status as a domestic violence victim. Although the court recognized that domestic violence discrimination can theoretically constitute sex discrimination under the FHA, plaintiff presented no evidence that the defendant's actions (communicating safety concerns and inquiring about the abandoned apartment) constituted discriminatory treatment or that she was treated differently than similarly situated tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to repair carpet and closet doors damaged during domestic violence incident
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish disparate treatment regarding repair of her unit. Although she alleged defendants failed to repair damage within six months, she provided no evidence that defendants treated other tenants differently or repaired similar damage for other tenants within a comparable timeframe, which is required to establish a disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide replacement unit or storage after fire damage
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that she requested and was denied a replacement unit or that defendants offered units to other tenants but refused her. Plaintiff chose to use her renter's insurance to obtain hotel accommodations rather than inquire about available units or apply to other Guardian-owned properties, and defendants did not prohibit such applications.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim for allowing tenants to smoke on property, resulting in fire damage
fha_claims.reasoning: The court adopted the magistrate judge's reasoning dismissing the negligence claim on summary judgment, finding no genuine dispute of material fact warranting trial.

case_name: Binti O. Mohamed v. Michael McLaurin
key_cases_cited: Hylton v. Friends of Mansion St. George
Gallagher v. 630 Real Estate Partners
Mojica v. Gannett Co.
Inland Mediation Bd. v. City of Pomona
Baker v. Waterford Square Homeowners Ass'n
Grady v. Affiliated Cent., Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment as a matter of law at close of plaintiff's evidence; final judgment for defendant
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on national origin. She presented no comparator evidence showing she was treated differently from similarly situated tenants. The court found all of defendant's actions (complaints about water damage, parking, lease violations, property damage) were based on legitimate business reasons unrelated to plaintiff's protected status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment as a matter of law at close of plaintiff's evidence; final judgment for defendant
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on gender. The court found that defendant's conduct toward plaintiff (complaints about lease violations, property damage, unauthorized occupants) was not motivated by discriminatory animus based on her gender, but rather by legitimate business concerns. The court found plaintiff's credibility severely compromised by false testimony on multiple material points.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with plaintiff's right to enjoy the apartment through harassment and hostile housing environment based on national origin and gender
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment as a matter of law at close of plaintiff's evidence; final judgment for defendant
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendant's conduct created a hostile housing environment sufficiently severe or pervasive to interfere with her enjoyment of the apartment. The court found that defendant's complaints about lease violations were legitimate business concerns, not harassment based on protected status. Even crediting plaintiff's version of disputed incidents (partial exposure, offensive comments), the conduct was not sufficiently severe or persistent to constitute a hostile environment. Plaintiff also failed to vacate within a reasonable time after conditions allegedly became intolerable, waiving any constructive eviction claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination against plaintiff's minor children based on national origin and plaintiff's gender
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment as a matter of law at close of plaintiff's evidence; final judgment for defendant
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's children's hostile housing environment claims fail for the same reasons as plaintiff's own claims. The court found no evidence that defendant's conduct toward the children (yelling when they left toys and bikes in common areas) was motivated by discriminatory animus based on their national origin or plaintiff's gender, but rather was a response to lease violations and property maintenance issues.

case_name: Elliott v. Versa CIC, L.P.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Soules v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to disability (Alzheimer's disease); specific accommodation type not detailed in this motion in limine ruling
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion in limine to preclude the reasonable accommodation claim as an untimely dispositive motion filed over one year after the summary judgment deadline and five months after the summary judgment order without timely reconsideration. The claim survived partial summary judgment denial and proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion in limine to preclude the disparate treatment claim, noting that defendants had invoked the disparate treatment standard in their own summary judgment brief and cannot now claim the claim was not pleaded. The claim survived summary judgment and proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements alleged under § 3604(c)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion in limine challenging the § 3604(c) discriminatory statements claim, holding that defendants' disagreement about whether statements are discriminatory is a defense to be asserted at trial, not grounds for precluding the claim. Whether statements violate § 3604(c) under the ordinary listener standard is a jury question.

case_name: College of the Ozarks, Inc. v. Biden
key_cases_cited: Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act challenge to HUD Memorandum interpreting Fair Housing Act's sex discrimination provisions to include sexual orientation and gender identity; First Amendment Free Speech and Free Exercise Clause challenge; Appointments Clause challenge; Religious Freedom Restoration Act challenge
fha_claims.reasoning: College lacked Article III standing because any alleged injury from the Memorandum was too speculative and not certainly impending. The Memorandum is an internal directive to HUD agencies, not a regulation of private parties, and does not directly impose restrictions or penalties on the College. HUD has never filed discrimination charges against a college exempt under Title IX, and the College failed to allege a credible threat of enforcement or actual chilling of speech.

fha_claims.reasoning: College lacked Article III standing because any alleged injury was too speculative and not certainly impending. The Memorandum is an internal directive to HUD agencies that does not impose restrictions on private entities or require HUD to determine the College's housing policies violate federal law. HUD has never filed discrimination charges against a college exempt under Title IX, and the College failed to show a credible threat of enforcement or actual chilling of speech.

source_file: 7804109_2022_Sailboat Bend Sober Living v. City of Fort Lauderdale, FL._ca11
case_name: Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, Florida

Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Center, Inc. v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 917
Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731
Vill. of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Zoning Ordinance treats individuals with disabilities more favorably than similarly situated non-disabled persons by allowing groups of more than three unrelated disabled persons to live together in residential zones while prohibiting the same for non-disabled persons. Under the FHA and ADA, discrimination requires less favorable treatment; favorable treatment cannot constitute discrimination. No prima facie case of disparate treatment established.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of automatic fire sprinkler system requirement; request to classify property as single-family dwelling exempt from Fire Code; request to narrowly tailor Fire Code based on residents' ambulatory status and ability to respond to fire emergencies
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the FHA and ADA, a plaintiff must prove the requested accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. Necessity requires a causal relationship between the disability and the need for accommodation. Plaintiffs failed to establish that residents' addiction-related disabilities caused their inability to afford higher rent; only one resident's affidavit at highest generality was insufficient to create a genuine issue of material fact. No evidence connected disability to inability to pay.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish intentional discrimination in the City's enforcement of the Fire Code using either direct or circumstantial evidence. Under McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework, plaintiffs conceded no disparate impact, provided no historical context, offered no evidence of community animus, and failed to show deviation from normal procedures. The Fire Code applied because the property housed more than three unrelated persons, not because of residents' disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claims analyzed in tandem with FHA claims. The same legal principles apply: no discrimination where disabled persons are treated more favorably; no necessary accommodation where disability does not cause the inability to pay; no intentional discrimination where Fire Code applied based on occupancy classification, not disability status.

case_name: Krystal Theresa Davis v. Daniel B. Rubin; Shannon Leigh McGroarty
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mount Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Phillips v. County of Allegheny, 515 F.3d 224 (3d Cir. 2008)
United States ex rel. Bookwalter v. UPMC, 946 F.3d 162 (3d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability-based discrimination in housing (mocking of disability alleged)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disability-based discrimination. The plaintiff's allegation that defendants mocked her disability was flatly contradicted by the attached letter itself, which controls over the complaint allegations under Vorchheimer.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing HUD discrimination complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately plead a causal connection between protected activity (HUD complaint filed in August 2019) and adverse actions (eviction notice dated July 25, 2019 and eviction complaint filed in early August 2019), which were almost exclusively earlier in time than the protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of deed covenants and restrictions to permit rental apartments instead of owner-occupied condominiums; approval of affordable housing development project
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's ripeness dismissal, holding that Village Green received a final, definitive decision from the Town Board when it filed a resolution stating the motion to approve 'fails for lack of second' and the town attorney conveyed that no further proceedings would be held. The court concluded the dispute was ripe for adjudication and remanded for further proceedings on the merits of the FHA discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination in contracts); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (property rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 with Fourteenth Amendment equal protection; Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process; Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment takings clauses; New York Executive Law § 296(5)-(6)
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court applied the Williamson County final-decision ripeness requirement to all of Village Green's non-FHA claims (§ 1981, § 1982, § 1983 equal protection, substantive due process, takings, and New York Executive Law § 296) and concluded that ripeness was satisfied by the same sequence of events establishing finality for the FHA claim. The court remanded all claims for further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Zoning Ordinance treats individuals with disabilities more favorably than similarly situated non-disabled persons by allowing groups of more than three unrelated disabled persons to live together in residential zones while prohibiting the same for non-disabled persons. Under the FHA and ADA, discrimination requires less favorable treatment; favorable treatment cannot constitute discrimination. Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of automatic fire sprinkler system requirement; request to classify property as single-family dwelling exempt from Fire Code; request to narrowly tailor Fire Code based on residents' ambulatory status and ability to respond to fire emergencies
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the FHA and ADA, a plaintiff must prove the requested accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. Necessity requires a causal relationship between the disability and the inability to afford the accommodation. Plaintiffs offered only one affidavit from one resident stating generally that living at the facility ameliorated his addiction, with no evidence that residents' disabilities caused their inability to afford higher rent. This scintilla of evidence was insufficient to create a genuine issue of material fact on the necessity element.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework. No direct evidence of discriminatory animus was presented. Under the Arlington Heights factors for circumstantial evidence: (1) no disparate impact on disabled persons was shown; (2) no relevant historical context was provided; (3) the sequence of events showed the City discussed the accommodation request at a public meeting and the property was reclassified based on its actual use as a Residential Board and Care Occupancy, not the residents' disability; and (4) no deviation from normal procedure was shown—the Fire Code applies to all buildings with more than three unrelated occupants regardless of disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claims were analyzed in tandem with FHA claims under the same legal standards. The court applied identical disparate treatment and reasonable accommodation frameworks to both statutes. All ADA claims failed on the same evidentiary grounds as the corresponding FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs presented direct evidence of quid pro quo sexual harassment through their own testimony that Oliver conditioned housing benefits (eviction assistance, repairs) on sexual favors. Under HUD's 2016 Final Rule, quid pro quo harassment does not require proof of an adverse housing consequence, and reasonable jurors could find Oliver exercised apparent authority over evictions and repairs. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs presented sufficient evidence of hostile environment sexual harassment through detailed testimony of severe and pervasive conduct spanning years, including unwelcome sexual comments, attempted touching, stalking, and repeated propositions. The totality of circumstances, evaluated under HUD's Final Rule factors, creates genuine issues of material fact for jury determination. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: DCHA is vicariously liable for Oliver's harassment under agency law and HUD's Final Rule. Oliver's position as housing manager facilitated the harassment, and genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Oliver had apparent authority and whether the agency relationship aided the harassment. Summary judgment on vicarious liability denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Myers's hostile environment claim is not time-barred under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations. Under National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan, the entire hostile environment claim is timely if at least one incident occurred within the limitations period. Myers testified to incidents in 2018, within two years of the March 10, 2020 filing date. Summary judgment on statute of limitations denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment equal protection claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Oliver did not move for summary judgment on Plaintiffs' § 1983 claim, so that cause of action proceeds without judicial determination at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged racial discrimination in enforcement of pet policy and eviction decision

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found sufficient evidence of intentional race discrimination and interference with fair housing rights under § 3617 against the Mamarils individually (based on racial slurs and harassment), creating a genuine factual dispute for jury determination. The pattern of harassment by the HOA president and former president could constitute attempted constructive eviction even without actual eviction, interfering with the Watters' post-acquisition enjoyment of their property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Watters' race discrimination claim under § 3604(a) against the HOA failed because they could not provide evidence that the HOA itself (as opposed to the individual Mamarils) engaged in discriminatory conduct or intent. The record was silent or contradicted their allegations of differential treatment regarding pet covenants, pool construction, covenant distribution, mailbox placement, paint color, and privacy fence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Privacy fence (six-foot tall vinyl fence) to mitigate PTSD triggers caused by seeing dogs; Terence requested this as a reasonable accommodation for his PTSD and terminal lung condition
fha_claims.reasoning: The failure to accommodate claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) failed at the second element because the HOA had no knowledge of Terence's PTSD, which was the disability forming the basis for the accommodation request. Although Terence had told one HOA member about his lung condition, he did not mention his PTSD in his accommodation request and provided no evidence the HOA knew of it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (equal property rights claim); race discrimination claim under § 1982
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1982 race discrimination claim against the Mamarils survived summary judgment because it requires the same proof of intent to discriminate as the FHA claim, and the Watters presented sufficient evidence of the Mamarils' discriminatory intent through racial slurs and hostile statements. The claim failed against the HOA for the same reason as the FHA disparate treatment claim—no evidence of HOA's discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide accessible information about hotel accommodations on reservation portals (ADA Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12182 and 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e))
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of Article III standing, holding that Laufer, as a disabled person denied statutorily-required accessibility information, suffered a concrete and particularized injury in fact under the ADA Reservation Rule, even though she was an ADA tester with no intent to book a room. The court applied Havens Realty (FHA tester standing precedent) by analogy and found that denial of information to which a plaintiff has a legal right constitutes concrete injury, with dignitary harm from discrimination providing additional adverse effects post-TransUnion.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court found sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent (racial slurs and 'you people' comment) and interference with housing rights through a pattern of harassment that could constitute attempted constructive eviction under § 3617. The Mamarils' conduct, viewed holistically and in light most favorable to plaintiffs, created a genuine factual dispute for jury determination regarding whether the pattern of racial harassment interfered with the Watters' post-acquisition enjoyment of their property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Watters' race discrimination claim under § 3604(a) against the HOA failed because they could not provide evidence that the HOA itself (as opposed to the individual Mamarils) engaged in discriminatory conduct. The record was silent or contradicted the Watters' allegations regarding differential treatment on pet covenants, pool construction, covenant distribution, mailbox placement, paint color, and privacy fence issues.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (equal property rights claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1982 claim against the Mamarils survives summary judgment because it requires proof of intent to discriminate, which the Watters established through the Mamarils' racial slurs and hostile statements. The claim fails against the HOA for the same reason as the FHA disparate treatment claim—no evidence of HOA's discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Privacy fence (six-foot tall vinyl fence) to mitigate PTSD triggers caused by seeing dogs, which Terence's doctors advised as necessary accommodation for his service-connected PTSD
fha_claims.reasoning: The failure to accommodate claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) failed at the second element because the HOA lacked knowledge of Terence's PTSD. Although Terence had informed one HOA member of his lung condition, he did not mention his PTSD in his accommodation request and provided no evidence that the HOA knew of his PTSD diagnosis. Without defendant awareness of the disability, the claim cannot proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The undisputed evidence showed that Interstate applied its income requirement uniformly to both disabled and nondisabled applicants, accepting disabled applicants who met the income threshold and rejecting both disabled and nondisabled applicants who did not. No reasonable jury could infer discrimination based on disability when the policy was facially neutral and applied equally regardless of disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no evidence that Interstate's income requirement had a disparate impact based on disability. The undisputed facts showed the policy was applied uniformly to all applicants regardless of disability status, and Akbar presented no statistical or other evidence of discriminatory impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 requires action under color of state law. Interstate, a private company, did not act under color of state law merely by receiving federal tax credits, which would make it a federal actor rather than a state actor. Section 1983 does not reach federal actors.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Recording of homeowners association board meetings or providing transcripts of meeting minutes immediately after meetings occur, to enable plaintiff with severe ankylosing spondylitis to access community information and participate in association governance despite inability to attend in-person meetings.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal at the motion to dismiss stage, holding that the district court erred by considering defendant's alternative accommodations before first assessing whether plaintiff's requested accommodations were facially reasonable. The court applied the Schaw framework, requiring that at the pleading stage, plaintiff bears the initial burden of showing the requested accommodation is facially reasonable, and undue burden/fundamental alteration are affirmative defenses for the defendant. The case was remanded for the district court to apply this framework in the first instance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide accessible information about hotel accommodations on reservation portals (ADA Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12182 and 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e))
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of Article III standing, holding that Laufer, as a disabled person denied statutorily-required accessibility information, suffered a concrete and particularized injury in fact under the ADA Reservation Rule, even though she was an ADA tester with no intent to book a room. The court applied Havens Realty's tester standing doctrine and found that denial of information to which a plaintiff has a legal right constitutes a concrete injury, with dignitary harm from discrimination providing additional adverse effects post-TransUnion.

fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found against plaintiff on failure to accommodate claim after trial. The court allowed defendant to present expert testimony challenging whether plaintiff met the threshold requirement of having a handicap under the FHA, which is an element plaintiff must prove.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court affirmed on grounds that there was no triable issue of fact as to whether defendant's conduct (open forum and litigation updates) would coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with plaintiff's FHA rights under § 3617. The conduct was merely factual representation of public record and reasonable measures to inform co-owners of litigation status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing made unavailable based on disability (epilepsy and autism)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court erred in granting summary judgment because sufficient evidence exists that A.R. qualifies as disabled under the FHA (either actually disabled or regarded as disabled), creating a genuine dispute of material fact precluding summary judgment on the § 3604(f)(1) claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Different terms, conditions, and privileges of rental housing based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: District court erred in granting summary judgment on § 3604(f)(2) claim because sufficient evidence exists that A.R. qualifies as disabled, creating a genuine dispute of material fact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statements expressing preference or discrimination based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), statements directed at an individual may violate the FHA's prohibition against statements indicating a preference based on handicap even if the individual is not disabled under the FHA, if an ordinary listener would understand the statements as classifying the individual as disabled and expressing discrimination. Aponte's text messages could reasonably be interpreted by an ordinary listener as indicating discrimination based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Misrepresentation that dwelling is not available for rental based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The 'ordinary listener' standard does not apply to § 3604(d) claims; instead, the 'actually disabled' or 'regarded as disabled' standards apply. Because sufficient evidence exists that A.R. qualifies as disabled, the § 3604(d) claim survives summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found Garden City's shift from R-M to R-T zoning was made with discriminatory intent based on Arlington Heights factors, including the abrupt sequence of events in response to vocal citizen opposition to affordable housing that reflected race-based animus. Appellate court affirmed, finding no clear error in the district court's determination that Garden City officials knowingly acquiesced to race-based citizen opposition.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found plaintiffs established prima facie case of disparate impact and that defendants failed to prove absence of less discriminatory alternative under prior Second Circuit precedent. Appellate court vacated and remanded because HUD's 2013 regulation (24 C.F.R. § 100.500(c)) shifted burden to plaintiffs to prove less discriminatory alternative available, abrogating prior circuit precedent. Court remanded for reconsideration under new regulatory framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Equal Protection Clause, Title VI of Civil Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found Garden City liable for violations of § 1981, § 1983, and Equal Protection Clause based on the same discriminatory intent findings as the FHA disparate treatment claim. Appellate court affirmed these findings without separate analysis, treating them as corollary to the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Nassau County's approval of Garden City's discriminatory R-T zoning and failure to exercise advisory veto power
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment dismissing disparate treatment claims against Nassau County, finding no genuine issue of material fact as to whether County had legal responsibility for Garden City's adoption of R-T zoning. Although plaintiffs raised genuine issue of fact as to whether County officials understood opposition was race-based, County's advisory veto power under § 239-m was non-binding and Garden City could override with majority-plus-one vote, which it did unanimously. Appellate court affirmed, finding County's causal role tenuous and plaintiffs' argument speculative.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of Civil Rights Act claim relating to Nassau County's steering of affordable housing to majority-minority communities
fha_claims.reasoning: District court dismissed Section 808 (affirmative obligation to further fair housing) claim as lacking private right of action but failed to address plaintiffs' parallel claims under § 3604(a) and Title VI relating to Nassau County's steering of affordable housing to low-income, majority-minority communities. Appellate court remanded for district court to address these claims in first instance rather than deciding them on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Landlord's failure to take prompt action to address tenant-on-tenant racial harassment (racial slurs, threats, intimidation by neighbor Endres)
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court dismissed under 12(b)(6), but Second Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that § 3617 encompasses landlord liability for failing to address tenant-on-tenant racial harassment where landlord knew or should have known of the conduct and had power to correct it. Claim survives motion to dismiss and proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental by tolerating and facilitating a hostile racial environment created by another tenant
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court dismissed under 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim under § 3604(b). Second Circuit vacated, holding that § 3604(b) reaches post-acquisition conduct and that plaintiff plausibly alleged intentional discrimination by landlord's deliberate indifference to known racial harassment despite power to evict. Claim survives and proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 (Civil Rights Act of 1866); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296(5) and (6) (New York State Human Rights Law); negligent infliction of emotional distress under New York common law
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court dismissed §§ 1981 and 1982 claims for failure to allege intentional discrimination. Second Circuit vacated, holding that deliberate indifference to racial discrimination can satisfy the intent element of §§ 1981 and 1982, and that plaintiff plausibly alleged such indifference. NYSHRL § 296 claims vacated and remanded as parallel to FHA claims. Negligent infliction of emotional distress claim affirmed as dismissed because emotional distress was directly caused by Endres's harassment, not landlord's breach.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to communal pool facilities without sex-based segregation of swimming hours
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied explicit facial discrimination analysis under § 3604(b) and found that although the pool schedule provided roughly equal aggregate swimming time, it discriminated against women by allocating substantially fewer evening hours (3.5 hours after 5 p.m. on weeknights for women vs. 16.5 hours for men) and assigning men the entire Friday afternoon period, reflecting overbroad generalizations about gender roles. The court reversed the district court's summary judgment and entered judgment for plaintiffs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sex-segregated swimming pool hours (disparate allocation of evening hours between men and women)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the condominium's sex-segregated swimming schedule constitutes per se facial discrimination in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b). The court rejected the defendant's justifications based on religious concerns of Orthodox Jewish residents, finding that generalizations about gender roles and religious modesty cannot justify disparate treatment, and that the defendant failed to present evidence of actual harm or necessity at the summary judgment stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent to Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher holders in predominantly white, non-Hispanic areas
fha_claims.reasoning: The panel majority affirmed the district court's Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, holding that the plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a disparate impact claim under the heightened 'robust causation' standard derived from Texas v. ICP II. The majority required the plaintiff to establish at the pleading stage that the defendant's policy caused the racial composition of voucher holders, which the dissent argued was an impossible burden at the motion to dismiss stage and exceeded what Twombly/Iqbal requires.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Perpetuation of residential segregation through refusal to rent to Section 8 voucher holders in predominantly white areas
fha_claims.reasoning: The panel majority dismissed the segregative-effect variant of the disparate impact claim on the same pleading-stage grounds, holding that the plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to show that the defendant's policy perpetuated segregation. The dissent argued that the plaintiff had plausibly alleged both a policy and a statistical disparity showing perpetuation of existing segregation, satisfying the Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court found that the City acted for reasons unrelated to race (dilapidation, crime, and planned park extension) and that one council member's prior racist comments were not shared by other council members. The court also found the City's HUD settlement agreement and redevelopment plan demonstrated lack of discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no disparate impact because: (1) the closure affects only a small fraction of Joliet's black population (about 3%), not a substantial fraction; (2) moving to newly constructed or voucher-available housing is not an injury given the dilapidated conditions; and (3) the condemnation is a one-time decision, not a policy subject to disparate-impact analysis under Inclusive Communities Project, and serves legitimate health and safety objectives.

source_file: 8443343_2017_Affordable Recovery Housing v. City of Blue Island_ca7
case_name: Affordable Recovery Housing v. City of Blue Island

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from sprinkler system installation requirement and special-use permit requirement to operate a recovery home for men with substance use disorders in a Single Family Residential zone
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the FHA does not apply because Affordable was not attempting to exclude handicapped persons from its facilities; rather, Blue Island's temporary exclusion of residents was quickly undone when Affordable discovered supervening state law preempting the sprinkler requirement. The court did not apply the reasonable accommodation framework because the FHA claim was not the basis for the district court's ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illinois Religious Freedom Restoration Act (775 ILCS 35/15) and Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-5(5))
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the compelling interest/least restrictive means test under both the Illinois RFRA and the federal RLUIPA, finding that Blue Island's fire-safety code was justified by an honest concern with fire hazards and that Affordable could have avoided the expulsion by researching applicable regulations before beginning operations. The expulsion was temporary and undone by discovery of preempting state law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II public accommodations claim regarding NCAA eligibility policy for former felons
fha_claims.reasoning: Judge Faber's concurrence argues that Title II does not authorize disparate-impact liability and contains only disparate-treatment claims requiring proof of intentional discrimination. Even if disparate-impact liability were cognizable, the business-necessity defense would protect the NCAA's felony-conviction policy as serving legitimate organizational interests in maintaining wholesome environments and good role models for youth.

Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
