fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenged county recorders' maintenance and publication of historical land records containing racially restrictive covenants, seeking injunctive relief to compel removal and redaction of such documents.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege a particularized, concrete injury traceable to the county recorders' conduct. The complaint did not allege that Mason intended to purchase or rent property, that any specific racially restrictive covenant affected him personally, or that he suffered economic harm. His generalized grievance about government non-compliance with law and alleged feelings of unwelcomeness were not sufficiently particularized injuries.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and 42 U.S.C. § 1985 claims challenging maintenance of racially restrictive covenant records
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing on all claims, including non-FHA statutory claims, for the same reasons: failure to allege particularized injury, lack of causal connection to defendants' conduct, and inability to demonstrate redressability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment for the defendant, holding that the sex-segregated pool schedule constitutes explicit facial discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) because it allocates unequal favorable swimming times to men and women (e.g., 16.5 hours for men vs. 3.5 hours for women after 5:00 p.m. on weeknights), reflecting overbroad generalizations about gender roles, even though aggregate swimming time is roughly equal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New Jersey state law claims regarding discrimination and condominium association rules
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims after granting summary judgment on the FHA claim; the appellate court left to the district court whether to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of Tenant Protection Vouchers to tenants at Sandpiper Cove following Notice of Default issued to property owner
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim as moot because the property was sold to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default, eliminating the statutory prerequisite for issuing Tenant Protection Vouchers. The court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the claim and therefore did not reach the merits of the FHA theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act challenge to HUD's decision not to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers; Fifth Amendment equal protection challenge
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims (APA and Fifth Amendment equal protection) as moot on the same jurisdictional basis: the sale of the property to a new owner eliminated the statutory prerequisites for relief, depriving the court of jurisdiction to adjudicate any claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination under the FHA because they could not show exclusion from services provided to others; cohabitation was not provided to any couples, so defendants could not have discriminated based on disability by denying a benefit provided to no one.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ability to cohabitate as a married couple in one of the defendants' group home facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked standing to seek the only available relief (injunctive relief) for reasonable accommodation claims under the FHA because they obtained the requested accommodation (cohabitation at East End) after filing suit, eliminating any immediate injury and rendering a permanent injunction request speculative.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, § 1983 Medicaid Act and Fourteenth Amendment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims against the State were barred by the Eleventh Amendment; claims against private group homes failed because plaintiffs did not plausibly allege state action; all claims seeking damages lacked standing because plaintiffs obtained the requested accommodation and could not seek the only available relief (injunctive relief).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Curfew Rule (children confined to home after sunset) and Loitering Rule (restrictions on congregating in streets, children confined after dark)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted partial summary judgment on facial discrimination under § 3604(b), finding the plain text of the Curfew and Loitering Rules discriminated against children by treating them differently than adults. However, the court left to the jury the question of whether the Rules were enforced in a discriminatory manner and whether such enforcement caused damages, as proximate causation is a required element of an FHA damages claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement (rental applications required copies of report cards for persons under 18)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court denied partial summary judgment on the Report Card Requirement, finding sufficient ambiguity in the rule's meaning (could be interpreted as vetting related to character, similar to adult background checks, or as age identification) such that a trier of fact must resolve whether it facially discriminates against families with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proper Attire Rule (requiring proper clothing; specifying 'Boys' shirtless and 'Girls' must wear cover-up over bathing suit)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court denied partial summary judgment on the Proper Attire Rule, finding the language was ambiguous—an ordinary reader could interpret 'Boys' and 'Girls' as referring only to male and female children, or to all males and females—such that a trier of fact must determine whether it facially discriminates based on familial status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Curfew Rule and Loitering Rule (enforcement and damages phase)
fha_claims.reasoning: After seven-day trial, jury found no liability despite the court's prior finding that the plain text of the Curfew and Loitering Rules violated § 3604(b). The jury determined that the Defendants either did not enforce the Rules in a discriminatory manner (enforced against all residents or not at all) or that the Plaintiffs failed to prove proximate causation and damages. Proximate causation is a required element of an FHA damages claim, and the Plaintiffs bore the burden of proving enforcement, causation, and damages.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement and Proper Attire Rule (trial phase)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found no liability on the Report Card Requirement and Proper Attire Rule claims after trial. The Plaintiffs did not appeal these verdicts, conceding the jury's determination on appeal.

source_file: 8682303_2017_Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Community Homeowners Ass'n_ca11

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court granted summary judgment on § 3604(b) claim regarding Loitering Rule, finding plaintiffs established prima facie case of intentional discrimination because the rule restricted only children and treated them differently than adults, and defendants' safety justifications were based on stereotypes rather than concrete evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court granted summary judgment on § 3604(b) claim regarding Curfew Rule, finding the rule facially discriminated against children by confining them to home after dark while allowing adults freedom of movement, with no legitimate nondiscriminatory justification supported by evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court granted summary judgment on § 3604(c) claim regarding Loitering Rule, finding that an ordinary reader would clearly conclude the rule discriminates against children based on its plain language and content.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court granted summary judgment on § 3604(c) claim regarding Curfew Rule, finding that an ordinary reader would clearly understand the rule as discriminating against children based on its plain language.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court denied summary judgment on § 3604(b) claim regarding Proper Attire Rule, leaving the issue for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court denied summary judgment on § 3604(b) claim regarding Report Card Requirement, leaving the issue for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(b), the district court granted partial summary judgment that the Loitering and Curfew Rules' text violated the FHA as a matter of law (prima facie case of intentional discrimination). However, at trial, the jury found the defendants not liable because plaintiffs failed to prove proximate causation—that the rules were enforced against only families with children and caused damages. The court held that proximate cause is a required element of an FHA damages claim, and the jury could reasonably conclude the defendants enforced the rules against all residents or not at all.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), the district court granted partial summary judgment that the Loitering and Curfew Rules violated the FHA as a matter of law under the 'ordinary reader' standard (facially discriminatory statements). At trial, the jury found defendants not liable because plaintiffs failed to establish a causal connection between the publication of the rules and the alleged damages. The jury may have concluded that the mere existence of facially discriminatory rules, which were eliminated before trial, did not cause the substantial damages claimed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement—rental applications required copies of report cards for any person under age 18
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Partial Summary Judgment Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment on the Report Card Requirement, finding sufficient ambiguity in the rule's meaning. An ordinary reader could conclude the report card was used as a means of identification or character vetting (applied to both adults and children), not solely as familial status discrimination. The issue was left for the jury to decide.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proper Attire Rule—required proper clothing when walking on streets; specified 'No Boys should be shirtless and Girls must wear a cover up over a bathing suit when walking to the pool'
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Partial Summary Judgment Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment on the Proper Attire Rule, finding the language was ambiguous. An ordinary reader could interpret 'Boys' and 'Girls' as referring to all males and females (not just children), or only to children. This ambiguity precluded summary judgment, and the issue was left for the jury to decide.

source_file: 8776095_2016_Civil Rights Education _ Enforcement Center v. Hospitality Properties Trust_cand

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equivalent wheelchair-accessible transportation services at hotels (Title III ADA claim for failure to provide equivalent accessible transportation at hotels that provide transportation to non-disabled guests)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion for class certification because plaintiffs failed to satisfy the commonality and typicality requirements of Rule 23(a) and the requirements of Rule 23(b)(2). The court found no common policy or practice across the 142 allegedly non-compliant hotels, and concluded that each hotel would require individualized proof of ADA violations, making class-wide relief inappropriate. The underlying Title III ADA claims survive but class certification is denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged various non-FHA claims including breach of duty against HUD, breach of contract and unjust enrichment against City of Pittsburgh and police officer, gross negligence and civil elder abuse against Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, and § 1983 claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court screened the amended complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and found it failed to coherently allege any facts supporting a viable cause of action. The court concluded the complaint was incoherent and that further leave to amend would be futile under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

case_name: Corla Jackson v. Siegel Group, L.L.C.
key_cases_cited: Alabama Ass'n of Realtors v. Dep't of Health & Hum. Servs., 141 S. Ct. 2485 (2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim; § 1982 claim; CDC eviction moratorium claim; Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court found no factual allegations to support claims under the Fair Housing Act or § 1982. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal, finding no reversible error of law or fact. The FHA claim was dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act (FCA) action alleging defendants submitted false Housing Assistance Payments (HAP) contracts to HUD regarding Section 8 subsidized housing units, misrepresenting compliance with Health Quality Standards (HQS) and Fair Housing Act requirements.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to satisfy Rule 9(b) particularity and materiality requirements for FCA implied certification claims. Although plaintiff adequately alleged particularity regarding the 2016 HAP contract (time, place, content, and defendant's knowledge), she failed to allege materiality by not demonstrating that HUD would have refused payment if aware of the HQS violations, nor did she clarify whether HUD's payment decisions rested on the HAP contract certification or independent property inspections.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver or exemption from the 650-foot separation requirement between sober living homes and state-licensed drug and alcohol treatment centers, to allow continued operation of existing sober living homes within 650 feet of other such facilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment to the City on the reasonable accommodation claims, finding that Appellants failed to establish that their residents were disabled under the FHA. The appellate court reversed, holding that the district court applied an incorrect legal standard by requiring individualized evidence of resident disability and by requiring proof of the City's subjective belief that residents were disabled under the 'regarded as' prong.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ordinances 14-13 and 15-11 imposed a 650-foot separation requirement and other restrictions on sober living homes (defined as group homes for persons recovering from drug and alcohol addiction and considered handicapped under state or federal law) that were not imposed on other residential uses.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the disparate treatment claim based on its finding that Appellants failed to establish that their residents were disabled. The appellate court reversed the summary judgment, holding that Appellants can establish disability on a collective basis through policies, procedures, and testimony, without individualized medical evidence of each resident's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: The 650-foot separation requirement and other permit conditions in Ordinances 14-13 and 15-11 have a disparate impact on sober living homes serving persons with disabilities (those recovering from drug and alcohol addiction).
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the disparate impact claim based on its finding that Appellants failed to establish that their residents were disabled. The appellate court reversed, holding that Appellants can establish disability on a collective basis and remanded for the district court to consider whether Appellants established a genuine dispute of material fact on the disability prongs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II, California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985–1986, California Government Code §§ 11135 and 65008, retaliation under the FHA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on non-FHA claims (ADA, FEHA, § 1985–1986, Cal. Gov't Code §§ 11135 and 65008, FHA retaliation, and § 1983) and awarded the City attorneys' fees, finding these claims were asserted in a frivolous fashion. The appellate court vacated and remanded the attorneys' fees awards without prejudice in light of the reversal on the disability prongs, but did not substantively address the merits of the non-FHA claims on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for an emotional support animal (dog) in violation of landlord's 'no dogs' policy
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed partial summary judgment on the reasonable accommodation claim, finding a genuine issue of material fact as to whether the defendant knew or reasonably should have known of the plaintiff's disability. The co-applicant's use of terms like 'verified support animal,' 'reasonable accommodation,' and the defendant's own use of 'service dog' created a triable issue on the knowledge prong of the Dubois test, precluding summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory statement: 'My policy has been not to accept dogs, even if service dogs'
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed summary judgment on the § 3604(c) claim, holding that an ordinary reader would not interpret a preference against dogs as indicating a preference against renters with disabilities. The statement indicated a preference against dogs specifically, not against disabled persons, making the connection too tenuous.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim based on landlord's duty to operate property free from unlawful discrimination; California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) claims under Cal. Gov't Code §§ 12927(c)(1), 12955(c)
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed summary judgment on the negligence claim because a landlord's failure to comply with the FHA's reasonable accommodation requirement constitutes a breach of the duty not to discriminate. Since the reasonable accommodation claim was remanded, the negligence claim must also be remanded as a question of fact remains.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver or exemption from the 650-foot separation requirement between sober living homes and state-licensed drug and alcohol treatment centers, allowing sober living homes to operate in closer proximity to other such facilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment to the City, finding that Appellants failed to establish that their residents were actually disabled or regarded as disabled under the FHA. The court applied an incorrect legal standard requiring individualized evidence of resident disability, which the appellate court reversed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinances (14-13 and 15-11) that imposed a 650-foot separation requirement and special permitting regime on sober living homes serving persons recovering from drug and alcohol addiction, while not imposing similar restrictions on other residential uses.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the disparate treatment claim based on its erroneous finding that Appellants failed to establish disability of their residents. The appellate court reversed, holding that Appellants can establish disability on a collective basis through policies and procedures, not individualized evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: The 650-foot separation requirement and special permitting regime for sober living homes, which facially targets group homes for persons with disabilities and has a disparate impact on persons recovering from drug and alcohol addiction.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the disparate impact claim based on its erroneous finding that Appellants failed to establish disability of their residents. The appellate court reversed, holding that Appellants can establish disability on a collective basis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II, California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985–1986, California Government Code §§ 11135 and 65008, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Appellants withdrew claims under §§ 1985–1986 and Cal. Gov't Code §§ 11135 and 65008. The district court granted summary judgment on the retaliation claim under the FHA and the § 1983 claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the FHA retaliation claim and the § 1983 claim, and awarded the City attorneys' fees on these claims, finding them asserted in a frivolous fashion. The appellate court vacated and remanded the attorneys' fees awards without prejudice in light of the reversal on the disability discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 regulatory takings, substantive due process, and equal protection claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Mohit's regulatory takings claims failed because his own allegations showed the farm retained economically beneficial uses (hay crop, twenty cows, twenty goats, five horses); substantive due process claims failed because they involved only state-created property rights and the officials were entitled to absolute legislative immunity for zoning ordinances; equal protection claims failed because Mohit did not plead facts showing he was treated less favorably than the similarly situated comparator (Grullon) or allege sufficient discriminatory animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for accessible parking with van-accessible space and access aisle; California Unruh Civil Rights Act claim; state law trespass counterclaim
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court reversed district court's judgment on Title III ADA claim, holding that the parking lot was a facility of a place of public accommodation (the Lobster Shop) subject to ADA requirements, and that actual usage—not lease terms—controls whether a facility is open to the public. Overwhelming trial evidence showed customers parked in the lot, establishing ADA violation. Court also rejected district court's adverse credibility determination against serial litigant plaintiff as based on impermissible legal reasoning under CREEC and D'Lil precedent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) retaliation claim for termination allegedly in retaliation for complaining about late wage payment
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's rejection of sovereign immunity but vacated and remanded the qualified immunity determination, holding that the antecedent question of whether qualified immunity applies to FLSA claims must be decided by the district court in the first instance. The court did not reach the merits of whether the plaintiff's termination violated the FLSA, but analyzed the clearly established law prong and found no clearly established right that the defendant violated a sufficiently specific version of the FLSA retaliation prohibition.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to provide accessible information on hotel reservation websites regarding accessible guest room features and reservation procedures
fha_claims.reasoning: District court dismissed for lack of Article III standing based on plaintiff's failure to allege definite travel plans to book a hotel room. Fourth Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that plaintiff has standing based on alleged informational injury under Havens Realty line of precedent, without requiring intent to actually use the services.

case_name: Elizabeth Fedynich; Nicole Fedynich v. Boulder Housing Partners

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation(s) under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's order granting defendants' motions to dismiss the amended complaint alleging FHA violations without substantively analyzing the reasonable accommodation claim on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. §§ 701-7961), Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 12101-12213), and due process claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal of non-FHA claims (Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and due process) without substantive merits analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to provide accessible information on hotel reservation websites regarding accessible guest room features and reservation procedures
fha_claims.reasoning: District court dismissed for lack of Article III standing based on plaintiff's failure to allege definite travel plans to the Baltimore area. Fourth Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that plaintiff has standing based on alleged informational injury under the ADA's Hotel Reservation Regulation (28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)), following Havens Realty, Public Citizen, and Akins precedents recognizing informational injury standing without requiring plaintiff to have intended to use the defendant's services.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that the requested accommodation 'may be necessary to afford [plaintiff] equal opportunity to use and enjoy [his] dwelling' under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B). The complaint did not establish the nexus between the disability and the need for the accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation in permit application approval process; § 1983 substantive due process claim; private nuisance claims; breach of fiduciary duty claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claim dismissed because permit application approval process is not a public 'service, program, or activity' in which plaintiff participates or receives; § 1983 claim dismissed because application of TCA § 332(c)(7)(B)(iv) is not arbitrary or conscience-shocking; nuisance claims preempted by federal TCA; breach of fiduciary duty claim time-barred under California law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on familial status under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing that he has children and thus could not be covered under the Act's familial status provision. This was a pleading-stage failure under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985 and 1986 conspiracy and failure to prevent claims; Protecting Tenants and Foreclosure Act of 2009 private right of action
fha_claims.reasoning: The Protecting Tenants and Foreclosure Act does not create a private cause of action, and the §§ 1985 and 1986 claims were premised on that non-existent right and therefore likewise not cognizable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for relocation to a ground-floor, three-bedroom apartment as an accommodation for osteoarthritis and obesity
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants failed to carry their initial burden under Celotex of identifying undisputed evidence demonstrating the absence of a genuine issue of material fact. Defendants offered only ipse dixit that the accommodation was unreasonable and provided contradictory testimony regarding availability of qualifying units, creating genuine disputes as to both the facial reasonableness of the accommodation and whether undue hardship was demonstrated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, and DCHRA retaliation claims arising from alleged retaliatory defamation lawsuit and mismanagement of rental account
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the McDonnell Douglas framework, plaintiff failed to establish that no reasonable jury could credit defendants' non-retaliatory reasons for filing suit (plaintiff's threats and abusive conduct toward management) and for rent collection efforts (plaintiff's nonpayment of rent from May 2017 to February 2019). Mere temporal proximity is insufficient to overcome defendants' legitimate, non-retaliatory explanations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Acceptance of housing choice voucher to supplement rent payments; exception to landlord's policy of not accepting vouchers except in limited circumstances
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that while the FHAA requires reasonable accommodations that directly ameliorate the effect of a handicap, the statute does not require landlords to accommodate a tenant's economic circumstances by accepting housing vouchers. The court reasoned that the duty of reasonable accommodation is limited to modifying rules or policies that hurt handicapped people by reason of their handicap, not by virtue of circumstances they share with others such as limited economic means. Accepting a voucher would alleviate downstream economic effects rather than directly ameliorate the disability itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims (unspecified in opinion; to be resolved at later time)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court proceeded to expedited bench trial on the federal FHA claim only, with state law claims to be resolved at a later time. The appellate opinion does not address the state law claims, which remain pending.

source_file: 9388716_2023_District of Columbia v. Proud Boys International, L.L.C._dcd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves civil conspiracy claims arising from the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot. The plaintiff (District of Columbia) seeks compensation for costs incurred in providing medical care to injured MPD officers and paid leave. Claims are brought under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985(1), 1986, and common law civil conspiracy (assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed Counts I and II (§ 1985 and § 1986 claims) on statutory standing grounds, finding the District of Columbia lacks standing under the zone-of-interests test because these statutes protect federal officers, not municipal financial interests. However, the court allowed Counts III–V (civil conspiracy claims for assault, battery, and intentional infliction of emotional distress) to proceed, finding the District plausibly pleaded a civil conspiracy under D.C. common law where the alleged overt acts were reasonably foreseeable consequences of the scheme.

Rupp's 50 years of landlord experience, knowledge of fair housing laws (including disability protections added in 1988 alongside familial status), and continued use of unlawful lease forms even after notice of the complaint supported the jury's verdict.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Religious meal accommodation (Halal diet) in prison; free exercise of religion claim under First Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court reversed district court's summary judgment dismissal on PLRA exhaustion grounds, holding that Morgan's single grievance adequately exhausted administrative remedies for a continuing violation of his free exercise rights regarding denial of religious meals, and remanded for consideration of the merits of his First Amendment claim.

P. 8(a)(2) and 10(b)) and local rules. Plaintiff was ordered to file an amended complaint by 28 February 2022 but failed to respond. fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that Robert Kellett be permitted to serve as her live-in aide as an accommodation for her disability. Defendants offered a stipulation in 2018 permitting Kellett to reside at the premises as a live-in aide despite his prior drug-related criminal conviction and lack of certification.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed summary judgment because the undisputed record revealed that Plaintiff was accorded a plainly reasonable accommodation. Defendants offered the exact accommodation Plaintiff sought—a stipulation permitting Kellett to serve as her live-in aide—and the fact that Plaintiff refused to sign the stipulation does not negate that Defendants made the offer of reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of retaliation because she could not demonstrate a causal connection between any protected activity and the adverse action (eviction). The eviction proceedings began before Plaintiff requested that Kellett serve as her live-in aide, and Defendants had agreed to her accommodation request, negating any inference of retaliatory motive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and New York State Human Rights Law discrimination and retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same legal standards under Section 504 and NYSHRL as under the FHA and affirmed summary judgment on all discrimination and retaliation claims brought under these statutes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to housing advertisements on Facebook Marketplace; plaintiffs allege Facebook's targeting methods excluded them from viewing housing ads available to non-protected class members
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that at the pleading stage, plaintiffs need only allege general factual allegations of injury and that Twombly/Iqbal are ill-suited to standing analysis. The court found plaintiffs plausibly alleged concrete injury—deprivation of truthful information and housing opportunities—through the comparative tester allegation that plaintiff's Caucasian friend received more housing ads using identical search criteria, even though plaintiffs could not identify specific ads they did not see.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to housing advertisements; plaintiffs allege Facebook's Ad Platform allowed housing advertisers to exclude protected categories (women, persons with disabilities, single parents, persons of color) from viewing housing ads
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of Section 230 immunity, holding that plaintiffs' claims challenge Facebook's conduct as a co-developer of content (by creating targeting categories, assigning users to categories via algorithms, and providing exclusion tools to advertisers) rather than as a mere publisher of third-party content. The court found Facebook materially contributed to the alleged illegality under the Roommates.com standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of shelter placement based on familial status (single man without children)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations that he was denied shelter placement because of his familial status as a single man without children do not support a claim under the Fair Housing Act, which defines familial status as one or more individuals under age 18 living with a parent or legal guardian. The complaint failed to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims against State of Delaware and state officials in official capacities; Title VI Civil Rights Act claim; state law negligence claims (negligent retention, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress); conditions of housing at motels
fha_claims.disposition: Sua sponte dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B); Eleventh Amendment immunity; qualified immunity; sovereign immunity
fha_claims.reasoning: The Eleventh Amendment bars § 1983 claims against the State of Delaware and state officials in their official capacities absent Congressional abrogation or state waiver, neither of which occurred. State law negligence claims against state and local officials are barred by sovereign immunity and qualified immunity under Delaware law. General allegations that motel conditions violated unspecified federal law lacked sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of Certificate of Continuing Occupancy (CCO) to permit Oxford House to operate as a community residence in a two-family dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Oxford House failed to demonstrate a reasonable likelihood of success on its disparate treatment claim under Arlington Heights because it presented insufficient evidence that the prospective residents' status as individuals with disabilities (substance use disorder) played any role in the Township's denial of the CCO. The court found that a single incident from 30 years prior, procedural irregularities, and a debatable zoning interpretation do not constitute clear evidence of discriminatory intent at the preliminary injunction stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of Certificate of Continuing Occupancy (CCO) to permit Oxford House to operate as a community residence in a two-family dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Oxford House failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact because it provided no statistical or other evidence demonstrating that the Township's decision had a greater adverse impact on individuals with disabilities than on others, relying instead on mere speculation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim for discrimination in denial of Certificate of Continuing Occupancy
fha_claims.reasoning: Oxford House's ADA claim, evaluated under the same Arlington Heights and disparate impact frameworks as the FHA claims, failed because Oxford House did not demonstrate that the prospective residents' disability status motivated the Township's denial or that the decision had a disparate impact on individuals with disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil liability under 18 U.S.C. § 1595 for sex trafficking; also Section 230 Communications Decency Act defense
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court reversed district court's dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged participant liability under 18 U.S.C. § 1595 by alleging Salesforce knew or should have known Backpage engaged in sex trafficking, participated in Backpage's venture through customized software and consulting, and knowingly benefited from that participation. Court also rejected Section 230 CDA defense because plaintiffs' claim does not depend on treating Salesforce as a publisher or speaker of third-party content.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint alleged disability discrimination under federal statutes
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against defendants Hein and Transition Projects, Inc. were barred by the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) for Fair Housing Act claims and Oregon state law for personal injury claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure policies and practices targeting minority borrowers (Count I: 'equity stripping scheme')
fha_claims.reasoning: Disparate-impact claim failed because the County's expert testimony (Drs. Lacefield and Cowan) was excluded under Daubert/Rule 702 as unreliable and untested. Without statistical evidence of a causal link between the banks' policies and the alleged disparities, the claim cannot survive summary judgment under Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged facially neutral mortgage servicing and foreclosure practices disproportionately affecting minority borrowers (Count II)
fha_claims.reasoning: Disparate-impact claim failed for the same reason as Count I: exclusion of expert testimony under Daubert eliminated the County's statistical evidence of causality between the banks' policies and disparate impact on minority borrowers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory 'integrated equity-stripping scheme' targeting minority borrowers through predatory lending practices
fha_claims.reasoning: Disparate-treatment claim failed because the summary judgment record did not support the existence of an integrated scheme; individual banks developed their own programs at different times for different reasons, and the County's own expert conceded such a scheme would not have made economic sense for the banks.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proximate causation under the Fair Housing Act; claims for property-tax revenue loss and municipal services costs
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017), the County as a tertiary injured party (government entity suffering indirect economic harm from borrower defaults) lacks proximate causation under the FHA. The directly injured parties are the borrowers; the County's injuries are too remote and attenuated to satisfy the 'first step' requirement of proximate cause doctrine.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged sufficient facts to survive motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly standard by alleging she is African-American, qualified for coverage under the master policy, and PPCA denied her coverage while allowing White residents to invoke the same policy for identical repairs. The fact that one other African-American resident received coverage does not negate the inference of racial discrimination at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for reporting fraud and waste of association financial resources while serving on the board
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege protected activity under § 3617 because reporting fraud and waste are not protected activities under the FHA's anti-retaliation provision unless the fraud/waste involved discriminatory housing practices. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege causation because the initial denial occurred in December 2014 before her board service began in 2015, and the alleged retaliatory denials (2018-2021) occurred two years after her board service ended (2016), which is too attenuated to suggest causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination claim (mentioned in complaint but not substantively addressed)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court determined that plaintiffs failed to prove their disparate impact claim. The appellate court did not disturb this finding on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow occupancy of 15-20 residents in a sober living home, exceeding the zoning ordinance limit of 8 unrelated disabled individuals plus 2 caretakers. Plaintiffs argued the higher capacity was therapeutically necessary for residents recovering from substance use disorders.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit held that the district court applied an incorrect legal standard by accepting that therapeutically beneficial treatment constitutes necessity. The court held that necessity requires proof that the accommodation is indispensable or essential—that without it, residents receive no ameliorative effect—not merely that it provides greater therapeutic benefit. The testimony that 15 residents provided increased therapeutic benefit over 8 was insufficient to meet this standard. The court vacated the district court's injunction and remanded.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow occupancy of 15-20 residents in a sober living home under a theory of financial necessity, exceeding the zoning ordinance limit of 8 unrelated disabled individuals plus 2 caretakers.
fha_claims.reasoning: District court determined that plaintiffs failed to prove their failure-to-accommodate claim under a theory of financial necessity. The appellate court did not disturb this finding.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing services (property maintenance and clean up, participation in committees and meetings, community notices) based on religion
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that the disparate treatment claim based on denial of housing services was not barred by res judicata because it required proof of different facts than the state defamation claim (comparing § 3604(a)-(b) to defamation elements), and remanded claims based on undated or post-April 2019 conduct.

source_file: 9448201_2023_Inner City Contracting LLC v. Charter Twp. of Northville_ca6

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disclosure of accessible room information on hotel websites under the ADA Reservation Rule (28 CFR §36.302(e)(1)(ii))
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court vacated the First Circuit's judgment as moot after plaintiff voluntarily dismissed her suit following sanctions against her attorney. The Court did not reach the merits of the standing question, though Justice Thomas's concurrence argued plaintiff lacked standing because the ADA does not create a statutory right to information (unlike the Fair Housing Act in Havens Realty), and plaintiff had no intent to visit the hotel, thus no concrete injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Short breaks and reduced stress; also challenged the district court's ruling that the January 2018 Letter (which sought changes to the daily office environment including compliance with Code of Ethics, adherence to defined roles, end to threats of termination, courtesy in communications, equal treatment, improved gender diversity, acknowledgment of team management, and written policies) was not an accommodation request
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that although Kelly informed the Town of his disabilities (anxiety, depression, high blood pressure), the January 2018 Letter did not adequately communicate a desire for accommodation because it lacked a logical bridge connecting the requested workplace changes to his disabilities. The letter's substance—focused on workplace governance, ethics, and personnel matters—did not make clear that Kelly was seeking assistance for his disabilities rather than addressing workplace grievances and personality conflicts. The court affirmed that to trigger the employer's duty to accommodate, an employee must communicate both his disability and his desire for an accommodation related to that disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Kelly failed to allege facts warranting a reasonable inference of disability discrimination. Although he plausibly alleged constructive discharge and that he was fulfilling the employer's legitimate expectations, he alleged no facts suggesting the Town harbored a discriminatory motive. The court held that temporal proximity between EEOC filings and adverse action supports retaliation claims but not discrimination claims, which require proof that disability was a but-for cause of the adverse action. Kelly's allegations that the Town mistreated multiple employees (not just him) undermined any inference that his disability motivated the conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not address the merits of the retaliation claim on appeal because Kelly's retaliation claim survived the motion to dismiss and proceeded to summary judgment. The district court had limited the scope of the retaliation claim by ruling that the January 2018 Letter was not an accommodation request, restricting the claim to allegations of escalating harassment following Kelly's EEOC filings. The court affirmed this limitation but did not reach the ultimate merits of the retaliation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Kelly failed to allege that the Town coerced, threatened, intimidated, or interfered with his exercise of ADA rights, or that the Town was motivated by an intent to discriminate. Although the Town's hostile conduct exacerbated his disabilities, he made no allegation that the Town engaged in this behavior to prevent him from filing EEOC charges, requesting accommodations, or pursuing other protected ADA actions. The court held that mere adverse effects on health do not constitute unlawful interference under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b).

fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment to defendants on the merits, finding plaintiff failed to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. Appellate court vacated only the fee award, not the underlying summary judgment, finding the district court applied post hoc reasoning in awarding fees but affirming that plaintiff's FHA claim lacked evidentiary support at summary judgment stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to violate Civil Rights Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA claims on the same basis as FHA claims—failure to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. Appellate court did not separately address these claims, focusing only on the fee award issue.

fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to meet minimal pleading standard under Rule 8(a); plaintiff fails to allege cogent facts sufficient to give defendants adequate notice of the legal claims, mixing discussion of medications and unrelated case law with vague housing discrimination allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleges discrimination based on disability, race, color, and national origin but fails to articulate any specific discriminatory conduct or harm; insufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish intentional discrimination through direct or circumstantial evidence under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework. No direct evidence of discriminatory animus; circumstantial evidence factors (discriminatory effect, historical background, sequence of events, departures from normal criteria) were insufficient to establish that disability played a role in the County's zoning decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing up to 55 residents (later conceded to 25-30 residents) in a residential zoning district; Vision Warriors legally permitted to house only 8 unrelated persons under existing zoning (4 per parcel plus domestic workers)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish necessity of the requested accommodation. Although the court did not reach the reasonableness/fundamental alteration question, it held that Vision Warriors did not demonstrate that housing 55 (or 25-30) residents would 'alleviate the effects' of residents' disability or that the accommodation was 'crucial to economic viability' compared to the 8 residents legally permitted. The necessity inquiry requires evidence that the accommodation would 'affirmatively enhance quality of life by ameliorating the effects of disability,' which plaintiff failed to provide.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves claims under Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act (UTPA) for misleading pricing representations on clothing items, not Fair Housing Act claims. The case concerns consumer fraud and false advertising in retail sales, not housing discrimination or reasonable accommodations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of monetary damages claims under the UTPA, holding that Clark adequately pleaded ascertainable loss under a 'purchase price theory' where she was induced to purchase items in reliance on misrepresented price history. The court affirmed dismissal of disgorgement/restitution claims for failure to plead inadequate remedy at law, and reversed dismissal of injunctive relief claim, finding Clark has Article III standing based on Davidson v. Kimberly-Clark Corp., though a dissent argued TransUnion undermined that precedent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed summary judgment for the defendant, holding that the anti-harboring statute does not plausibly create criminal liability for landlords merely leasing to undocumented immigrants in the ordinary course of business. The statute requires active concealment or harboring with intent to shield from detection, not passive housing. The court found Waples failed to meet its burden at Step Two of the Inclusive Communities framework because the policy did not serve a legitimate, plausible interest in avoiding prosecution, and the record was too thin to support a business necessity defense given Waples's inconsistent enforcement and failure to evict noncompliant tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of business license requirement to open utility accounts in the name of the Oxford House group homes
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-element failure-to-accommodate test and found that plaintiffs failed to establish the necessity prong. The accommodation (waiver of business license requirement) was not necessary to address the effects of residents' substance use disability because: (1) therapeutic arguments lacked evidentiary support—residents would not be the ones filing licenses, and no evidence showed that filing a license would harm familial bonds or the Oxford House model; and (2) financial arguments were speculative and lacked concrete evidence that residents' addiction created inability to afford potential rent increases.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs asserted an intentional discrimination claim but did not appeal the district court's grant of summary judgment in the City's favor on this claim; the appellate opinion does not substantively address the merits of the disparate treatment theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maintenance issues and safety complaints
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's amended complaint failed to plausibly allege discrimination because of race, sex, disability, or any other legally cognizable protected class; the allegations regarding maintenance and safety issues did not illustrate discrimination based on a protected characteristic.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims; Pennsylvania Address Confidentiality Program (ACP) violations under 23 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 6707
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court sua sponte dismissed the ACP claim without analyzing whether the statute implies a private right of action; the appellate court vacated and remanded for the District Court to consider in the first instance whether § 6707 implies a private right of action and whether plaintiff plausibly stated a claim. ADA claims were not separately analyzed on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessibility information on hotel websites regarding accessible rooms, as required by the ADA Reservation Rule (28 CFR § 36.302(e)(1)(ii))
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court vacated the First Circuit's judgment as moot after Laufer voluntarily dismissed her case with prejudice following sanctions against her attorney. The Court did not reach the merits of the standing question, though Justice Thomas's concurrence argues Laufer lacked Article III standing because she alleged no violation of her own rights—the ADA prohibits discrimination based on disability, not failure to provide information, and Laufer disclaimed any intent to visit the hotel.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of zoning ordinance limiting occupancy to four unrelated persons to allow seven unrelated recovering alcoholics and substance abusers to reside together in a single-family home in an R-1 zone
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment for plaintiffs, holding that genuine issues of material fact existed regarding whether the requested accommodation was reasonable and necessary. The court found that plaintiffs failed to present sufficient evidence to the City Council demonstrating that seven residents were indispensable (rather than merely preferable) for therapeutic purposes, and that financial viability of the business alone cannot justify an accommodation without proof that sober homes as a category need such accommodations. The court applied the burden-shifting framework requiring plaintiffs to prove reasonableness and necessity, with defendant able to rebut by showing undue burden or fundamental alteration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court did not rule on the disparate treatment claim, noting only that genuine issues of material fact existed. The appellate court declined to grant summary judgment in favor of the City on appeal, holding that the district court should have the initial opportunity to address this claim on remand, and that disputed factual issues preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court did not rule on the disparate impact claim, noting only that genuine issues of material fact existed. The appellate court declined to grant summary judgment in favor of the City on appeal, holding that the district court should have the initial opportunity to address this claim on remand, and that disputed factual issues preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claims for failure to provide reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment/disparate impact discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed FHA and ADA claims together under the same legal framework, as both statutes apply to municipal zoning decisions and use nearly identical language regarding disability and reasonable accommodations. The ADA reasonable accommodation claim was reversed on the same grounds as the FHA claim—genuine issues of material fact regarding necessity and reasonableness precluded summary judgment for plaintiffs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1691(a)); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (civil rights contract claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the Individuals' ECOA and § 1981 claims for failure to state a plausible claim. The court held that guarantors are not 'applicants' under the ECOA except for purposes of the signature rules, which were not alleged here. For § 1981, the court found the Individuals lacked statutory standing because they failed to identify injuries flowing from their own contractual relationship with the bank, only from CDMR's proposed relationship. The appellate court affirmed on all grounds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts supporting intentional discrimination based on race or disability. The complaint contained only legal conclusions (that the failure to maintain was 'disparate treatment') and bare allegations of protected class membership without factual allegations connecting Defendants' conduct to discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of D.C. housing laws (Counts III, IV, V); violations of 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 371, 1341 (Counts I, VI, VII, VIII)
fha_claims.reasoning: Criminal statutes (§§ 241, 242, 371, 1341) do not create private causes of action. D.C. law claims lack federal question jurisdiction and diversity jurisdiction is absent because plaintiffs and defendants share D.C. citizenship. Court declined supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for more time to move/delay of eviction due to disability (Crohn's disease)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing he was disabled within the FHA definition (did not allege how Crohn's disease substantially limits major life activities beyond hospitalization and transfusion). Additionally, even if disability were established, the requested accommodation (delay of eviction) is not facially reasonable because it does not address the needs created by the disability and would constitute a fundamental alteration requiring removal of the 'hump' rather than merely saddling the camel.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim fails due to temporal sequence: AMH initiated eviction proceedings on March 4, 2021, and sent multiple move-out notices on March 9, 10, 15, and 19, but plaintiff did not send his accommodation request until March 20, 2021. Because the allegedly retaliatory action (eviction notices) preceded the protected activity (accommodation request), plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to support a retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 procedural due process claim; Fourth Amendment claim (not renewed on appeal)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a constitutionally protected property interest necessary for a procedural due process claim. The building was never demolished, and plaintiff has no property interest in procedures themselves or in market consequences of a notice of an appealable building-code order.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow plaintiff to keep a registered emotional support animal (dog) in rental property despite landlord's 'no dogs' policy
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found that defendant had constructive knowledge of plaintiff's disability based on rental application disclosing 'registered support animal' and subsequent emails identifying it as an emotional support animal; defendant's blanket 'no dogs' policy violated FHAA § 3604(f)(3)(B) by failing to provide reasonable accommodation. Appellate court affirmed, finding no clear error in the district court's factual findings regarding defendant's knowledge and the violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) § 12955 violation; state negligence law claim
fha_claims.reasoning: District court held that defendant violated FEHA § 12955 (parallel to FHAA) and state negligence law by denying rental application based on no-dogs policy; appellate court affirmed the judgment without separately analyzing the non-FHA claims, indicating they were resolved on the same factual and legal basis as the FHAA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves claims under the Communications Decency Act § 230(c)(1), not the Fair Housing Act. The claims are: (1) negligence, (2) breach of contract, (3) breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, (4) violation of California's Unfair Competition Law (UCL), and (5) unjust enrichment, all arising from Meta's alleged failure to prevent fraudulent third-party advertisements on its platform.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of non-contract claims (negligence, unjust enrichment, UCL) under CDA § 230(c)(1) immunity because they seek to treat Meta as a publisher or speaker of third-party content and do not require Meta to materially contribute to the unlawfulness. The court vacated dismissal of contract claims (breach of contract and breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing) because they derive from Meta's contractual duty to moderate advertisements, not from its status as a publisher, and thus § 230(c)(1) does not apply.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for Exception to Payment Standard under Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher program to increase the subsidy cap above the standard payment amount, allowing the landlord to finance accessibility modifications (bathroom and structural modifications) and recoup costs from the increased subsidy payments.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that as a matter of law, landlords are not required under the FHA to apply for government funding or exception payment standards as a reasonable accommodation. The court rejected the expansion of FHA obligations to require landlords to petition housing authorities for such accommodations, finding no case law or regulatory support for this theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged refusal to rent the unit to plaintiff based on his disability status.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no genuine dispute of material fact regarding discriminatory motive. Defendants established a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for cancellation (inability to afford $30,840 in modifications and lack of government funding), and plaintiff failed to present evidence beyond speculation that this reason was pretextual or that animus against disabled persons motivated the decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) disability discrimination claim, Unruh Civil Rights Act § 51 claim, retaliation claims under FHA and FEHA, and negligence claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed FEHA and Unruh Act claims coextensively with FHA claims under the same reasonable accommodation framework and applied the same legal standards. All state law claims failed on the same bases as the FHA claims: the requested accommodation was not legally required, and there was no evidence of discriminatory motive. Retaliation and negligence claims were not separately analyzed but were encompassed in the summary judgment ruling.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the ground that Plaintiff failed to demonstrate immediate and irreparable injury due to unreasonable delay in seeking relief (more than five years from initial move-in, fourteen months through DFEH process, nearly one year in federal court before filing the motion). The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself, noting that dispositive motions are under submission and trial is forthcoming.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Upgrade of Plaintiff's apartment windows to double-paned windows to reduce noise intrusion as an accommodation for his disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction for the window upgrade on the ground that the cost of windows is easily calculable and compensable in damages, and thus does not constitute irreparable harm warranting mandatory injunctive relief. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Civil Code § 54.1 (disability discrimination) and negligence claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on procedural grounds (failure to demonstrate irreparable injury and unreasonable delay) without reaching the merits of the state law claims. The claims survive and remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff's claims for unpaid rent under California Civil Code § 1951.2 and fraudulent inducement/promissory fraud. Defendant's counterclaims for Fair Housing Act violations (42 U.S.C. § 3604), violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1982, and state law claims for discrimination, stalking, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's partial motion for summary judgment on his state law claims (unpaid rent and fraud) because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the gas leak's impact on habitability and rent obligation, and fraud claims involve fact-intensive issues of intent and reliance unsuitable for summary judgment. Defendant's FHA counterclaims were not addressed in this opinion as the motion targeted only plaintiff's claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Upgrade of windows in plaintiff's apartment unit to reduce external noise exacerbating plaintiff's disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court classified the window upgrade request as a reasonable modification under § 3604(f)(3)(A) rather than an accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), because it requires a physical change to the premises. Under the FHA, the tenant bears the expense of modifications, and it is undisputed that plaintiff refused to pay for the windows, so the claim fails as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assignment of the Preferred Parking Space (located directly in front of plaintiff's unit) as reserved parking to accommodate plaintiff's mobility disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the parking accommodation claim on two independent grounds: (1) defendants failed to serve plaintiff with the unredacted moving memorandum, depriving plaintiff of notice of defendants' arguments; and (2) defendants failed to meet their burden as the moving party by not including material facts in their Statement of Uncontroverted Facts necessary to support their argument that alternative parking was offered at no cost and that relocation was reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Upgrade of windows in plaintiff's apartment unit to reduce external noise exacerbating plaintiff's disability (California Disabled Persons Act claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the California Disabled Persons Act § 54.1(b)(4), modifications of property are explicitly not required, so plaintiff's DPA claim based on the window upgrade request fails as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assignment of the Preferred Parking Space as reserved parking to accommodate plaintiff's mobility disability (California Disabled Persons Act claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the DPA parking accommodation claim on the same grounds as the FHA claim: defendants failed to serve the unredacted memorandum and failed to meet their burden by not including necessary material facts in their Statement of Uncontroverted Facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence and negligence per se claims under California common law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the negligence and negligence per se cause of action because the duty to provide reasonable accommodations is premised on statutory obligations under the FHA and DPA, not on common law theories of negligence, and plaintiff abandoned the issue by not opposing it.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff proved defendant reasonably should have known of plaintiff's handicap and violated the reasonable accommodation provisions of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B). Plaintiff awarded $14,800 in compensatory damages for out-of-pocket losses in securing alternative housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) failure to reasonably accommodate claim; negligence claim
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) - Court Trial on the Briefs
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff proved violation of Cal. Gov't Code § 12955(c) (FEHA reasonable accommodation) and negligence claim. Both claims resulted in judgment in favor of plaintiff with compensatory damages award.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant VooRooGoo raised Fair Housing Act noncompliance as a potential defense to an unlawful detainer action, but no specific accommodation was requested or at issue.
fha_claims.disposition: Remand (12(b)(1) — lack of subject matter jurisdiction)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that defendant's allegation of FHA violation constitutes a potential defense or counterclaim, not a federal question presented on the face of plaintiff's properly pleaded complaint. Under the well-pleaded complaint rule and Caterpillar, federal law defenses do not confer federal question jurisdiction, and the court remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction without reaching the merits of any FHA claim.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that defendants failed to meet their burden of proving fraudulent joinder of the non-diverse defendant (Mr. Picano) by clear and convincing evidence. The court concluded there remained a non-fanciful possibility that a state court could find plaintiffs could state a claim against Mr. Picano under California law, thus diversity jurisdiction was lacking.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned handicapped parking space in front of plaintiff's apartment (the 'Requested Space'), which was located in a General (unassigned) parking area
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted judgment as a matter of law on the issue of whether the Reserved Parking Option (the alternative accommodation offered by defendant) was reasonable. The court found that substantial evidence established C.R. was capable of walking to the Reserved Parking Option space, which posed no greater risks than his routine community outings, and that Joffe's testimony to the contrary was inconsistent and amounted only to a scintilla of evidence. The court also granted JMOL on causation and damages, finding no legally sufficient evidence that PLB's refusal caused C.R. emotional harm or that any damages award was supported by evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Move to a different apartment unit with all desired amenities, including a Reserved parking space immediately near the unit (the 'Move Option')
fha_claims.reasoning: The court upheld the jury's verdict that the Move Option was not a reasonable alternative accommodation. Drawing all inferences in favor of C.R., substantial evidence supported that moving would be too traumatic for C.R., given his prior move in 2011 led to a partial six-month hospitalization and that changes to his routine or environment trigger dysregulation. The jury could credit Joffe and Curcio's testimony over the defendant's expert's contrary opinion regarding causation of the prior hospitalization.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Whether plaintiff's request for an assigned handicapped parking space constituted a request for an 'accommodation' (change to rules/policies) versus a 'modification' (physical alteration to premises)
fha_claims.reasoning: On the Rule 50(b) motion, the court upheld the jury's verdict that C.R.'s request was for an accommodation, not a modification, finding substantial evidence in testimony that Joffe wanted PLB to change its parking policy to allow her to reserve the Requested Space based on proximity, not handicap accessibility. However, on the Rule 59(a) motion for new trial, the court found the verdict against the clear weight of evidence, noting Joffe's written requests expressly sought 'an assigned handicapped parking space' with supporting medical documentation, and that Joffe's later testimony that she meant only a policy change was not credible given her education and sophistication.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant withheld rent claiming plaintiff discriminated against defendant in violation of the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff's complaint presented only a state law unlawful detainer claim; any federal FHA defense or counterclaim by the defendant cannot serve as a basis for federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, as federal jurisdiction must appear on the face of the plaintiff's complaint.

fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that defendants violated FEHA, awarding $98,000 in compensatory damages to the minor daughter. Unruh, Unfair Business Practices, and Negligence claims were voluntarily dismissed on the eve of trial.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court reviewed amended complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and concluded it did not state a viable FHA claim over which the court possessed subject matter jurisdiction. After multiple opportunities to amend and warning of futility, plaintiff failed to file a second amended complaint by the deadline, and the court dismissed the FHA claim without leave to amend.

fha_claims.disposition: Dismissal; supplemental jurisdiction declined under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims (fraud, Unruh Act, FEHA) under § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims over which it had original jurisdiction were resolved. Claims dismissed without prejudice; statute of limitations tolled for 30 days.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for complaining about neglect, mistreatment, exploitation, and abuse; claims he was either evicted or treated so harshly he had to leave for his own safety.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting an inference that he engaged in activity protected under the FHA. The complaint does not allege that his complaints addressed conduct that could reasonably be believed to constitute unlawful discrimination based on disability under the FHA, which is required to establish protected activity for a retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 504 Rehabilitation Act discrimination and harassment claims; ADA Title III discrimination, harassment, and retaliation claims; state law negligence, negligent hiring/retention/training/supervision, felonious injury, and menacing claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims dismissed for lack of Article III standing to seek injunctive relief (no allegation of likelihood to return to facility) and unavailability of damages under Title III. § 504 discrimination and harassment claims dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing denial of services or discrimination 'by reason of' disability—allegations focused on quality of medical care rather than equal opportunity to participate in services. § 504 retaliation claim failed because plaintiff did not allege protected activity under the Rehabilitation Act. State criminal statute claims (felonious injury, menacing) dismissed because the statutes establish only criminal offenses without creating private civil causes of action.
