S. Middlesex Opportunity Council, Inc. v. Town of Framingham, 752 F. Supp. 2d 85 (D. Mass. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statements indicating preference or intention to discriminate based on disability of intended residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c), the court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether defendants' statements (press releases, public forum statements, media interviews, emails) conveyed a prohibited preference or discrimination based on disability to an ordinary listener. The 'ordinary listener' standard is fact-intensive and requires jury determination of intent and interpretation, not summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making housing unavailable through series of discriminatory actions including cease and desist orders, tax exemption denials, and petitions to state agencies
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f), the court found sufficient record evidence for a reasonable jury to find that defendants acted with discriminatory intent to make housing unavailable based on disability. The 'otherwise make unavailable' language is broad and encompasses a series of actions imposing burdens on protected class members. Discriminatory intent can be inferred from totality of circumstances, including strong community opposition to which officials were responsive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of tax exempt status to 461 Main Street property in January 2018, after plaintiffs filed lawsuit to enforce FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, the court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether defendants retaliated against plaintiffs for exercising FHA rights. Prima facie elements are satisfied: protected activity (filing FHA lawsuit), defendants' awareness, adverse action (tax exemption denial despite prior grants), and causal connection (temporal proximity and pattern of discriminatory treatment).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claims based on same facts as FHA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same legal analysis to ADA and Section 504 claims as to FHA claims, finding that intentional discrimination claims under all three statutes are analyzed in tandem. Because genuine issues of material fact exist on the FHA claims, summary judgment is also denied on the ADA and Section 504 claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing in fraternity houses based on gender; plaintiffs sought membership in fraternities which would have entitled them to housing benefits
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish standing under the Fair Housing Act because the alleged injury (denial of housing) was not fairly traceable to the conduct of the landlords but rather to the fraternities' failure to admit women. The predicate act of denial of membership and the separate act of denial of housing do not necessarily follow from one another, and plaintiffs never alleged they sought to rent the same properties and were denied based on gender.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Discriminatory Housing Practices Act claim; Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act claim; Negligent Misrepresentation claim; Breach of Contract claim; Breach of Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing claim; Civil Conspiracy claim; Public Accommodations claims under Connecticut law
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Connecticut housing discrimination claims failed for the same reasons as the FHA claim. CUTPA and negligent misrepresentation claims lacked sufficient factual specificity and relied on recycled allegations already deemed legally insufficient. Breach of contract claims failed because plaintiffs could not identify specific contractual promises distinct from general educational quality obligations, which would constitute impermissible educational malpractice claims. Civil conspiracy claims failed because they depended on underlying tort claims that were themselves dismissed. Public accommodations claims failed because plaintiffs did not adequately plead that the fraternity houses constituted places of public accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3604(c) applies only to notices, statements, or advertisements with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling. The discriminatory statements made by inspectors during post-acquisition property inspections do not fall within the scope of § 3604(c) because they were not made with respect to the sale or rental of the dwelling itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3604(b) applies to post-acquisition conduct affecting the terms, conditions, or privileges of a dwelling when there is a contractual connection between the defendant's conduct and the terms and conditions related to the plaintiff's purchase. Here, the mortgage servicing relationship and the right to inspect the property under the mortgage deed constitute such a contractual connection, allowing the claim to survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3605 covers discrimination in the terms or conditions of residential real estate-related transactions, which includes not only the making of loans but also the purchasing of loans and providing financial assistance. The mortgage servicing relationship constitutes a residential real estate-related transaction, and the plaintiff has alleged discrimination in the terms and conditions of that transaction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 prohibits coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference with the exercise or enjoyment of FHA-protected rights. The plaintiff has alleged that she was engaged in the protected activity of living in her home, that defendants were aware of this activity, that they took adverse action through intimidation and threats, and that they explicitly connected her race to their conduct, satisfying all four elements of a § 3617 claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Trespass, negligent supervision, RESPA violation, CUTPA violations (unfair practices, deceptive practices, intentional/reckless violations)
fha_claims.reasoning: The trespass claim survives because the mortgage deed permitted only 'reasonable' entries and inspections, and the plaintiff has alleged facts that could establish the entries were unreasonable. The negligent supervision claim survives because the plaintiff has alleged that defendants knew or should have known that property inspection services involved an unreasonable risk of causing emotional distress and failed to adequately supervise. The RESPA claim survives because the plaintiff's qualified written request involved servicing of her loan by requesting a CARES Act forbearance and disputing incorrect information about lump sum repayment. The CUTPA claims survive because the plaintiff has alleged unfair and deceptive practices causing ascertainable loss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges racial slur uttered by security guard at DSS office, not a housing-related accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that § 3617 protects rights related to sale and rental of housing and real estate transactions. fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 Equal Protection claim; § 1983 due process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff failed to allege a direct causal link between a municipal policy or custom of New Haven and the security guard's utterance of a racial slur, as required under Monell and City of Canton. Plaintiff did not allege that New Haven had a policy directing such conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on race and cited 42 U.S.C. Chapter 21 (civil rights statutes) and § 3617 (Fair Housing Act retaliation/interference provision); also alleged harassment and intimidation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to state a cognizable claim because the facts alleged (store clerk asking plaintiff to change his shirt and replacing a mask string) do not demonstrate discriminatory intent based on race. Additionally, § 3617 claim failed because it applies only to housing and real estate transactions, and the events occurred at a secondhand store unrelated to housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing opportunity at Allure Apartments (sister property)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts supporting a plausible inference of discriminatory motivation. Although plaintiff alleged she was denied housing because of her race, the factual allegations contradicted this, suggesting instead that a neutral policy prevented tenants from breaking leases to move to newer buildings. Conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Differential treatment in terms and conditions of rental (noise policy enforcement and quiet hours)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing differential treatment of similarly situated persons based on race. The allegations suggested management treated 'friends' differently than plaintiff, but contained no factual allegations supporting the inference that differential treatment occurred because of plaintiff's race rather than personal relationships.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statements indicating preference or limitation based on race in rental advertisements or notices
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts that defendants or their agents made statements indicating a preference or limitation based on race with respect to rental of a dwelling, as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for exercising fair housing rights; hostile housing environment based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts that defendants had discriminatory animus motivating their actions or inactions, or that defendants subjected plaintiff to a hostile housing environment because of her race. Conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cited 42 U.S.C. § 3617 (Fair Housing Act interference/coercion provision) but complaint contains no facts relating to housing or real estate transactions.
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 of the Fair Housing Act safeguards protected class members from coercion and interference in exercise of FHA rights, but the complaint includes no facts relating to housing or real estate transactions, and therefore the FHA provisions are inapplicable and insufficient to confer subject matter jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (civil rights deprivation under color of state law); state law claims including sexual assault, assault and battery, emotional distress, and various Connecticut statutory violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claim against YNHH fails because YNHH is a private hospital with no allegations that it acted under color of state law; section 1983 claim against City of New Haven fails because plaintiff alleged only isolated acts by unidentified officers without pleading facts showing municipal policy, custom, or widespread practice required for municipal liability.

fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 prohibits interference with Fair Housing Act rights only as enumerated in sections 3603-3606, which define substantive violations in housing sales, rentals, and brokerage services. Plaintiff failed to allege that the clerk interfered with rights protected by the FHA, and the claim arises from a retail store transaction unrelated to housing, placing it outside the FHA's scope.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 2000a public accommodations discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 1981 racial discrimination, Ind. Code § 35-45-2-1 intimidation, Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act, common law tort, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-571c civil harassment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacks diversity jurisdiction (both parties are Connecticut citizens) and fails to state cognizable federal claims. Title VII does not apply absent an employment relationship; § 2000a claim lacks required administrative notice to CHRO; § 1981 claim fails because plaintiff alleges no facts connecting race to the alleged discrimination; remaining claims arise under state law or are not cognizable, and the court declines supplemental jurisdiction.

Plaintiff failed to identify any protected class basis for the alleged discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for prior complaint about an employee
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to allege facts suggesting coercion, intimidation, threatening, or interference with FHA rights under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. Allegations are conclusory and lack factual detail necessary to state a plausible retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI claim alleging discrimination in federal program receiving federal funding
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against HUD dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on sovereign immunity. HUD, as a federal agency, is shielded by sovereign immunity, and plaintiff failed to identify an applicable waiver of sovereign immunity under the Civil Rights Acts or the APA. Dismissal without prejudice as to Title VI claim to allow plaintiff to challenge HUD's Title VI compliance determination under the APA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the § 3617 claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint alleges no facts relating to housing or real estate transactions; § 3617 protects rights granted under FHA §§ 3603-3606, which are housing-specific, and the underlying allegations concern only a grocery store detention.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 2000a (public accommodations discrimination); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination in contract); 15 U.S.C. § 45c (unfair/deceptive practices); 28 U.S.C. § 4101 (defamation); 47 U.S.C. § 230 (internet platform immunity); 10 U.S.C. § 920 (military sexual assault); state law claims (CUTPA, common law defamation, battery, IIED, harassment, Tom Bane Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction: § 2000a claim failed because C-Town is a retail grocery store not covered by the statute and plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies with CHRO; § 1981 claim failed because plaintiff did not allege race was a but-for cause; § 45c, § 4101, § 230, and § 920 claims failed because they do not provide private rights of action or are inapplicable to the facts; state law claims cannot provide federal question jurisdiction and supplemental jurisdiction was declined.

Court found allegations lacked sufficient factual support under Iqbal/Twombly standard.

Claim survived motion for judgment on pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of reasonable accommodation for disability (unspecified accommodation and disability)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged CHRO denied reasonable accommodations for disability but failed to allege facts establishing what disability she has or what specific accommodation was denied. Allegations were conclusory and insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (discrimination in property rights), state law breach of contract, state law fraud
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1982 discrimination claim failed for same reasons as FHA discrimination claim (conclusory allegations). fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie case of national origin discrimination. Stray remarks by non-decisionmaker Kimberly Lindemann were speculative and unconnected to Board's decision. Comparators cited were not similarly situated. Defendants articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons (failure to obtain prior Board approval and alleged building code violations), and Plaintiffs failed to prove pretext by showing discrimination was the real reason.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' gender discrimination claim failed because evidence of alleged conduct by Board members (refusing to discuss rule violations, excluding Ledeneva from budget discussions) does not establish gender animus. Kimberly Lindemann's comments about others' motives were speculation without personal knowledge. Ledeneva's subjective belief of bias is insufficient to support inference of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Familial status discrimination claim failed because denial of playset while Kozo had trampoline does not establish discrimination based on family status. Both Plaintiffs and Kozo had children, so they were not treated differently because of familial status. Familial status discrimination requires showing adverse conduct based on presence of children, not differential treatment between families with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing discrimination complaint and threatening to defend rights in court, including removal of Ledeneva from Board
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants failed to adequately address retaliation claims in their motion, making only fleeting, conclusory reference in reply brief. Arguments not made in initial brief cannot be raised for first time in reply. Plaintiffs alleged retaliation after October 10 and October 12, 2018 protected activity (threatening court action and filing discrimination complaint), and genuine issue of material fact exists as to whether removal from Board and other conduct constituted retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged quid pro quo harassment: demand that Plaintiffs pave driveways for all homeowners as condition of approval
fha_claims.reasoning: Kozo's email comment that Plaintiffs should pave everyone's driveway was not a 'demand' under quid pro quo harassment standard. No reasonable juror could find the comment was a demand or that it was based on or related to national origin, gender, or familial status. Quid pro quo harassment requires unwelcome request or demand made a condition of housing-related benefit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged hostile housing environment based on national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: Hostile environment claim failed because evidence does not give rise to inference that Plaintiffs were harassed because of national origin or other protected status. Alleged conduct (false statements about building code violations, accusations of threats, threats of fines, statements about moving) was not sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter conditions of housing arrangement. Congress did not intend FHA to remedy every neighbor dispute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence (failure to train, monitor, supervise officers/Board members on FHA compliance); Negligent and Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (based on false accusations and unreasonable denial of step request); Defamation and Defamation Per Se (false statements in CHRO proceeding that Kalashnikov threatened physical violence); Perjury; Harassment; Extortion
fha_claims.reasoning: Negligence claim for failure to train/supervise on FHA compliance failed because no cognizable duty exists under FHA to train employees on fair housing laws. Negligent infliction of emotional distress failed because no evidence Defendants should have foreseen emotional distress causing illness or bodily harm. Intentional infliction failed because alleged conduct (denying request, false accusations, threats of fines) does not meet extreme and outrageous standard under Connecticut law. Defamation claims barred by absolute privilege for statements made in quasi-judicial CHRO proceedings. Perjury, harassment, and extortion are criminal offenses with no private civil causes of action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim of intimidation by store manager regarding mask-wearing policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 of the Fair Housing Act applies only to coercion, intimidation, threats, and interference in the context of 'the sale or rental of housing,' 'residential real estate-related transactions,' and 'the provision of brokerage services.' A restaurant mask-wearing policy falls outside the scope of FHA jurisdiction, making the claim frivolous as applied to this defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1964 discrimination claim; § 1981 racial discrimination claim; California CCP § 527.6 civil harassment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim under § 1981, which requires allegations of (1) membership in a racial minority, (2) defendant's intent to discriminate on the basis of race, and (3) discrimination concerning an enumerated activity. Plaintiff alleged no facts of racial discrimination. State law claim under CCP § 527.6 dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction due to absence of diversity of citizenship and decline of supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that CoreLogic does not 'make unavailable or deny' housing under § 3604(a)-(b) because the housing provider, not CoreLogic, makes all material decisions regarding applicant qualification, configuration of criminal record filters, access to records, and final acceptance/denial. CoreLogic's role is too tenuous to establish FHA liability; it merely provides information that housing providers use according to their own policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiffs failed to prove CoreLogic intentionally discriminated on the basis of race or national origin. The evidence showed CoreLogic's CrimSAFE product is a customizable tool controlled entirely by housing providers; CoreLogic does not make housing decisions and therefore cannot be liable for discriminatory intent in denying housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA); Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) §§ 1681g, 1681h
fha_claims.reasoning: Court ruled in favor of CoreLogic on CUTPA claims (which failed for the same reasons as FHA claims—CoreLogic does not make housing unavailable). Court ruled in favor of Mr. Arroyo on FCRA claims, finding CoreLogic violated 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681g and 1681h by requiring Ms. Arroyo to furnish a power of attorney (legally impossible for a conserved person) as a condition for disclosing Mr. Arroyo's consumer report from June 30, 2016 to November 14, 2016. fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of Fair Housing Act § 3617 (interference, coercion, or intimidation in connection with housing rights)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3) (racial discrimination); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (conspiracy to violate equal protection); Connecticut state law claims of nuisance, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, slander, negligent infliction of emotional distress, CUTPA violation, and anti-intimidation statute violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury returned a verdict for the defendants on all federal civil rights claims (§§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3), § 1983) and most state law claims. The jury found liability only on two state law claims (slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress) but awarded zero damages on both, which the court upheld on the motion for new trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim: denial of credit increases and personal loan to 92-year-old Lillian Clark
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint lacks sufficient factual detail regarding loan applications, dates, reasons for denials, and fails to allege that Santander continued business with younger applicants. Conclusory and vague allegations do not satisfy Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Race discrimination claim: poor customer service at bank branch based on plaintiff's Asian descent
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff fails to allege he was attempting to engage in a residential real estate transaction or credit transaction. Insufficient allegations that poor customer service was based on race rather than other factors. Individual defendants not alleged to be involved in discriminatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Redlining claim: denial of credit increases and personal loan based on property location in working-class/blue-collar town
fha_claims.reasoning: Allegations are vague and conclusory. Complaint lacks specific details about applications, dates, and reasons for denials. Cannot support plausible redlining claim under Fair Housing Act or ECOA without more concrete factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal criminal statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 1005, 1341), FDCPA (15 U.S.C. § 1692e), Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. § 1125), state law claims (negligence, abuse of process, breach of contract, emotional distress, wrongful death, CUTPA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Federal criminal statutes do not provide private rights of action. Fraud claims fail Rule 9(b) heightened pleading standard—bare-bones allegations without specificity as to fraudulent statements, speakers, time/place, and reasons for fraud. FDCPA claim against Santander fails because Santander is a creditor, not a debt collector. Lanham Act claim fails because consumers lack standing under the statute. State law claims barred by res judicata, collateral estoppel, litigation privilege, or failure to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation (42 U.S.C. § 12203), state law tort claims, First Amendment retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA retaliation claim dismissed for failure to allege plaintiff was an employee or establish any element beyond bare retaliation allegation. First Amendment retaliation claim improper against private defendants. Grullon v. City of New Haven, 720 F.3d 133 (2d Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges racial discrimination in foreclosure conduct, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead FHA violations with specificity required by Twombly and Iqbal. Allegations of racial discrimination based solely on Carla Karlen's race, without disparate impact analysis, case law citations, or factual examples of discriminatory intent, are conclusory and insufficient to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges unlawful practices in selling, brokering, and appraising premises.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' allegations lack legal analysis and factual basis. The claim invokes 24 C.F.R. § 135 but provides only circular logic ('as a result of such actions, Plaintiffs have been damaged by an incalculable amount') without connecting facts to any legal violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory conduct during foreclosure and subsequent litigation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs tie conclusory statements to no violation of law and allege no real damage. The pleading fails to meet Twombly and Iqbal standards for plausibility.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges racial animus and malicious behavior during foreclosure action and subsequent litigation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Four mentions no law at all and fails to allege facts sufficient to state a plausible claim under Twombly and Iqbal. Additionally, Connecticut's litigation privilege doctrine bars claims related to conduct of legal proceedings, and plaintiffs fail to allege abuse of process required to overcome the privilege.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Effective communication accommodations including permission to pass notes during Board meetings and requirement that other members face plaintiff when speaking; auxiliary aids and services for elected Board member with autism and hearing impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found defendants violated Title II of the ADA and Section 504 by failing to provide effective communication and auxiliary aids and services to plaintiff as an elected Board member; jury rejected defendants' undue burden defense, finding that providing accommodations would not have imposed an undue burden.

case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Robert Rizzo, et al.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court liberally construed pro se allegations and found plaintiff adequately alleged harassment and retaliation under § 3617 based on complaints about unsafe conditions and alleged course of conduct that was threatening and intimidating, allowing plaintiff to proceed against specified defendants on this claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II or Title III disability discrimination claim; 18 U.S.C. § 241 conspiracy claim
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA and Fair Housing Act claims based on events prior to February 25, 2018 are barred by the applicable two-year statute of limitations period, as the complaint was filed February 25, 2020. Criminal conspiracy claim under 18 U.S.C. § 241 dismissed as frivolous because plaintiff lacks standing to prosecute criminal charges; only the United States Attorney may bring criminal prosecutions.

case_name: David Q. Webb v. State of Delaware, et al.
key_cases_cited: Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275 (2001)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing at New Castle County Hope Center based on familial status (plaintiff is a single male without minor children)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for FHA discrimination because he is a single male without minor children and therefore does not fall within the protected class of 'familial status' as defined by 42 U.S.C. § 3602(k). The FHA prohibits discrimination against families with minor children, and plaintiff's allegations do not speak to discrimination based on any protected characteristic under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI Civil Rights Act claims; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims (Counts II-VI); Ninth Amendment claim (Count V); deliberate ignorance claim (Count VII); housing conditions claim under Section 8 of the Housing Act (Count IX); state law negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and vicarious liability claims (Counts X-XIII)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI claims dismissed for conclusory allegations without factual basis for intentional discrimination. § 1983 claims against state and state officials in official capacities barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity; claims against county executive Meyer fail to plead Monell liability. Ninth Amendment claim not cognizable under § 1983. Deliberate ignorance claim not cognizable under federal law. Housing conditions claim under Section 8 fails because no private right of action exists. State law negligence claims barred by sovereign immunity and Delaware State Tort Claims Act. IIED claims fail to identify specific outrageous conduct with sufficient factual detail. Vicarious liability claim fails because underlying claims are not cognizable.

case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Robert Rizzo, et al.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Lloyd v. Presby's Inspired Life, 251 F. Supp. 3d 891 (E.D. Pa. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations against NCCHA Defendants fail to state a plausible § 3617 retaliation claim because: (1) requesting bank statements and raising rent in response to non-compliance are not retaliatory acts—they are authorized regulatory actions; (2) failure to provide documents is not a protected activity; (3) biennial inspection schedule was compliant with regulations; and (4) alleged deficiencies existed in prior inspections, breaking any causal link between complaints and adverse actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations against Greenlawn Defendants and Fairville Management Company fail to state a plausible § 3617 interference claim. Requesting renters' insurance after water damage is reasonable and not retaliatory (same request made to similarly situated neighbor). Service providers entering apartment for scheduled appointments, while potentially questionable under state law, does not rise to the level of severe or pervasive interference required under § 3617, as distinguished by case law involving sustained harassment campaigns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff references 'Source of Income Discrimination' and alleges wrongful eviction attempts, refusal to cooperate with rental assistance program (DEHAP), and unauthorized rent increases, but does not clearly identify which FHA provisions apply or what specific accommodation is sought.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, finding it unclear under which FHA provisions plaintiff was attempting to bring her claims and that she alleged precious few factual allegations with specificity. Plaintiff was granted leave to file an amended complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether disability was the but-for cause of denial versus financial unqualification (failure to meet 30% rent-to-income ratio). Salazar presented evidence of legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for rejection, and disputes exist as to rental application requirements and Root's qualifications.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), Salazar's undisputed statements expressing preference against renting to a person with mobility impairments (e.g., 'Renting that building to a handicap person with challenging mobility motor skills will be doing a dishonesty') satisfy all three elements: statement made, with respect to rental, indicating preference/discrimination based on handicap. An ordinary listener would understand these statements as expressing a preference against renting to persons with mobility disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Orlando City Code §§ 57.48 and 57.49
fha_claims.reasoning: Orlando City Code § 57.48 is substantially identical to 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1) and receives the same analysis; summary judgment denied on same grounds as federal disparate treatment claim. Orlando City Code § 57.49 is substantially identical to 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) and receives the same analysis; summary judgment granted on same grounds as federal discriminatory statements claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mold remediation and repair of water damage to the home caused by Hurricane Irma, necessary to address the effects of S.C.'s severe asthma triggered by mold exposure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged all four elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim: disability (severe asthma substantially limiting major life activities), request for accommodation (mold remediation), necessity (to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling), and refusal. The court rejected defendants' argument that mold remediation cannot be a reasonable accommodation, finding that the consequences of mold exposure to S.C. require greater care than for an average tenant, and that mold remediation is not specifically required by Florida law for non-disabled tenants, making it a disability-specific need.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Same mold remediation and water damage repair claim brought under the Florida Fair Housing Act (FFHA), Fla. Stat. § 760.23(9)(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FFHA claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to allege compliance with the mandatory administrative exhaustion requirement under Fla. Stat. § 760.34, which requires filing a complaint with the Florida Commission on Human Relations and participating in the statutory conciliation process before commencing a civil action. The court followed binding intermediate Florida appellate court precedent holding that administrative exhaustion is a condition precedent to filing a judicial action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that defendants made housing unavailable under § 3604(a). The court found that defendants, as a law firm offering foreclosure assistance services, lacked the power to make housing unavailable—only the lenders held that power. Reverse redlining theory did not transform an unactionable claim into an actionable one.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected § 3604(b) claim for discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of sale/rental or in provision of services. Plaintiffs failed to allege that defendants provided services recognized as actionable under the FHA. Offering assistance in obtaining mortgage modifications from third-party lenders is not the same as providing the types of services (insurance, lending, etc.) contemplated by § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs failed to allege facts plausibly supporting that defendants' business includes engaging in residential real estate-related transactions under § 3605(a). Providing assistance with obtaining mortgage modifications does not constitute providing 'financial assistance' within the meaning of § 3605(b)(1). Defendants did not provide funds to clients; they merely assisted with paperwork.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3617 claim for failure to clearly identify which FHA rights were allegedly infringed and how defendants interfered with those rights. Plaintiffs' theory was shifting and unclear, with the United States merely tracking statutory language without explanation and Intervenors changing their theory in their response brief. Dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the United States' § 3614 pattern or practice claim because it is derivative of the underlying FHA violations under §§ 3604, 3605, and 3617. Since plaintiffs failed to allege plausible violations under those provisions, they could not establish a pattern or practice of violations. Dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Correction of improper walkway/ramp grades for access to office, swimming pool, gym, and apartment; removal of obstructed paths; provision of accessible handicap parking spaces; replacement of noncompliant doorknobs and latches; correction of noncompliant sink, tub, shower, and toilet in apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under Twombly/Iqbal standard, finding that structural improvements and construction/repair are not reasonable accommodations under § 3604(f)(3)(B), which applies only to accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services, not physical alterations to property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remedy of defective construction including entrance grades, doors, and locks in common areas and apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under §§ 3604(f)(1) and (2), which do not provide relief for failure to remedy defective construction and do not constitute independent acts of prohibited discrimination. Court noted that such claims must be brought under § 3604(f)(3) and only against the property owner involved in initial design and construction.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3604(a) claim (making unavailable or denying a dwelling based on national origin) as failing to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard; allegations did not plausibly connect Defendants' conduct to denial of housing based on national origin.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3604(b) claim (discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental based on national origin) as failing to state a plausible claim; allegations fell outside the scope of that provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3605 claim (discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions based on national origin) because Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that Defendants' business included engaging in residential real estate-related transactions as defined in that section.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss § 3617 claim (coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference with exercise of housing rights), finding that Plaintiffs' allegations were sufficient to state a plausible claim under the broad language and remedial purpose of the FHA, even though the facts differed from typical § 3617 cases.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss § 3614 claim (pattern or practice of resistance to full enjoyment of FHA rights), finding that because the § 3617 claims survived, the § 3614 claim alleging a pattern or practice of § 3617 violations also survives as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; opinion addresses settlement approval procedure only, not substantive claims
fha_claims.disposition: Settlement approval motion denied without prejudice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to approve the proposed settlement because the parties failed to submit the executed settlement agreement and did not address whether non-disclosure provisions were appropriate for filing in the public record. The court did not reach the merits of any underlying claims, including the FHA claim referenced in the Amended Complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Selective enforcement of Florida Statute § 316.212 (golf cart prohibition on sidewalks) to permit use of golf cart as mobility device; Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims for denial of reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found plaintiffs plausibly alleged all elements of Title II ADA and Section 504 claims by asserting they are disabled and denied benefit of using sidewalks due to failure to provide reasonable accommodation of selective enforcement. Court rejected defendant's arguments that plaintiffs failed to state a claim, finding fact-specific reasonableness inquiry appropriate for summary judgment stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to repair sliding glass doors in unit; denial of access to BuildingLink online forum; denial of access to records
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Counts One and Two sufficiently pleaded under Twombly standard; allegations of discriminatory acts (failure to repair common elements, blocking from message board) gave defendants adequate notice of claims and survived motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Condominium Act violation; Breach of Fiduciary Duty; Breach of Association Covenants
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count Six (Florida Condominium Act) because statutory immunity for officers/directors does not apply to willful violations of rights; Count Seven (Breach of Fiduciary Duty) survived as to Daly, Schwartz, and Petruzzella but was dismissed in part as to Walters with leave to amend for lack of clear fiduciary basis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial discrimination under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Federal Fair Housing Act, Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, and premises liability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because only defendants may remove an action from state court to federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a). Plaintiff, as the party who initiated the action, lacked authority to remove it herself. The case was remanded to state court.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff, proceeding pro se, improperly removed the case from state court. Removal statutes contemplate removal only by state-court defendants, not by plaintiffs. The case was remanded to state court without reaching the merits of any claim.

source_file: 9642893_2022_Suntree Master Homeowners Association, Inc. v. Frison_flmd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendants asserted a Fair Housing Act defense regarding Plaintiff's inspection, but no specific accommodation was requested or at issue.
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that removal was improper because the FHA claim was raised only as a defense to the plaintiff's state-law claims for unpaid assessments, not as an independent federal question in the complaint. Federal defenses do not provide a basis for removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1331.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use of golf cart as mobility device on public sidewalks in Pasco County; Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiffs' motion to exclude expert testimony regarding whether the requested accommodation (golf cart use on sidewalks) was reasonable and safe under the ADA and Section 504. The case involves Title II ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, not FHA claims. The motion was procedural (Daubert gatekeeping); the underlying reasonable accommodation claim on the merits remains pending for trial.

source_file: 9643667_2022_Weekley Homes, LLC v. Board of County Commissioners_flmd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from School Impact Fee for age-restricted community (Communities for Older Persons) under FHA Housing for Older Persons Act exemption; plaintiff sought exemption despite Encore Declaration lacking mandatory 30-year irrevocable non-revocation clause required by County Ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Weekley Homes failed to state a plausible 'class of one' Equal Protection claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it could not identify a similarly situated comparator—all other communities that received the exemption had the required 30-year irrevocable non-revocation clause that Encore lacked, making them dissimilar as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Equal Protection claim; Florida Statutes Chapter 86 declaratory judgment claims regarding constitutionality of County School Impact Fee Ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law declaratory judgment claims (Counts II and III) because they raised novel issues of Florida state law, all federal claims were dismissed, and comity, judicial economy, and fairness favored remand to state court where the case was originally filed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as a shotgun pleading for failure to provide adequate notice of claims and grounds. Plaintiff alleged national origin discrimination based on leasing agent's statement that she 'does not like Cubans,' but complaint failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure pleading requirements through vague, conclusory allegations and improper incorporation of counts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim dismissed for failure to plead the third element of prima facie retaliation—causal link between protected activity and adverse action. Plaintiff alleged defendants used 'endless delays' as retaliation but provided no factual explanation of how the delay was causally related to his verbal complaint, merely reciting legal conclusions without supporting facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI claims dismissed as shotgun pleading. Plaintiff failed to substantiate that defendants received federal financial assistance (required element of Title VI), and individual defendants (Ms. Moran and Mr. Diaz-Gines) are not proper defendants under Title VI, which applies only to 'programs or activities' receiving federal funds, not individual employees. Complaint failed to place defendants on adequate notice of which defendants were liable under which statute.

source_file: 9644128_2022_Rood v. Town of Ft. Myers Beach_flmd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Special exemption to build a dune walkover (elevated structure traversing two coastal lagoons) across environmentally critical zoning land to provide beach access from plaintiff's property
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to request an accommodation (vague wheelchair references in environmental proceedings did not constitute clear notice of disability or accommodation need); even if a request had been made, the Dune Walkover would fundamentally alter the Town's environmentally critical zoning scheme, was not necessary to address plaintiff's actual disability (cane use for balance, not wheelchair use), and would provide preferential treatment rather than equal access, as plaintiff had alternative public beach access options available.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cites FHA §§ 3603-3606 and § 3617 alleging discrimination and harassment in connection with homeowner's association disputes over pool deposit return and assessment charges; no disability or protected class basis identified.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to identify any protected class status (race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin) and the conduct complained of (pool deposit delay and assessment misclassification) does not fit within any prohibited discrimination enumerated in § 3604. The FHA claims are wholly insubstantial and frivolous, insufficient to confer federal question jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim of racial discrimination in mortgage lending under the Fair Housing Act because they did not allege that defendants knew of Shanita Lane's race, did not specify which FHA provisions were violated, failed to allege disparate treatment compared to similarly situated applicants, and did not allege any injury. The conclusory allegations and email correspondence provided were insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the two-dog rule to allow Parisi's support dog (Rokco) to remain in the residence along with Clark's two pet dogs (Soonie and Riley), for a total of three dogs.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself. The opinion addresses only whether certain affirmative defenses should be stricken. The Second Affirmative Defense (failure to exhaust) was denied as properly asserted, and the Fourth Affirmative Defense (that the accommodation is not reasonable) was stricken as not a proper affirmative defense but rather a denial of an element plaintiffs must prove. The claim survives and proceeds to further litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illegal intimidation and threats under the FHA.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the interference/coercion claim. The opinion addresses only affirmative defenses and does not substantively analyze the elements of this claim. The claim survives the procedural ruling and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illegal discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of the sale or rental of a dwelling based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing plaintiff to keep emotional support animal (assistance dog) despite dog's involvement in altercation with another resident's dog
fha_claims.reasoning: At the motion to dismiss stage, plaintiff plausibly alleged that defendant made housing unavailable because of his disability by forcing him to choose between his home and his assistance animal. Although defendant claimed it terminated the lease for violation of pet removal notice, plaintiff adequately alleged the adverse action was taken because of his disability, citing defendant's knowledge of the animal's status and failure to conduct individual assessment or explore less drastic alternatives.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing plaintiff to keep his emotional support dog (Zena) under mitigative measures such as keeping the dog on plaintiff's property and not allowing it off-leash
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged all four elements of a failure to accommodate claim: disability (mental health impairment), request for accommodation (through brother's letter), necessity (emotional support animal needed for disability), and refusal (defendant's denial). Court rejected defendant's argument that the request was not for an accommodation to rules/policies and that it was facially unreasonable, finding that reasonableness is a question of fact and plaintiff adequately alleged mitigative measures and lack of significant threat.

fha_claims.reasoning: The Fair Housing Act claim is time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which provides a two-year statute of limitations. The allegedly discriminatory acts occurred in summer 2018, over two years before the May 25, 2023 complaint was filed, and plaintiff offered no basis for tolling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment claim; § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment race discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claims are time-barred under the four-year statute of limitations applicable in Florida. The eviction occurred in August 2018, over four years before the May 25, 2023 complaint was filed. Additionally, the § 1983 claims fail because plaintiff alleges no facts showing that PMM, a private landlord, acted under color of state law, which is required for § 1983 liability.

The court found that the tolling provision under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(B) applies to administrative proceedings, and the status of the HUD complaint is unclear from the complaint itself, so the claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of no-pets policy and pet deposit requirement for service dog (German Shepherd named Kai trained to assist plaintiff with disabilities) under Tampa Code of Ordinances § 12-82
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts III and IV (Tampa ordinance claims) are time-barred because the statute of limitations began to run in May 2019 when the discriminatory act occurred and expired in May 2021. The Tampa Code of Ordinances § 12-113(a)(1) provides a two-year statute of limitations with no tolling provision for administrative proceedings, unlike the federal FHA. Plaintiff did not file the complaint until August 23, 2022, more than a year after expiration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to have emotional support animal (cat) in common areas of dorm building, not confined to plaintiff's room
fha_claims.reasoning: Eleventh Amendment immunity bars FHA claims against state university board of trustees. The FHA does not contain an explicit waiver of sovereign immunity, and Congress did not make unmistakably clear its intent to abrogate state sovereign immunity under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on disability in housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Eleventh Amendment immunity bars FHA disparate treatment claims against state university board of trustees and property owner acting as state agent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for requesting accommodation (emotional support animal in common areas), including imposition of sanctions, lease termination, lock-out, and removal of personal belongings
fha_claims.reasoning: Eleventh Amendment immunity bars FHA retaliation claims under § 3617 against state university board of trustees. Ex parte Young exception does not apply because plaintiff asserted no § 1983 claims against state officers for prospective equitable relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation for emotional support animal; breach of contract; fraudulent inducement; breach of implied covenant of good faith; unconscionability; tortious intimidation; unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II does not protect emotional support animals, only service animals; consequently the ADA claim fails as a matter of law. Eleventh Amendment immunity bars breach of contract, tort, and quasi-contractual claims against state university in federal court. Florida has not waived sovereign immunity for these claims.

The temporal gap between the second accommodation request and the eviction notice made the causal connection implausible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing Friedel I lawsuit and submitting accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found it implausible that the eviction was retaliatory for filing Friedel I or submitting accommodation requests when the most plausible explanation was that Park Place prevailed at trial proving the dog was dangerous and plaintiffs refused to remove it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing; tortious business interference
fha_claims.reasoning: Breach of covenant claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to identify any express provision of the lease agreement that was breached, as required under Florida law. Tortious interference claim dismissed because the alleged interference (eviction) was justified by the jury verdict in Friedel I.

The prior judgment was final and on the merits, and Defendant is in privity with HHA as an employee whose conduct formed the basis of the claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 false arrest and Fourth Amendment violations; state tort law false arrest claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 false arrest and Fourth Amendment claims, along with state tort false arrest claims, are barred by res judicata because they arise from the same May 17, 2016 incident and nucleus of operative facts as claims adjudicated in Hilliard I. The summary judgment order in Hilliard I granted judgment for HHA on the § 1983 false arrest claim (Count I) following substantive merits analysis, constituting a final adjudication on the merits that precludes relitigation of these claims against Defendant in privity with HHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact regarding all three elements of a § 3617 interference claim: plaintiff exercised protected right to be free from sexual harassment, defendant's posting of lease violation notices and eviction attempt constituted interference, and close temporal proximity of a few days established causal connection between protected activity and interference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida state law claims under § 760.37 and § 760.23(2), Florida Statutes
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the same McDonnell Douglas framework and causation standards to the parallel Florida state law claims as to the FHA claims, finding genuine issues of material fact on all elements and denying summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act discrimination claim; CARES Act federal eviction ban violation; Civil Rights Act violations
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction; Colorado River Abstention
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the removed state-court eviction case because removal was improper (counterclaims cannot form the basis for federal question jurisdiction), diversity jurisdiction was not established (incomplete diversity and amount in controversy insufficient at $7,736.42), and removal was procedurally untimely (filed 80 days after the 30-day removal deadline). Additionally, even if the court had original jurisdiction, it would abstain under Colorado River because the federal and state proceedings involve substantially the same parties and issues, creating potential for piecemeal litigation and forum shopping.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant asserted Fair Housing Act discrimination and Title VII race discrimination as a defense/counterclaim to eviction, but the complaint itself does not allege any FHA claim on its face.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the state court complaint is a straightforward unlawful detainer action under Florida law. Federal question jurisdiction does not exist on the face of the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint; defenses or counterclaims based on federal law (including the FHA) cannot confer federal question jurisdiction. The court never reached the merits of any FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of alternative temporary residency within an Extended Stay America Hotel and discharge from Camillus House residential facility despite disability (extreme angina) and homelessness.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as an impermissible shotgun pleading that fails to provide defendants adequate notice of claims and grounds, violates Rule 10(b) by combining multiple defendants, incidents, and legal theories in single paragraphs, and fails to separate distinct causes of action into different counts. Court did not reach substantive merits of FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of federal housing based on color, race, and national origin as a disabled senior citizen.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as shotgun pleading lacking minimum clarity and coherence required by Rules 8 and 10. Court did not reach substantive merits of discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges coercion, intimidation, threatening, and interference by defendants.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as shotgun pleading. Court did not reach substantive merits of interference/coercion claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA violations (42 U.S.C. §§ 12101, 12102, 12203), Fourth Amendment violations, Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection violations, False Claims Act violations (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729-3733), Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, § 1983 state actor liability, § 1985 conspiracy, § 1986 failure to prevent, deliberate indifference to medical needs.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as shotgun pleading that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which act. Court did not reach substantive merits of non-FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory conduct and harassment based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I (§ 3617 retaliation/interference claim) dismissed for failure to plausibly allege that the Association endorsed or approved the racist motion or engaged in conduct severe and pervasive enough to constitute actionable interference under § 3617. Plaintiff alleged only vague, conclusory statements that hate speech was 'common and accepted' without sufficient factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory enforcement of Association rules (no-renter rule, guest policy) based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II (§ 3604(a)-(b) disparate treatment claim) dismissed because § 3604 applies only to conduct directly impacting accessibility to housing through sale or rental. Plaintiff's allegations of discriminatory enforcement of Association rules against a unit owner who already owned the property do not implicate § 3604, which regulates the sale or rental of housing, not post-purchase enforcement of cooperative rules.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory effect of Association rules (no-renter rule, guest policy) based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III (§ 3604(a)-(b) disparate impact claim) dismissed on the same basis as Count II: § 3604 is limited to conduct affecting the sale or rental of housing and does not extend to post-purchase enforcement of cooperative rules. The court found no statutory basis for a disparate impact claim under § 3604 in this context.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that someone other than Anna Strickstein-Zandman interact with plaintiff regarding business matters related to his residency, due to stress-related disability and antagonistic relationship with the board president.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded personal involvement by the individual defendant in the discriminatory acts and that the allegations of willful discrimination fall within the exception to state statutory immunity, allowing the claim to proceed past the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for access to gym and recreational amenities despite medical restrictions; plaintiff's therapist cleared him to use the gym, but defendants required clearance from their own treating physician.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded that the individual defendant personally determined he was not healthy enough to use the facilities and that these allegations of willful discrimination survive the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Imposition of discriminatory terms and conditions regarding use of gym and recreational facilities based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendants discriminated against him under different terms and conditions than non-disabled residents and that the individual defendant was personally involved in these discriminatory acts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of lease renewal in retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation and asserting FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendants retaliated against him by refusing to renew his lease because of his disability and that the individual defendant was personally involved in this retaliatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing in violation of Florida Fair Housing Act § 760.23(1); supplemental state law claims under Fla. Stat. § 760.20 et seq., specifically §§ 760.23(2), 760.23(8), 760.23(9)(b), and 760.37.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss on the state law claim (Count IV), finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded personal and deliberate discrimination by the individual defendant, which survives the motion to dismiss stage under supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal link between his protected activity (filing the prior lawsuit) and the adverse action (non-renewal of lease). The approximately one-year gap between the lawsuit and non-renewal is insufficient under Eleventh Circuit precedent, which requires temporal proximity to be 'very close' and has found three to four months insufficient. Plaintiff also failed to rebut Defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason (problematic behavior documented in warning letters) by showing it was pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation claim (Count I); Civil Rights violations under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1985 (Count III); Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (Count IV); Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress (Count V)
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts I, III, IV, and V were dismissed with prejudice on motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim. The ADA retaliation claim (Count I) and civil rights conspiracy claims (Count III) were dismissed as legally insufficient; emotional distress claims (Counts IV and V) were also dismissed at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of emotional support animal (dog) application for Mr. Tomlinson based on the dog's size and breed; plaintiff submitted application with pet form, photographs, and letter from psychiatrist on May 29, 2022; denied June 14, 2022.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff, as a person associated with Mr. Tomlinson (who has a disability), has standing to bring a failure-to-accommodate claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f). Plaintiff adequately pleaded that Mr. Tomlinson is disabled, that she requested an accommodation (ESA), and that defendants refused it. At the motion to dismiss stage, these allegations are sufficient to survive under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleaded all three elements of a § 3617 retaliation claim: (1) protected activity (filing HUD complaint regarding denial of reasonable accommodation), (2) adverse action (denial of lease renewal for Unit 304 and denial of lease approval for Unit 311), and (3) causal connection (defendants' letter explicitly cited the ongoing legal matter as grounds for denial). Allegations are sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with plaintiff's contract to lease Unit 311 by defendants' denial of board approval based on the ongoing legal matter regarding the ESA denial in Unit 304.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff adequately pleaded a § 3617 interference claim by alleging that defendants interfered with her contract for Unit 311 because of the disability-related denial regarding Mr. Tomlinson's ESA in Unit 304. The plain text of § 3604(f)(1)(C) covers discrimination against a renter because of a handicap of a person associated with that renter, and plaintiff's allegations fit squarely within this provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Conveyance of publicly owned land (Perkins Field) for affordable housing development in downtown Warner Robins
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege a policy or practice with disparate impact. The complaint alleged only a one-time decision to renege on the Perkins Field development and did not establish that the City implemented a policy of confining affordable housing to less desirable areas, as the prior Pennrose developments were not alleged to have been shunted away from downtown by the City. Robust causality between any policy and harm to African Americans was not plausibly alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval and conveyance of Perkins Field for affordable housing development; reversal of prior commitments to the development
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged FHA disparate treatment claim under circumstantial evidence theory. The City initially rolled out the red carpet, enthusiastically solicited and supported the development through multiple steps, then abruptly reversed course when community opposition surfaced—opposition characterized by coded language about low-income housing and rising crime. The sequence of events, discriminatory effect on African Americans (primary consumers of affordable housing), and departure from normal criteria plausibly infer intentional discrimination based on race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (Ground Lease Agreement); specific performance to compel lease of Perkins Field; Contract Clause violation (rescission of commitment resolution and defunding of Development Authority)
fha_claims.reasoning: Breach of contract claim against Development Authority dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege how the Authority could breach by failing to lease property it did not own when the City prevented conveyance. Specific performance claim dismissed because no valid contract existed between plaintiffs and the City. Contract Clause claim dismissed because the rescission of the commitment resolution was not a 'law' under the Contract Clause, and the defunding vote was not plausibly alleged to have caused the injuries alleged in the complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Specific accommodation not detailed in this order; plaintiff alleged failure to accommodate related to disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff leave to proceed in forma pauperis and allowed the Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed following frivolity review under § 1915(e)(2)(B), meaning the claim survived the initial screening and was not found to be frivolous or indisputably meritless.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Road maintenance and repair (not an accommodation claim; plaintiff alleges discriminatory denial of road maintenance services based on race, disability, sex, and age of homeowners)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA discrimination claims are barred by res judicata because he had a full and fair opportunity to litigate discrimination theories in his prior state court suit seeking the same relief (road maintenance) and failed to raise them. Claim preclusion forecloses litigation of matters that should have been advanced in the first suit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process, Title VI, Title II ADA, § 504 Rehabilitation Act, age discrimination (42 U.S.C. §§ 6101–6107), Fourteenth Amendment equal protection
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims are barred by res judicata on the same basis as the FHA claims. Additionally, to the extent plaintiff sought to assert claims on behalf of other homeowners, he lacked standing as a pro se litigant under 28 U.S.C. § 1654.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to plaintiff's mental health disability; the opinion does not detail the specific accommodation requested
fha_claims.disposition: Allowed to proceed following frivolity review
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff leave to proceed in forma pauperis and allowed the Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed following § 1915(e) frivolity review, without dismissing the claim on the merits. The opinion does not substantively analyze the elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of railings on the retaining wall in front of plaintiff's duplex unit to address plaintiff's paranoia and anxiety triggered by fear of falling
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that plaintiff's request for retaining wall railings constitutes a request for modification under § 3604(f)(3)(A), not an accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), because it involves a structural change to common use areas. The court did not apply the reasonable accommodation standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of railings on the retaining wall in front of plaintiff's duplex unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the six-element test for FHA modifications and found that plaintiff failed to establish: (1) disability under the FHA (no documentation provided to defendant by close of discovery; diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia came over one year after the request); (2) reasonableness and necessity (plaintiff could play catch in other areas of the property and enjoyed his unit equally to other residents); and (3) willingness to pay at plaintiff's own expense (plaintiff's post-deposition declarations contradicting his deposition testimony were treated as sham affidavits).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Hallmark four-factor test for discriminatory intent in local governmental decisions and found that plaintiffs failed to establish that the City acted with racial discriminatory intent when rescinding the Commitment Resolution. The court found no evidence that community opposition was based on racial animus, that City officials were aware of allegedly racist social media posts, or that the City was not justified in rescinding based on the reduction in commercial retail space.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs established a prima facie case of retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 based on defense counsel's threats of criminal investigation and revocation of the LIHTC award made during depositions and follow-up emails in response to plaintiffs' exercise of FHA rights. The court held that the City's proffered legitimate nonretaliatory reasons were pretextual and that genuine issues of material fact remain for trial, except that plaintiffs are entitled to summary judgment that they have suffered no economic or special damages to date.
