fha_claims.accommodation_description: Availability of Spanish-speaking representative to discuss mortgage servicing matters
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a plausible FHA violation. The Fair Housing Act does not impose an obligation on mortgage servicers to retain Spanish-speaking representatives. Plaintiff did not allege that anyone refused his calls because of his national origin or Puerto Rico origin, only that calls were transferred between departments. Lack of Spanish-language service is a business practice issue, not an FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Advancement of funds for post-closing property taxes; face-to-face meeting within 200-mile radius; loss mitigation services; compliance with National Housing Act 24 C.F.R. § 203.604 and § 203.605; TILA and RESPA violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state plausible claims under the National Housing Act, TILA, RESPA, and state tort law. The mortgage agreement clearly imposed the obligation to pay property taxes solely on plaintiff, not the servicer. Section 203.604(d) explicitly exempts servicers from face-to-face meeting requirements when the property is more than 200 miles away. Section 203.605 loss mitigation duties do not apply to reverse mortgages with no monthly installments. Plaintiff did not explain how TILA or RESPA were violated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicap parking space at the second-floor elevator entrance to Tower I of the condominium
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Rivera pled sufficient facts to state a prima facie case for FHA reasonable accommodation claim under the four-element test (disability, defendant's knowledge, reasonable and necessary accommodation, refusal). Failure to respond to accommodation request can constitute constructive refusal; interactive process required. Claim survives motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicap parking space near Tower I entrance for Dávila (deceased husband); defendant offered space at Tower II entrance instead
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations state prima facie case for Dávila's reasonable accommodation claim but expressed concern about statute of limitations timing. Dismissal inappropriate without clear allegation of when denial occurred; claim survives motion to dismiss pending clarification of temporal facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policy or practice resulting in no designated handicap parking spaces at Tower I
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to analyze disparate impact theory at motion to dismiss stage because neither party briefed the issue. Court directed plaintiff to clearly spell out theories in future filings but did not dismiss the theory; claim remains pending clarification.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for discrimination in public accommodations (parking area)
fha_claims.reasoning: Residential condominiums are not covered by Title III ADA as public accommodations. No commercial space alleged within the condominium. Dismissed without prejudice; plaintiff may amend if additional facts show ADA applicability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible handicap parking spaces (172, 173, and 178) at the second-floor door entrance to the elevator in Tower 1 of Torre Cibeles condominium
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a prima facie case of reasonable accommodation discrimination under the FHAA because: (1) Mora ceased administration of the building in 2014 and could not have known of plaintiff's disabled status when she requested accommodation in 2021; (2) plaintiff never requested accommodation from Mora after the parking space sales; and (3) Mora could not refuse an accommodation it had no ability to provide. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations without factual support for how the sale of designated handicap spaces violates the FHAA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claims regarding accessible parking and reasonable accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's ADA Title III claims were dismissed in a prior order (Docket No. 101) for failure to state a claim. The court noted that plaintiff largely relied on ADA allegations to frame her claims but those claims were not viable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow complainant Fernández-Montero, who is legally blind, to keep a service dog in a rental apartment despite the landlord's no-pet policy
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants actually denied the accommodation and the timing of any subsequent offer. The court held that under FHA, a violation occurs when a disabled resident is first denied reasonable accommodation, irrespective of remedies granted later, and that failure to accommodate can be inferred even without explicit denial. The defendants' initial refusal to rent due to the no-pet policy, followed by a delayed offer only after HUD complaint and conciliation, presents factual disputes precluding summary judgment for defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a larger unit to accommodate plaintiff's disabled son who came to live with him
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint is utterly lacking in plausible factual allegations required under Twombly and is at serious risk of dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6). The court found the complaint so vague that it is impossible to ascertain what plaintiff is alleging, though based on hearing representations, plaintiff may potentially have a viable disparate impact claim under Graul.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and IDEA claims related to failure to accommodate disabled son
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state plausible claims under the ADA and IDEA due to lack of factual allegations. The court found the complaint conclusory and at serious risk of dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to meet Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked personal jurisdiction over the defendants under the Massachusetts long-arm statute and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(f) because the defendants' contacts with Massachusetts were insufficient and the alleged discriminatory conduct (refusal to sell based on race) occurred in Rhode Island. The case was transferred to the District of Rhode Island rather than dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent reduction during interim and annual recertifications based on job loss and income decrease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie disparate treatment by showing she was denied rent recertification while similarly situated white women received recertifications despite incomplete forms; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether defendants' proffered race-neutral reasons (income verification requirements) are pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent reduction during interim and annual recertifications based on job loss and income decrease under RIFHPA
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Rhode Island Fair Housing Practices Act, plaintiff established prima facie disparate treatment; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to pretext, applying same McDonnell Douglas framework as FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to process recertification paperwork, calling police and seeking temporary restraining order, issuing non-compliance notice and pursuing eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie retaliation under FHA § 3617 by showing protected activity (complaints of racial discrimination), adverse actions (refusal to process paperwork, police call, eviction), and causal connection; defendants' proffered non-retaliatory reasons contradicted by their own documentation showing complaints of discrimination were the driving cause.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to process recertification paperwork, calling police and seeking temporary restraining order, issuing non-compliance notice and pursuing eviction under RIFHPA
fha_claims.reasoning: Under RIFHPA anti-retaliation provisions, plaintiff established prima facie case with same three elements as FHA claim; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether defendants acted in retaliation for discrimination complaints.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, Rhode Island Civil Rights Act of 1990, Rhode Island Fair Housing Practices Act (disparate treatment claims)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI and RICRA disparate treatment claims analyzed under same McDonnell Douglas framework as FHA; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to pretext for defendants' actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1437f (Section 8 Housing Program) - alleged violation of rent recertification and hardship exemption regulations
fha_claims.reasoning: No implied private right of action exists under 42 U.S.C. § 1437f or its implementing regulations; applying Cort v. Ash four-factor test, statute focuses on obligations of entities receiving federal funds rather than rights of beneficiaries, and Supreme Court disfavors implying private remedies in regulatory statutes.

case_name: Madeliene Y. Jeffreys v. Marcia L. Fudge, Secretary of U.S. Housing & Urban Development, et al.
key_cases_cited: UNDETERMINED

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certification and recertification as a live-in aide for plaintiff's disabled daughter and grandson in Section 8 housing
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed for lack of private right of action under FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (FHA) does not establish a private right of action for money damages, and therefore dismissed plaintiff's direct FHA claim. The court noted that while the FHA regulations require PHAs to approve live-in aides as reasonable accommodations, the FHA itself provides no private remedy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; deprivation of property interest in continued Section 8 housing assistance and live-in-aide status through obstruction of recertification process
fha_claims.disposition: Survives motion to dismiss; case proceeds against properly named defendants
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiff stated a plausible § 1983 due process claim by alleging that the WHA obstructed the recertification process by refusing to provide a duplicate form while insisting documentation be submitted on that withheld form, combined with allegations of false evidence and an arbitrary deadline. The court found a sufficient property interest in continued Section 8 assistance to warrant due process protection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on failure to use preferred name (Hope instead of Scott) and alleged passive-aggressive behavior by defendant.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous and failing to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to allege facts that might reasonably support a housing discrimination claim based on defendant's failure to use plaintiff's preferred name. The court found that while such behavior was insensitive and disrespectful, it did not constitute actionable housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that a reasonable jury could conclude that Childress was subjected to racial harassment that was sufficiently severe and pervasive to alter his housing conditions and create an abusive environment, satisfying all four elements of a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA: unwelcome conduct, based on race, severe or pervasive, and imputable to defendants. The cumulative effect of multiple race-based incidents in 2015, including racial slurs and discriminatory statements, created a genuine issue of material fact precluding summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance to build a carport on residential property to accommodate plaintiff Patricia Witt's physical disability
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only discovery disputes (motion to compel) regarding the underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The court did not reach the merits of whether the Town of Irmo unlawfully refused to provide a reasonable accommodation for the zoning variance. The case remains pending on the substantive FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance to permit construction of a 24-foot by 11-foot carport with attached ramp to cover mobility ramp and driveway, to protect Ms. Witt from slippery surfaces due to her mobility disability (four hip surgeries, knee replacement needed, use of walker and cane, history of falls).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-pronged Bryant Woods Inn test (reasonable, necessary, equal opportunity) and found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the carport as designed would have an ameliorative effect on Ms. Witt's disability and the degree of benefit it would provide. The court found the reasonableness element satisfied (no undue financial/administrative burden, no fundamental alteration), but could not resolve the necessity and equal opportunity elements without speculation, requiring denial of both parties' summary judgment motions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modification under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A) to permit Ms. Witt to make modifications to her existing premises (carport construction) at her own expense.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court noted that the elements for establishing a prima facie case of discrimination for failure to permit a reasonable modification under § 3604(f)(3)(A) are the same as for failure to grant a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and therefore did not provide separate analysis. The claim survives summary judgment on the same basis as the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination because of disability in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not separately analyze the disparate treatment claim; the opinion focuses on the reasonable accommodation and reasonable modification theories under § 3604(f)(3)(A) and (B). The claim survives summary judgment as part of the overall denial of both parties' motions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Fair Housing Act § 3617 retaliation claim; specific accommodation not identified
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff's Fair Housing Act § 3617 retaliation assertions insufficient to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly, noting that although plaintiff alleged her adult son is disabled, she failed to assert that any defendant acted adversely due to protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights claims arising from state court foreclosure action
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Rooker-Feldman doctrine to preclude federal review of state court foreclosure judgment; additionally, § 1983 claims failed because the Court of Common Pleas is not a 'person' subject to suit, judges are entitled to judicial immunity, and neither Suntrust Bank nor Joseph Partain are state actors as required by § 1983.

key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co.
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged various constitutional violations (Thirteenth and Fourth Amendment), Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act 1968, § 1983 due process claims, § 1988 attorneys' fees, 18 U.S.C. § 873 (blackmail/extortion), and state law claims including discrimination, conspiracy, breach of contract, and property damage.
fha_claims.disposition: Recommended for summary dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all claims as frivolous or lacking arguable basis in law or fact. Constitutional claims against private defendants failed because they are not state actors under § 1983. § 873 claims failed because no private right of action exists. Discrimination claims were conclusory without factual support. Conspiracy claims lacked concrete facts of mutual understanding. § 1988 claim failed because pro se litigants cannot recover attorneys' fees. State law claims were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims failed.

The opinion does not substantively analyze the FHA claim or any specific accommodation request.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to deny the JumpStart defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Buchanan plausibly alleged the defendants were state actors or had been delegated statutory government authority. The FHA claim was not separately analyzed on the merits; it survives the motion to dismiss along with the other claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Various accommodations and services for juveniles with disabilities in state custody, including accessible conditions and disability-related services
fha_claims.reasoning: The court reversed the magistrate judge's recommendation to dismiss for lack of standing, finding that organizational plaintiffs (NAACP, DRSC, Justice 360) had alleged concrete and particularized injuries—diversion of resources and impairment of advocacy activities—caused by alleged violations of the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and IDEA, and that such injuries were redressable by favorable judicial decision. The court rejected the magistrate's requirement that organizational injuries must align with interests protected by the underlying statutes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged discriminatory intent under the Iqbal/Twombly standard by alleging racially coded language by Council members, intense public opposition characterized by racist euphemism, and departures from the County's regular zoning practices. The Court found sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory purpose to survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: At the motion to dismiss stage, Plaintiffs satisfied step one of the disparate impact burden-shifting framework by demonstrating a robust causal connection between the County's denial of the zoning application and disparate impact on Black residents through statistical evidence showing Black residents are nearly eight times as likely as White renters to receive subsidized housing support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' perpetuation of segregation claim, characterized as an alternate avenue of pleading disparate impact, survived the motion to dismiss. Plaintiffs plausibly alleged using statistical evidence that the County's denial prevented racial integration that Porter's Landing would have provided and that the policy perpetuates segregated housing patterns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment), 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1983 Equal Protection claim survived because they plausibly alleged discriminatory intent and a causal connection between the County's zoning decision and the alleged injury, satisfying Monell's requirement of an official policy or custom. Plaintiffs' §§ 1981 and 1982 claims survived because they satisfied the § 1983 requirement of an official policy or custom of discrimination, as required by the Fourth Circuit in Dennis v. County of Fairfax.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination claims under Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and retaliation
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal question jurisdiction because the FHA and other federal claims were raised as counterclaims in a state eviction action, which cannot serve as a basis for removal under the well-pleaded complaint rule. The court also lacked diversity jurisdiction because the defendant was a South Carolina citizen and failed to allege damages exceeding $75,000 or establish complete diversity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Delay in removal/eviction to allow plaintiff's son to obtain mental health treatment and medication adjustment from his medical provider
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that the requested accommodation (delay in eviction) would directly ameliorate the effect of her son's mental impairments or ensure the safety of other residents. Under Bryant Woods Inn, an accommodation that provides no direct amelioration of the disability's effect cannot be 'necessary' under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that plaintiff's retaliation claim, including allegations that filing a fair housing complaint was followed by forced early rent payment, removal of online payment ability, and delayed maintenance, is best adjudicated at the summary judgment stage and survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory terms and conditions of rental, including forced early rent payment and removal of online payment ability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court deferred substantive discussion of the discriminatory terms and conditions claim to the summary judgment stage because the retaliation claim will move forward and the claims are interrelated. The claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (state tort); breach of contract; perjury; civil conspiracy to commit perjury and perjury by omission; civil conspiracy to commit infliction of emotional distress; ADA Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of intentional infliction of emotional distress, even when considered together, do not rise to the level of conduct 'utterly intolerable in a civilized community' as required under South Carolina law. The court found that inconsiderate and insulting behavior is insufficient to state an IIED claim.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court found amended complaint failed to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard. Complaint consisted primarily of legal citations and conclusions without sufficient factual allegations to establish prima facie case of discrimination based on disability or failure to accommodate.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO violations, EFTA violations, FCRA violations, Ex parte Young doctrine claims, § 1985(3) civil rights conspiracy, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, covenant of quiet enjoyment, deceit, conversion, trespass, abuse of process, unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all non-FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Rule 12(b)(6). Complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to support RICO, EFTA, FCRA, § 1985(3), or state law tort claims. Claims against Judge Eldridge also dismissed on judicial immunity grounds and Ex parte Young claims against Judge Eldridge and Director Deiter dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loan approval and funding amount; plaintiff alleges discrimination in loan qualification calculations and reduction of funding amount
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case under the FHA disparate treatment standard because she did not allege facts showing she was qualified for the loan (the USDA letter documented discrepancies in her application) and did not allege that the USDA approved loans for similarly situated applicants; her speculation about future conduct does not constitute plausible factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Timely appraisal date to preserve grant funding availability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that the denial of the accommodation was because of her disability; she alleged only that Steinley failed to perform the appraisal on time, without connecting this failure to her handicap as required under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing a Federal Tort Claims Act petition and state small claims case
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's alleged protected activity (filing a FTCA petition and state court case) does not constitute a right granted or protected by 42 U.S.C. §§ 3603, 3604, 3605, or 3606, which are the only activities protected under the FHA retaliation statute, 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691(e)), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause (U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1), Ex parte Young doctrine (209 U.S. 123)
fha_claims.reasoning: ECOA claim failed because plaintiff did not allege she was qualified for the loan or that the USDA approved loans for similarly situated applicants; Section 504 claim failed because plaintiff did not establish she was a 'qualified individual with a disability' given the documented discrepancies in her application; Fourteenth Amendment claims failed because the defendants are federal actors to whom the Fourteenth Amendment does not apply; Ex parte Young claim failed because defendant Gross is a federal employee and the doctrine does not apply to federal officers.

The court has not yet addressed the merits of the Section 504 reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Six-foot wooden privacy fence to prevent son with autism and sensory processing disorder from eloping and to provide safe outdoor access
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the necessity element of the reasonable accommodation test and found that although a fence may be necessary for equal enjoyment, plaintiffs failed to show that the HOA-approved six-foot wrought iron fence would not adequately address their concerns. The court held that consideration of reasonable alternatives is built into the necessity analysis, and plaintiffs' preference for wood over wrought iron does not establish necessity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to HOA covenant restrictions on fence type and material (wooden vs. wrought iron) based on disability accommodation request
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed the necessity element and found that plaintiffs failed to establish that a wooden fence was necessary when the HOA approved a six-foot wrought iron fence that could serve the same safety purpose. The necessity inquiry requires showing that without the specific requested accommodation, the disabled person would be denied equal opportunity to enjoy the housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination in denial of wooden fence request based on disability status
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's analysis of the necessity element under § 3604(f)(3)(A) and (B) encompasses the disparate treatment claim, as the court found no evidence that the HOA treated plaintiffs differently based on disability; rather, the HOA offered an alternative accommodation (wrought iron fence) and fee deferral.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of a six-foot wooden privacy fence at plaintiffs' home to accommodate their son's special needs
fha_claims.reasoning: The court ruled on a motion to strike expert testimony regarding the necessity of the fence accommodation, not on the underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim itself. The court excluded opinion testimony by the treating physician regarding whether a six-foot wooden fence was necessary, but allowed testimony limited to the physician's treatment of the child and his medical diagnoses. The FHA claim on the merits remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing four unrelated persons with mental disabilities to reside together in a single-family home in an R-1 zoning district under the same terms and conditions as residents without disabilities; exemption from special permit requirement for group homes housing persons with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States and City agreed to a comprehensive settlement resolving claims that the City discriminated by refusing to allow Quality Lifestyle to operate a group home for four persons with mental disabilities. The Decree requires the City to amend its zoning ordinance to allow residences for persons with disabilities to operate as of right without special permits, protecting housing for persons with mental illness, intellectual disabilities, and emotional disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing opportunity based on disability status through discriminatory zoning and land use practices
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States alleged that the City discriminated on the basis of disability by refusing to allow four persons with mental disabilities to reside together in a single-family home under the same terms and conditions as residents without disabilities, in violation of FHA §§ 3601-3619. The settlement requires the City to amend its zoning ordinance to eliminate discriminatory practices and ensure equal housing opportunities for persons with disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA discrimination claim; Title V ADA interference/retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States alleged violations of Title II of the ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12132) and Title V of the ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12203(b)) based on the City's discriminatory zoning practices and interference with the exercise of ADA rights. The settlement resolves these claims through comprehensive injunctive relief requiring amendment of zoning ordinances and implementation of non-discrimination policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning amendment to allow plaintiff's sober living recovery facility to operate in an RS-1 residential zoning district
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment in part on April 19, 2024, but reserved the question of whether plaintiff's proposed accommodation was reasonable and necessary as defined by the FHA and ADA for trial on May 6, 2024. The motions in limine address evidentiary issues for the pending trial, not the merits of the accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), and Equal Protection Clause claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff brought claims under the ADA, RLUIPA, and Equal Protection Clause in addition to the FHA. Summary judgment was granted in part on April 19, 2024, but the opinion does not specify which non-FHA claims survived or were dismissed. The case proceeds to trial with the reasonableness and necessity of the accommodation remaining at issue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process claim regarding termination from Shelter Plus Care Program; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act discrimination claim; ADA Title II intentional discrimination claim; ADA Title II reasonable accommodation claim; Shelter Plus Care Program claim; Section 8 claim; TCPA claim; retaliation claim under ADA/Section 504
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff has a legitimate property interest in continued receipt of Shelter Plus Care benefits and that the statute requires due process protections upon termination; court cannot determine from pleadings whether MHA provided minimum required process, so claim survives screening.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and dismissed the FHA discrimination claim against the original defendants for failure to state a claim. The claim was not allowed to proceed past initial screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, Tennessee Consumer Protection Act
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed under Rule 4(m) for failure to effect service
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found colorable claims under Title II ADA and Due Process but dismissed the action without prejudice under Rule 4(m) because plaintiff failed to effect service on the remaining defendant (MHA) within 90 days and did not respond to the show-cause order despite ample opportunity and notice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that McGuire's allegations, construed liberally and in light most favorable to plaintiff, plausibly alleged retaliation under FHA § 3617 by showing she engaged in protected activity (advocating for FHA compliance), was terminated, and there was a causal connection (King's email stating 'We need to let [McGuire] go today' shortly after her FHA advocacy emails). The motion to dismiss was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 1915(e)(2) screening (applying the same Iqbal/Twombly standard as Rule 12(b)(6)), the court found McGuire failed to allege sufficient facts to support a Title VII retaliation claim because she did not allege she opposed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and did not allege the defendants terminated her for opposing such employment discrimination. Her complaints focused on FHA violations, not Title VII-protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under Tennessee Human Rights Act § 4-21-301(a)(1)
fha_claims.reasoning: The Magistrate Judge recommended denial of Defendants' motion to dismiss the THRA retaliation claim, finding it survived the 12(b)(6) pleading standard. The District Court adopted this recommendation, allowing the THRA retaliation claim to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII retaliation claim, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal of the Title VII retaliation claim pursuant to § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) as frivolous or failing to state a claim. The District Court adopted this recommendation and dismissed the Title VII claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to accommodate a mixed-breed service dog used to care for two disabled family members (plaintiff's mother with end-stage liver disease and three-year-old daughter with brain tumor). The service dog alerts when mother has high ammonia episodes and when daughter stops breathing.
fha_claims.reasoning: At the § 1915(e) screening stage, the court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found that the plaintiff plausibly alleged she sought an accommodation for a service dog necessary to fully enjoy the rental dwelling and that defendants arbitrarily denied the request. The court did not apply the substantive reasonable accommodation framework (five-element test) but rather determined the complaint stated a colorable claim sufficient to survive initial screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendants initiated eviction procedures and made misrepresentations about plaintiff's financial condition after denying the service dog accommodation request, allegedly to intimidate and interfere with plaintiff's exercise of FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: At the § 1915(e) screening stage, the court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found that the plaintiff plausibly alleged the defendants acted to intimidate or interfere with the plaintiff's enjoyment of FHA rights through retaliatory eviction procedures and misrepresentations. The court did not apply the substantive three-element test for § 3617 interference claims but determined the complaint stated a colorable claim sufficient to survive initial screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Designated accessible parking space for disabled tenant; defendants provided space but failed to prevent regular use by non-disabled tenants, forcing plaintiff to park in visitor parking far from apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations sufficient to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim under Iqbal/Twombly: plaintiff alleged disability, requested reasonable accommodation (dedicated disabled parking), defendants knew of disability, refused accommodation by failing to prevent non-disabled use, and suffered injury as result. Claim survives initial § 1915(e) screening and proceeds to service of process.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations sufficient to state a plausible FHA interference claim under § 3617: plaintiff exercised FHA right to request reasonable accommodation; defendants intentionally harassed, intimidated, threatened, and coerced plaintiff through improper eviction notice, threats, and harassment; causal connection existed between plaintiff's accommodation request/injury remedies and defendants' retaliatory conduct; plaintiff suffered damages. Claim survives initial § 1915(e) screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I and Title III claims; ADA retaliation and interference claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title I claims dismissed because defendants do not qualify as 'covered entities' under 42 U.S.C. § 12111(2) (employers, employment agencies, labor organizations, or joint labor-management committees); plaintiff did not allege defendants were her employers. ADA Title III claims dismissed because private apartment complex parking lots, walkways, entryways, and stairwells are not 'places of public accommodation' under 42 U.S.C. § 12182, and no private right of action for money damages exists under Title III.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence and fraud claims under Tennessee state law; FDCPA claim under 15 U.S.C. § 1692k
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Negligence claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to identify any Tennessee authority recognizing a duty of care owed by opposing counsel to a litigant based on allegedly excessive damages claims, and plaintiff provided no legal argument supporting such a cause of action. Fraud claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to plead the reliance element with particularity under Rule 9(b), as the parties openly disagreed regarding their respective obligations rather than plaintiff relying on false representations. FDCPA claim against McCoy remains pending.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately alleged that defendant William L. Belew, Jr. personally participated in the design and construction of a noncompliant building, establishing plausible individual liability under the FHA and 24 C.F.R. § 100.7(a). The court rejected defendant's argument that corporate form shields him from liability where he was directly involved in the discriminatory conduct.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA and TILA claims on the ground that both statutes apply only to residential transactions, and the complaint failed to allege that the secured property was Mitchell's principal dwelling. The property was a commercial nursing home facility, not Mitchell's residence, so the FHA's protections did not apply.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of quiet enjoyment, breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to strike defendant's affirmative defense. The underlying state law claims for breach of quiet enjoyment and breach of contract remain pending.

case_name: Alexander v. Lexington Associates II, L.P.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, Fla., 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation to keep an assistance animal (dog named Bonnie, later Rebel) in her apartment due to mental disability. Defendant Clark initially granted verbal approval with weight/breed restrictions, then demanded removal of first dog as 'pit bull-like,' and later required new accommodation form for second dog.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed claims against Lexington (property owner) for failure to plead plausible facts establishing vicarious liability. Plaintiff alleged no agency or employment relationship between Lexington and the individual defendants (Clark and Triplett) who allegedly denied or interfered with the accommodation. Without pleading an agency relationship, vicarious liability cannot be established under traditional tort principles incorporated into the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged harassment and interference with plaintiff's exercise of FHA rights, including issuance of baseless lease violation notices, surveillance, photographing plaintiff off-premises, removal of assistance animal by animal control, and entry/ransacking of unit.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed retaliation/interference claims against Lexington under § 3617 for the same reason: plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing that Lexington, as property owner, was vicariously liable for the alleged coercive conduct of its agents Clark and Triplett. No agency relationship was alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide accessible information about guest rooms and accessible booking functionality on third-party hotel reservation websites (ADA Title III violation)
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot; Leave to Amend Granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion to amend her complaint to cure the standing deficiency identified in defendant's motion to dismiss. The court held that plaintiff's amended allegations of a plausible intent to visit Henderson in summer 2022 and revisit the booking websites satisfy Article III standing requirements under Lujan. The motion to dismiss was denied as moot without prejudice to file a subsequent motion after amendment.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the TRO motion on the ground that plaintiff failed to establish immediate and irreparable harm, not on the merits of the underlying claims. The court noted that no valid FHA claim was before it in either the original or proposed amended complaint, and the underlying non-FHA claims remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to sell property to plaintiff; sale to third party at lower price
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify any facially neutral policy or practice; claim stems from single act of refusal to sell, and complaint lacks allegations that anyone other than plaintiff is affected by the challenged conduct, making disparate impact claim implausible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to sell property to plaintiff based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint contains only conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent without supporting factual allegations; plaintiff does not allege how defendant knew her race or provide any factual basis for intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (race discrimination in contracts), § 1982 (race discrimination in property sale), § 2000d (Title VI), § 1983 (equal protection/Fifth Amendment), § 1985(3) (civil conspiracy), 18 U.S.C. §§ 1962(b)-(d) (RICO)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims fail under Iqbal/Twombly: § 1981 and § 1982 claims lack allegations of discriminatory intent; § 1983 claims fail because neither defendant is a state actor (Fannie Mae is not a state actor per Sixth Circuit precedent; Tigert is private individual); § 1985(3) conspiracy claim contains only conclusory allegations without factual support; RICO claims fail because plaintiff alleges single scheme targeting single victim, not pattern of racketeering activity, and conspiracy allegations are conclusory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide adequate information about accessible features in hotel reservations system; violation of ADA regulation 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)(1)(ii) requiring hotels to identify and describe accessible features in enough detail for disabled individuals to assess independently whether accommodations meet their needs
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish Article III standing because she did not allege a concrete injury in fact. The court distinguished Havens Realty (which involved affirmative misrepresentation motivated by discrimination) from mere failure to provide information online. The court found that informational deprivation alone, without a traditionally recognized harm or impact on plaintiff's ability to access services, does not constitute a concrete injury sufficient for Article III standing, even though a regulatory violation may have occurred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I employment discrimination claim; Tennessee Disability Act (TDA) employment discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found plaintiff established prima facie case of disability discrimination under both ADA and TDA through temporal proximity of disability disclosure (January 29, 2018) to termination (February 2, 2018) and evidence of fabricated disciplinary charges. Defendant articulated legitimate nondiscriminatory reason (misconduct), but plaintiff created genuine dispute of material fact regarding pretext, precluding summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to construct a three-sided fence around the back half of plaintiff's backyard (between jogging path and lake) to exclude public access and allow plaintiff to safely use the sunlit area given his compromised immune system from cancer treatment.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to establish the first element of the reasonable accommodation framework—that he is handicapped under the FHA. The court held that 'being in close proximity to persons unknown to him' is not a major life activity protected by the FHA, and that even if being in the sun were a major life activity, it would be recreational rather than central to daily life. Without establishing disability, plaintiff cannot establish discrimination based on failure to accommodate.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance to allow up to fifteen unrelated disabled persons (recovering drug and alcohol addicts) to live in a sober living home in a single-family residential district (SF-7 zone), in violation of occupancy limits in the zoning ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the facial challenge to the ordinance under the direct-evidence theory of disparate treatment, finding that the ordinance treats unrelated disabled persons better than unrelated non-disabled persons (allowing 8 disabled unrelated residents versus 4 non-disabled unrelated residents), and therefore does not facially discriminate against persons with disabilities under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ordinance limiting occupancy of sober living homes to fewer residents than permitted for family households
fha_claims.reasoning: Under McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting, plaintiffs established a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on differing occupancy limits; defendant articulated legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons (promoting general welfare, family values, and controlling residential density); the court found that plaintiffs raised a genuine issue of material fact regarding whether defendant's stated reasons were pretextual for discrimination, precluding summary judgment on the circumstantial-evidence theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only the FHA claims on the motion for summary judgment; ADA claims are mentioned in the complaint but not substantively analyzed in this opinion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim

fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to stay discovery pending resolution of standing, finding that plaintiff satisfied all three elements of Article III standing under the FHA's broad definition of 'aggrieved person.' The court held that plaintiff need not have intended to rent the property to have standing, and that her personal encounter with accessibility barriers constituted a cognizable injury. The design and construction claim itself was not addressed on the merits but survives the procedural challenge.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans With Disabilities Act claim regarding public accommodation status; breach of contract, intentional infliction of emotional distress, harassment, stalking, and gross negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the ADA claim legally insufficient because plaintiffs failed to establish that the residential property was a place of public accommodation subject to ADA coverage. The alleged service animal accommodation claim was unrelated to any common-use areas. State-law claims were dismissed without prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that although plaintiffs presented some circumstantial evidence of pretext, they failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that Plano's enactment of the ordinance was intentionally discriminatory. The court found Plano's legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the ordinance (protecting single-family neighborhoods) were not pretextual, and plaintiffs' arguments that Plano sought only minimal compliance with federal law or lacked empirical data did not establish discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs' disparate-impact claim was actually a disparate-treatment claim in disguise because plaintiffs failed to identify a facially neutral policy with a disproportionately adverse effect on individuals with substance use disorders. Additionally, even assuming plaintiffs had identified such a policy, they failed to establish the 'robust causation' required under the Supreme Court's framework in Texas Department of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from zoning ordinance to allow occupancy of 15 residents in a sober living home located in an SF-7 single-family residential zone, which ordinance limited household care facilities to 8 residents
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs satisfied all four elements of the reasonable-accommodation claim: (1) WESL residents are disabled (individuals in recovery from substance use disorders who cannot live independently without relapsing); (2) plaintiffs requested an accommodation and Plano denied it; (3) the requested accommodation of 15 residents is reasonable because it imposes no undue financial or administrative burden on Plano (no documented problems with traffic, noise, or nuisance; only two minor complaints in two years of operation; no evidence Plano expended resources) and does not fundamentally alter Plano's zoning scheme (the home operates as a single-family residence); and (4) the accommodation is necessary—therapeutically necessary—to afford WESL residents equal opportunity to live in the dwelling of their choice, as established by expert testimony that 15 residents constitute the critical mass needed to prevent isolation and support recovery, whereas 8 residents would lead to isolation that counteracts therapeutic benefits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim; same facts and legal theories as FHA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed the ADA Title II claim using the same framework as the FHA claims, finding that plaintiffs prevailed on the reasonable-accommodation theory under the ADA. The court noted that the FHA and ADA provide similar protections and that courts often analyze the two statutes together. Plaintiffs failed on disparate treatment and disparate impact under the ADA as well, but prevailed on the failure to provide reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that GHA disregard plaintiff's criminal history as an accommodation for alleged mental illness disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately plead a qualifying disability under the FHA. Non-specific references to mental illness without allegations of how the disability limits major life activities are insufficient to state a plausible failure-to-accommodate claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; Section 8 statutory and regulatory claims; ADA failure-to-accommodate claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible municipal liability claim under § 1983 (no official policy or custom alleged); no private cause of action exists under Section 8 statutory provisions; ADA failure-to-accommodate claim fails for same pleading deficiency as FHA claim (insufficient disability allegations).

fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the City failed to reasonably accommodate plaintiffs' request for a variance to operate a 15-resident sober living home for individuals with substance use disorders. The court applied the FHA reasonable accommodation framework and determined the City's denial violated the FHA, though the court awarded only nominal damages ($1) because plaintiffs failed to prove compensatory damages (mental anguish and lost profits) to a reasonable certainty.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim related to permanent injunction prohibiting City from retaliating against plaintiffs for pursuing FHA and ADA complaints
fha_claims.reasoning: The court issued a permanent injunction prohibiting the City from retaliating against plaintiffs for having pursued housing-discrimination complaints under the FHA and ADA, indicating the court found retaliation liability on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) failure to accommodate claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the City liable for failing to accommodate plaintiffs under the ADA. However, under Fifth Circuit precedent, compensatory damages under the ADA require a showing of intentional discrimination, which the court found was not present. The court distinguished the ADA from the FHA, which permits compensatory damages for non-intentional discriminatory practices.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the case to the Eastern District of Texas for improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b). All non-FHA statutory claims were transferred along with the FHA claims. The merits of these claims were not addressed.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a claim under FHA § 3604(a) because uninhabitability (pest infestations, mold, sewage leaks, structural defects) does not render a dwelling 'unavailable' within the meaning of the statute; the Fifth Circuit has established that uninhabitability is distinct from unavailability under § 3604(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a claim under FHA § 3604(f)(1) because that section uses identical operative language to § 3604(a) ('unavailable'), and uninhabitability does not constitute unavailability under either provision.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked standing under Title VI because they failed to allege facts showing that Defendant received federal funds and used those funds in a discriminatory manner; conclusory allegations of federal funding without factual support cannot survive a 12(b)(6) motion. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice as supplemental jurisdiction was declined after dismissal of the federal anchor claims.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff failed to adequately allege a handicap (allergies, autoimmune disease, and joint condition without establishing how they substantially limit major life activities) and failed to allege that defendant knew of the disability and its consequential limitations. Conclusory allegations that conditions 'substantially impact her ability to live a normal life' do not meet the individualized assessment standard required by the ADA Amendments Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for injunctive relief
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to establish standing for injunctive relief under Title III of the ADA. Plaintiff did not allege a real and immediate threat of repeated injury; she alleged only that she would be placed at the head of the waitlist for the next available unit, which does not establish a likelihood that she will need accommodations or be denied them. The principal relief sought (top of waitlist ahead of current residents) addresses a past wrong, not an anticipated one.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to meet the robust causation requirement under Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015). The statistical disparities in the Section 8 voucher population preexisted the policy and plaintiff pleaded no facts showing the policy caused those disparities, only that the policy would disproportionately affect Black or African-American voucher holders.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policy prohibiting rental properties from being used for Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a reasonable inference of intentional race discrimination. The allegations that the policy was motivated by race were conclusory, conjectural, and speculative, relying on assumptions that the voucher population is predominantly Black or African-American without adequate factual support that defendant knew this fact or considered race in enacting the policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policy prohibiting rental properties from being used for Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1982, plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to support a prima facie case of intentional race discrimination. Like the FHA disparate treatment claim, the allegations of discriminatory intent were conclusory and lacked adequate factual support that defendant had a racially discriminatory motive in enacting the policy.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege with particularity the nature of the equal opportunity denied due to disability, the impact of an additional extension, and how that extension would directly ameliorate the effect of his disability to provide equal opportunity to obtain housing. The complaint lacks the requisite nexus between the requested accommodation and the equal opportunity standard.

fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims are either reiterations of the reasonable accommodation theory (which failed to state a claim) or lack factual allegations of denial of direct access to the voucher program itself. The methods of administration claim similarly lacks a basis independent of the reasonable accommodation denial.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under Younger abstention doctrine (equitable relief would interfere with pending state court proceeding) and ripeness doctrine (City has not issued final decision on permit applications, so factual development is required). FHA claim was included in the complaint but was not separately analyzed; it was dismissed along with all other claims on jurisdictional grounds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to disclose accessible features and allow booking of accessible guest rooms on third-party hotel booking websites in violation of ADA regulations 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)(1)
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot; Motion to Amend Granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint to cure standing defects by alleging a plausible intent to return to the non-compliant websites during a planned trip to Adamsville in July 2022. The court held that plaintiff adequately alleged an injury-in-fact under Article III standing doctrine and that the amended complaint would survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss. The original motion to dismiss was denied as moot pending the filing of the amended complaint.

Purely conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent are insufficient under Iqbal, and the complaint failed to connect specific adverse actions (firing, eviction) to discriminatory animus rather than legitimate reasons.

fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed in part, reversed in part

Court reversed dismissal of § 33-1381 retaliatory threats claim, holding that district court erred in concluding no remedy was available under Arizona law; remanded for further proceedings on that claim.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim for intentional discrimination under the Fair Housing Act because they did not allege facts showing that the current owner (Winnie Street) had received a Notice of Default, which is a statutory prerequisite for HUD to issue vouchers under the Consolidated Appropriations Act. The complaint's allegations regarding a prior owner's Notice of Default do not satisfy the statutory requirement that 'the owner' (present tense) has received such notice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claim for arbitrary and capricious agency action; Fifth Amendment equal protection claim for intentional discrimination on basis of race and ethnicity; statutory claim for violation of HUD's obligations under Consolidated Appropriations Act § 219
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim under the Administrative Procedure Act and Fifth Amendment because they did not allege facts demonstrating that the current owner had received a Notice of Default, which is the statutory prerequisite for HUD to issue vouchers. The complaint is devoid of facts meeting this condition, and the court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard at the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to raise a plausible inference of race-based discrimination. The complaint alleged only a property dispute with a neighbor and subjective impressions of facial expressions, which do not support a plausible inference that race was a but-for cause of the alleged discriminatory treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proposed FHA § 804(b) disparate-impact claim based on alleged application of one-of-a-kind policies to plaintiff
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to explain how a singular impact on one person satisfies the legal requirements for a disparate-impact claim under the FHA, which requires showing that a facially neutral policy disproportionately burdens a protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (racial discrimination), 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process and equal protection), 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to interfere with constitutional rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA federal claims failed under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards. Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support a plausible inference of intentional racial discrimination or racial animus on the part of any defendant. The alleged facts—a property dispute, subjective impressions of facial expressions, and a disputed email reference—do not support a plausible inference that race was a but-for cause of defendants' actions.

The psychologist's letter contained only formulaic legal conclusions without factual detail, and plaintiff did not allege facts showing the accommodation was both reasonable and necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing renewal based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the first element of a discrimination claim under § 3604(f)(1)(A) and (f)(2)(A) by failing to allege facts demonstrating a qualifying handicap with sufficient specificity regarding the nature and limitations of the alleged mental impairment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting accommodation and threatening to report BU to City of Boston
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately alleged all three elements of a retaliation claim under § 3617: (1) protected activity (self-advocacy requesting accommodation), (2) adverse action (interference with housing portal access and denial of renewal), and (3) causal link (complaint alleges accommodation requests motivated the decision, with the missing consent form offered as a pretext). At the motion to dismiss stage, construing facts in plaintiff's favor, the complaint states a plausible claim for relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA retaliation claim under the doctrine of claim preclusion (res judicata) because Alvarez's 2022 lawsuit (Case No. 22-3631) resulted in a final judgment on the merits of his FHA retaliation claims based on the same November 2022 termination from subsidized housing, and the new evidence (Zoom video) does not overcome the preclusive effect. Alternatively, the claim fails on the merits because Alvarez did not allege that he was a member of a protected class or that he was discriminated against based on a protected characteristic, which is fatal to any FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims against HUD for breach of duty to maintain fair housing rights; claims against CLS for alleged conflict of interest in representation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against CLS as specious because there were no allegations that CLS was responsible for the termination of subsidized housing or any plausible basis for any claim against CLS. Claims against HUD based on alleged breach of duty to maintain fair housing rights were conclusory and failed to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: Amber Reineck House v City of Howell Michigan

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs established a prima facie case of discriminatory intent in enacting the Moratorium under the Arlington Heights factors, creating a genuine dispute of material fact for jury determination. However, the court granted summary judgment against plaintiffs on their disparate treatment claim regarding Ordinance 929, finding no reasonable jury could conclude it was enacted with discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on their § 3617 interference claim, holding that discriminatory effect alone does not establish the required discriminatory animus element. The court found a genuine dispute whether the Moratorium was enacted with discriminatory intent versus legitimate regulatory purposes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to the moratorium on special land use applications to allow immediate consideration of plaintiff's application for a sober living home for six women in recovery from substance use disorders
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiffs established that the first accommodation (moratorium exemption) was necessary to provide equal housing opportunity for women in recovery, as no sober living homes for women existed in the city and the moratorium prevented approval. However, whether the accommodation was reasonable presented a genuine factual dispute regarding the balance of benefits to disabled residents against administrative burdens to the city.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to nine procedural and substantive zoning requirements including public hearing requirements, public notice requirements, site plan review, planning commission review, and one-year expiration of permission
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the second accommodation request, finding that while waiver of public hearing and notice requirements might have been necessary, plaintiffs failed to establish that exemption from all nine requirements was necessary. The court found that requirements like the one-year expiration of permission were not essential to afford equal housing opportunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Michigan Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (MPDCRA) §§ 37.1501-07 (real estate transaction provisions); ADA Title II discrimination and reasonable accommodation claims; ADA Title V retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed MPDCRA §§ 37.1501-07 claims as outside the court's jurisdiction because those provisions govern only real estate transactions and broker actions, not municipal zoning decisions. The court treated FHA and ADA claims as interchangeable with MPDCRA § 37.1302 claims and proceeded on the FHA/ADA framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rezoning of 42-acre parcel from R-1-8 (8,000+ sq ft lots) to R-1-6 (6,000 sq ft lots) to permit development of affordable/moderately priced homes ($125,200-$159,800) rather than large-lot, higher-priced homes ($258,000-$386,000)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs established prima facie disparate impact using HMDA data showing Hispanics disproportionately priced out of market by rezoning denial (45% Hispanic in proposed price range vs. 30% in higher price range); genuine issues of material fact remain as to whether city's stated justifications (neighborhood character, preliminary plat reliance, buffer compromise) were necessary to achieve legitimate zoning goals and whether less discriminatory alternatives existed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rezoning denial based on discriminatory intent/animus against Hispanic homebuyers
fha_claims.reasoning: Ninth Circuit reversed district court's dismissal of disparate treatment claim, finding plausible allegations that city council's denial was motivated by racially charged code words in neighbor opposition (e.g., 'group of people' with incomes under $75k 'statistically account for 91% of rape, murder, assault'), unanimous planning commission approval, and city's three-year history of approving rezoning requests. Case remanded for further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection and substantive due process claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; violations of Arizona constitutional and statutory law
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted motion to dismiss all non-FHA claims under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim; only FHA disparate impact claim survived initial motion to dismiss.

source_file: BOARD OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS OF JOHNSON COUNTY v. Jorgensen
case_name: BOARD OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS OF JOHNSON COUNTY v. Jorgensen
key_cases_cited: Summers v. City of Fitchburg, 940 F.3d 133 (1st Cir. 2019)
Davis v. Echo Valley Condominium Association, 945 F.3d 483 (6th Cir. 2019)
Giebler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Alexander v. Choate, 469 U.S. 287 (1985)
Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from state fire code (K.S.A. 31-132 et seq.) for group homes housing four or five developmentally impaired adults; categorical exclusion from fire prevention and safety requirements such as panic bars, fire retardant doors, interconnected smoke alarms, and sprinkler systems
fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed on appeal from district court denial of relief
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that a blanket categorical exemption from an exhaustive regulatory scheme does not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA because it amounts to a fundamental alteration of the regulatory scheme rather than a tailored modification of specific requirements. The court applied the Rehabilitation Act framework prohibiting accommodations that work a fundamental alteration in a program, and found that Johnson County's request failed because it sought to exclude all group homes from fire code coverage entirely, posed threats to public safety of vulnerable residents, and was not a mere moderate adjustment to policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of sex discrimination were conclusory and devoid of specific factual averments suggesting disparate treatment because of sex, failing to meet the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate treatment based on race within the limitations period, including delayed repairs, differential treatment regarding security devices, and differential insurance coverage, sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation and removal of mold from unit; repair of leaking exterior sliding doors; provision of remediation services covered by community master insurance policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted in footnote 2 that Plaintiff may be alleging failure to accommodate her disabilities (severe allergies triggered by mold), and although many allegations appear barred by claim preclusion, the amended complaint sufficiently states a failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed past the pleadings stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged all four elements of retaliation under § 3617: protected activity (complaints to Association, HUD, MCCR, and courts), Defendant's awareness, adverse action (delayed repairs, refusal to communicate), and causal connection (repairs scheduled differently and later due to protected activity).

key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination on the basis of race in denial of donated vehicle from donation program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged race discrimination in denial of vehicle from donation program but failed to allege supporting facts or draw a nexus between race and the alleged denial. Conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of transportation services, including denial of ability to purchase a vehicle and denial of receipt of donated vehicle; alleged denial of access to Cassell House based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a nexus between his alleged handicaps (arthritis, use of wheelchair/cane/walker, anxiety, possible diabetes and high blood pressure) and the defendants' actions. Plaintiff did not explain how he was precluded from housing because of his handicap or how the complained-of actions constituted discrimination based on handicap.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional claims under First, Fourth, Fifth, and Eighth Amendments; ADA Title III claims for discrimination and failure to provide reasonable modifications; assault and related state law claims against co-resident Michael Huggins
fha_claims.reasoning: Constitutional claims dismissed because defendants are private actors not acting under color of state law. ADA Title III claims for monetary damages dismissed because Title III provides only injunctive relief. ADA claims also fail on merits because plaintiff failed to allege he was qualified for any program or excluded because of disability. State law assault claims against co-resident remanded to state court.

case_name: Rickey Banks v. Ryan Ross et al.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race in denial of vehicle from donation program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a claim of race discrimination under the FHA. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support regarding the vehicle donation program or defendants' involvement in excluding plaintiff based on race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of transportation services and vehicle; denial of receipt of donated vehicle; denial of ability to purchase vehicle without repercussions
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a nexus between his alleged disability and the denial of transportation services or vehicle receipt. The complaint does not explain how he was discriminated against based on his handicap or how defendants' actions constituted disability-based discrimination in violation of the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on disability in denial of vehicle from donation program and other services
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a claim of disability discrimination under FHA § 3604(f). The complaint does not establish which alleged medical condition constitutes the handicap at issue, does not explain how plaintiff was precluded from housing because of that handicap, and fails to draw a sufficient nexus between the alleged disability and defendants' challenged actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III discrimination; constitutional claims (First, Fourth, Fifth, Eighth, Fourteenth Amendments); state law claims (elder abuse, assault by fellow resident)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims seeking monetary damages fail as a matter of law; constitutional claims fail because defendants are private actors not subject to § 1983 and constitutional protections do not apply to private conduct; state law claims lack federal jurisdiction and should be dismissed without prejudice to re-filing in state court.
