fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy for operation of Oxford House (group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse/alcoholism)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations supporting an inference of discriminatory intent. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support; the mere fact that no Oxford Houses exist in the Township, without more, is insufficient to support discriminatory intent; and the possibility that Defendant misapplied zoning laws does not evidence intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy for operation of Oxford House (group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse/alcoholism)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to respond to Defendant's disparate impact arguments in its opposition brief, resulting in waiver of any arguments in opposition to the disparate impact claim. The Amended Complaint does not contain the phrase 'disparate impact' and does not allege facts supporting such a theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim was analyzed under the same framework as the FHA disparate treatment claim and failed for the same reasons (insufficient factual allegations of discriminatory intent). The NJLAD claim was not cognizable in federal court.

source_file: PLAYERS PLACE II CONDO. v. KP
case_name: Players Place II Condominium Association, Inc. v. K.P. and B.F.
key_cases_cited: Oras v. Hous. Auth. of Bayonne, 373 N.J. Super. 302, 861 A.2d 194 (App. Div. 2004)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (dog named Luna weighing 63 pounds) in violation of condominium pet policy limiting pets to 30 pounds or less
fha_claims.reasoning: The New Jersey Supreme Court held that the trial and appellate courts erred in dismissing defendants' LAD and FHA reasonable accommodation claims. The court established a framework requiring: (1) plaintiff to show disability and that accommodation may be necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwelling; (2) housing provider to prove accommodation is unreasonable through fact-specific balancing of costs/benefits and whether it would fundamentally alter operations or impose undue burden. The court found B.F. established disability (bipolar II disorder, depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADD) and that Luna ameliorated symptoms, but remanded to Law Division for jury determination on whether the Association proved the accommodation unreasonable, as no interactive process occurred and Luna caused no documented problems.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep a 63-pound emotional support dog (Luna) in violation of condominium pet policy limiting pets to 30 pounds or less
fha_claims.reasoning: The New Jersey Supreme Court held that the trial and appellate courts improperly dismissed the reasonable accommodation claim. The court established a burden-shifting framework: plaintiff must show disability and necessity of accommodation; housing provider must then prove unreasonableness through fact-specific balancing of costs/benefits and whether accommodation would fundamentally alter operations or impose undue burden. The court found B.F. established disability and presented evidence of necessity (Luna ameliorates symptoms), and the Association failed to engage in interactive process or prove unreasonableness. The case was remanded to the Law Division for jury determination on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Cooperation with and provision of documentation to support defendant's application for rent assistance from the Salvation Army, allegedly necessary due to disability-related financial hardship
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant failed to plead sufficient facts establishing that she had a disability within the meaning of the FHAA (i.e., a condition substantially limiting a major life activity). She alleged only that she had health issues that were being managed or had resolved, and provided a generic description of relapsing polychondritis without specifying how it substantially limited any major life activity. Additionally, she failed to inform defendants that her request for assistance was related to a disability until after they terminated the tenancy, so defendants could not have known of any disability when they denied the accommodation request.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the FHAA, defendant failed to plead that she engaged in protected activity (requesting an accommodation for a disability) because she did not sufficiently allege that she informed defendants her request was related to a disability. Additionally, defendants terminated the tenancy before defendant framed her request as a possible accommodation request, so there was no causal connection between any protected activity and the adverse action.

source_file: Pinnacle Treatment Centers Inc v City of Crown Point Indiana

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the City's enforcement of the zoning ordinance was motivated by discriminatory animus against substance abuse disorder patients. Circumstantial evidence of community opposition animated by bias, combined with evidence of mayoral involvement in closed-door sessions and official questioning suggesting animus, precluded summary judgment for either party. The court held that credibility determinations and weighing of competing evidence required jury resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance to permit up to eight unrelated individuals to reside in the group home in an R-1 residential district, notwithstanding the city's five-person family definition restriction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Seventh Circuit's burden-shifting framework for reasonable accommodations in zoning cases, requiring plaintiff to show the accommodation is (1) reasonable, (2) necessary, and (3) affords equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing. The court found genuine disputes of material fact: (1) whether the variance is reasonable given the therapeutic benefits of peer support in a larger group home and the absence of demonstrated harm to the neighborhood; (2) whether the accommodation is necessary because disabled residents require community-based residential facilities to have equal opportunity to live in residential neighborhoods; and (3) whether the City's denial was pretextual discrimination rather than legitimate zoning enforcement. Delegatto's lay testimony regarding therapeutic benefits was admissible, and the absence of complaints post-opening supported Pinnacle's position.

source_file: Portnoy v. MEI CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, INC.
case_name: Eli Portnoy v. MEI Condominium Association, Inc.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that someone other than Anna Strickstein-Zandman interact with plaintiff regarding business matters related to his residency, based on medical advice to reduce stress and stressful communications due to disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded individual liability of board member under FHA and that state law immunity does not bar federal FHA claims. Allegations of willful discrimination fall within exception to state immunity. Claim survives at pleading stage but merits not yet reached.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of access to gym and recreational facilities based on disability; discriminatory terms and conditions of provision of services and facilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss under § 3604(f)(2), finding plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendant personally involved in denying gym access based on disability and that individual board member can be held liable under FHA despite state law immunity arguments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of lease renewal in retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation and asserting FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss retaliation claim under § 3617, finding plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendant refused to renew lease because of plaintiff's disability and in retaliation for requesting accommodation, with allegations of willful discrimination sufficient to overcome state immunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing (non-renewal of lease) based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count IV (state law claim under Florida Fair Housing Act § 760.23(1)), finding plaintiff adequately pleaded personal and deliberate discrimination by individual defendant, sufficient to survive pleading stage and overcome state immunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal Equal Protection Clause (§ 1983), Michigan state equal protection claim, Title VII employment discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: State of Michigan is not a 'person' subject to § 1983 liability; state equal protection claim barred by Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity; Title VII claim fails because plaintiff did not plausibly allege state employment and Title VII was not designed to protect convicted felons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim regarding public housing eligibility based on criminal history
fha_claims.reasoning: FHA does not mandate housing availability to individuals whose tenancy would constitute a direct threat to health or safety; public housing authorities retain discretion to deny applications based on history of convictions for property and assaultive crimes; plaintiff did not name Detroit Housing Commission as defendant.

fha_claims.reasoning: This is a research summary/statistical compilation of 802 FHA cases classified across multiple procedural stages (motion to dismiss, summary judgment, trial, appeal) and outcomes (defendant win 57.9%, plaintiff win 8.5%, mixed 9.2%). No individual case opinion is provided for substantive legal analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This is a research summary/statistical compilation of 1,029 FHA cases, not a single case opinion. No individual claim can be extracted.

It contains statistical distributions of accommodation types, disability categories, outcomes, procedural postures, parties, and courts, but does not present a single case opinion with extractable claims, holdings, or reasoning.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Johnson Controls framework for facial discrimination and held that RSS failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination because community residences are not singled out or treated differently from similarly situated uses (apartment buildings and rooming houses also require use variances), and RSS presented no evidence that community residences are materially similar to uses permitted as of right or by special permit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance requiring use variance for community residences in R-2A residential zone
fha_claims.reasoning: Because the court found the ordinance is not facially discriminatory and RSS failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination, the court did not need to reach or analyze any disparate impact theory; the grant of summary judgment on the disparate treatment claim was dispositive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court treated FHA and ADA claims as interchangeable in the zoning discrimination context and applied the same Johnson Controls framework, holding that the ordinance is not facially discriminatory under either statute because community residences are not singled out or treated differently from similarly situated non-disabled uses.

The motion was vague as to which accommodations remained at issue and did not address the March 2023 grant letter.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, Fourteenth Amendment due process, and ineffective communication claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the Title II ADA prima facie test (qualified individual with disability, exclusion/denial of benefits, discrimination by reason of disability) and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act test (disability, otherwise qualified, denied benefits solely because of disability, program receives federal assistance), finding the evidence insufficient to warrant summary judgment because the March 2023 grant of the three-bedroom accommodation created a factual dispute as to whether plaintiffs were denied benefits.

fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim because the driveway apron was not part of the 'premises' of plaintiff's dwelling under the FHA—it was located on an adjacent property outside plaintiff's property line. The court held that while exterior accessible routes may be required, plaintiff sought to alter a public way outside a neighboring property, not to modify the premises she occupied. fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA Title II claim because the driveway apron was not a 'service, program, or activity' provided by the City—it was a privately permitted driveway created for a neighboring commercial property. Plaintiff did not allege that any actual City service (such as sidewalks or curb ramps) was inaccessible to her because of her disability. The court also noted that Title II does not require public entities to engage in an interactive process.

source_file: State Financial Bank National Association v City of South Milwaukee

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing availability through efforts to prevent construction and raze Lake Bluff Apartments; alleged steering of tenants to segregated public housing (Parkcrest)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact on disparate impact claim. Evidence showed Lake Bluff tenants were disproportionately African American (16% vs. 1.39% of city population), City's zoning and moratorium decisions had greater adverse impact on African Americans, and City's subsequent steering of tenants to segregated Parkcrest housing perpetuated segregation. Court applied Arlington Heights II four-factor test and found sufficient evidence of discriminatory effect, intent, and City's interest to preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disabled tenants at Lake Bluff: whether granting housing preference at Parkcrest public housing is adequate; whether City should consider alternative accommodations rather than razing apartments; accessibility of Parkcrest units for mobility-impaired tenants
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether Parkcrest housing preference constitutes reasonable accommodation for disabled Lake Bluff tenants. Evidence showed 11 of 56 Lake Bluff households had mobility-impaired members, scarcity of affordable accessible family housing, and Parkcrest's accessibility limitations (only 3 accessible units, two-story townhouses precluding wheelchair access, centralized heat system). Court could not resolve as matter of law whether preference at Parkcrest is reasonable accommodation without further factual development.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II Americans with Disabilities Act claim; § 1983 due process claim (dismissed by separate order)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on ADA Title II claim, finding genuine issues of material fact regarding whether City engaged in unlawful practice continuing into limitations period through moratorium, rezone ordinance, and subsequent steering practices. Court rejected City's argument that these were discrete acts outside statute of limitations. § 1983 due process claim was dismissed by separate order (not addressed in this opinion).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for special exception to zoning ordinance to permit ten unrelated residents (persons in recovery from alcoholism and drug addiction) to occupy a single-family dwelling as a 'functional family equivalent,' rather than the standard three-unrelated-person limit
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the Third Circuit's burden-shifting framework, the court found genuine disputes of material fact on both prongs: (1) whether plaintiffs established necessity for ten residents (conflicting expert testimony on optimal occupancy levels), and (2) whether defendants demonstrated unreasonableness (undefined zoning terms 'nonprofit' and 'transient,' plaintiffs' offer to limit parking, and factual questions about whether accommodation would fundamentally alter the zoning program). fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 12132

source_file: Support Ministries for Persons With AIDS Inc v Village of Waterford NY

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of zoning approval to establish a residential facility for HIV-positive homeless persons through enactment and application of Local Law No. 2 of 1990, which amended the definition of 'boarding house' to exclude facilities for persons with illnesses requiring medical care
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Local Law No. 2 of 1990 was enacted with discriminatory intent to prevent Support Ministries from establishing a residence for HIV-positive persons, based on the timing of the amendment, the legislative history showing the board's intent to block the specific project, community opposition rooted in fear and prejudice against PWAs, and the board members' own statements opposing the facility. The HIV-positive status of the proposed residents was at least one factor, and probably the primary factor, motivating the discriminatory ordinance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enactment and application of Local Law No. 2 of 1990, which banned occupancy by persons suffering from or recovering from any illness or disease requiring medical or nursing care, thereby excluding virtually all handicapped persons from boarding or rooming houses in Waterford
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-pronged Arlington Heights disparate impact test and found: (1) strong showing of discriminatory effect on handicapped persons; (2) evidence of discriminatory intent; (3) defendants failed to establish a legitimate, bona fide governmental interest—their actions were based on unfounded fear of AIDS and prejudice, not legitimate zoning concerns; and (4) plaintiffs sought only to restrain defendants from interfering with private property use, not to compel affirmative provision of housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Coercion, intimidation, threats, and interference with Support Ministries' attempts to establish a residence for PWAs, including the mayor's call for all opponents to stand at a public meeting, appointment of known opponents to zoning positions, unprecedented call for a referendum on zoning matters, and communication of anonymous threats to burn the building
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that defendants violated 42 U.S.C. § 3617 by coercing, intimidating, threatening, and interfering with Support Ministries' exercise of FHA rights through multiple actions: the mayor's orchestration of public opposition, appointment of petition signers to zoning positions, unprecedented referendum proposal, and communication of threats to burn the facility, all contributing to a threatening and coercive environment designed to dissuade the project.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance or reasonable accommodation to permit operation of an unlicensed housing with services establishment for elderly individuals with Alzheimer's disease or dementia in a single-family residential (S1) zoning district without obtaining a variance from the Board of Zoning Appeals
fha_claims.reasoning: The trial court found that Willow Haven's unlicensed housing with services establishment does not fall within the UDO's express definition of 'group home' (which requires licensing), and thus a variance was required. The court held that whether federal and state law mandate a variance be granted or a reasonable accommodation be made is a matter for the Board of Zoning Appeals to decide, not the City Director. source_file: Woodfield Equities LLC v Incorporated Village of Patchogue

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use variance or special permit to operate a residential recovery center for recovering alcohol and drug addicts in a single-family residential zoning district; rental permit for expanded occupancy
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the claim was not ripe for adjudication because plaintiffs never applied for the required use variance or special permit before or after purchasing the property, failing to exhaust administrative remedies. The court held that ripeness requires either a final determination by a decision maker (a denied application) or a showing that further administrative efforts would be futile, neither of which plaintiffs demonstrated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that condemnation of property was pretext for discrimination against use as residential recovery center for individuals with substance use disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Applying the Arlington Heights intentional discrimination framework, the court found no evidence of discriminatory intent. The Village had legitimate, documented reasons for condemnation predating plaintiffs' purchase (relocation of community services), minimal community opposition compared to similar cases, no departures from normal condemnation procedures, and plaintiffs' own failure to apply for required zoning relief undermined any inference of pretext. The timing of condemnation was based on property vacancy, not the identity of occupants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II and Rehabilitation Act § 504 claims alleging failure to provide reasonable accommodation and discrimination in municipal zoning decisions
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied preliminary injunction relief on ripeness grounds applicable to all three statutes (FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act). Plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies by never applying for required zoning variance or special permit, and the condemnation proceeding was not yet final under New York EDPL § 207, which requires appellate review. The court declined to act as a substitute zoning board.

source_file: Yates Real Estate Inc v Plainfield Zoning Board of Adjustment

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variances and waivers (38 variances and 33 waivers) to permit construction of a 25-unit apartment building in a historic district zoned for single/two-family residential use, including use variance, density variance (36.2 units per acre vs. 2 permitted), height variance, bulk variances, and waivers from minimum unit size requirements (500 sq ft minimum; proposed units ranged from 256-595 sq ft), parking requirements (11 spaces vs. 45 required), and storage space requirements.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the initial burden on necessity and equal opportunity elements. The court found: (1) plaintiff failed to establish a protected class because it did not commit to limiting residency to veterans with PTSD, only to veterans generally; (2) plaintiff failed to show the specific size of the facility (25 units) was necessary for therapeutic benefit, as general testimony about group living benefits did not establish that 25 units or 36 residents were required; (3) plaintiff failed to show financial necessity because the expert's pro forma was based on unverified figures from the developer, including a purchase price inflated from $100,000 to $300,000, and comparable facilities (All Saints Apartments, Basking Ridge veterans housing) operated viably without such accommodations; and (4) even if plaintiff met its burden, the municipality demonstrated the accommodation was unreasonable because it would fundamentally alter the city's zoning scheme by requiring 38 variances and 33 waivers that would undermine historic preservation goals, violate minimum unit size protections, create severe parking deficiencies, and increase density 18 times the permitted maximum.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of zoning variances and waivers based on alleged discriminatory animus toward veterans with PTSD.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory purpose. Although plaintiff pointed to certain board member comments during testimony about veterans with PTSD and trust issues, the court found these comments, when read in context, did not evince discriminatory animus or NIMBY concerns. The board presented legitimate, neutral, and persuasive reasons for denial based on zoning compliance, historic preservation, parking, unit size standards, and density restrictions. There was no indication the denial was guided by negative attitudes toward the disabled or discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Rehabilitation Act, and New Jersey Municipal Land Use Law (MLUL) claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied FHAA analysis to the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, finding the same deficiencies in establishing necessity and equal opportunity, and the same reasonableness of the municipality's denial. The MLUL claim was not briefed by plaintiff on the preliminary injunction motion and was therefore not addressed. The court noted that even under the MLUL's rational basis standard of review, the zoning board's decision was supported by the record and not arbitrary or capricious.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Construction of a five-foot-wide elevator shaft on the side elevation of a four-story oceanfront townhouse to accommodate the property owner's mobility disability (inability to safely navigate stairs). The accommodation required variances from zoning regulations requiring a ten-foot side yard setback and a two-foot, six-inch landscape area.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the Board's determination that the requested variances constituted a reasonable and necessary accommodation under Title II of the ADA. The court applied a balancing test considering: (1) whether the accommodation undermined legitimate zoning purposes (it did not, as the Town Code expressly permits variances and recognizes ADA accessibility needs); (2) whether less intrusive alternatives existed (substantial evidence showed the side yard was the only practical location given the building's floor plan, parking requirements, and structural constraints); and (3) the costs to surrounding property owners (the Board properly discounted the real estate broker's opinion regarding property value loss, as credibility assessment is entrusted to the administrative agency). The court found substantial evidence that Mr. Peroutka's disability prevented safe stair use and that the elevator was necessary to allow him continued use of his property.
